# PAROL6

> Documentation for the PAROL6 desktop robotic arm by Source Robotics.

Every page of this site is also available as Markdown at its address followed by `index.md`, with its links absolute; `llms-full.txt` holds every page in one file. The version box on the landing page names the release the pages describe.

Full text of every page, in the order of the site's navigation. Source: https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/

**Revision:** 2026.A

[Quick start](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/quick-start/) [About this manual](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/about/)

Source Robotics d.o.o. publishes this document as part of the open-source PAROL6 project. It is revised as the
product changes; the document number, release, revision and date above identify the version you are reading, and
the document history on the About page says what changed. Take care that the release named under *Applies to*
matches the robot in front of you, and that the Python API version matches what `pip` installed: the version
selector in the header switches between releases. The text and the images are licensed CC BY-SA 4.0, the code
examples MIT.

# Quick start

From the PAROL6 you have just built to one that is homed and moves on command, on one page. It assumes the robot
is assembled and wired as in the [Build guide](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/build/) ([Mechanical assembly](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/build/mechanical-assembly/),
[Electronics and wiring](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/build/electronics-and-wiring/)), and nothing more: no firmware uploaded yet, no software
on your PC, and no experience with Python or a terminal. Every step ends with a link to the page that explains it;
follow it when a step is not clear or something fails.

!!! danger "Read first"
    PAROL6 has no brakes: when the power goes, the arm falls. It has pinch points, it moves fast, and it moves by
    itself while homing. Anchor it to the table, keep the E-stop within reach, keep hands out of the arm's path, and
    read the [Safety](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/02-safety/) chapter: it is five minutes long.

## 1. What you need

| | Where to get it |
|---|---|
| **Your PAROL6**, assembled and wired, with the control board inside the base | the [Build guide](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/build/); the parts in the [BOM](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/build/bill-of-materials/), or as kits from [the shop](https://source-robotics.com/) |
| **A 24 V power supply**, 5 A | the [BOM](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/build/bill-of-materials/) names one; any 24 V 5 A supply works |
| **A mains switch within reach**, on the supply's mains side: a switched socket strip will do | it is the stop that still works when the PC software has frozen ([Emergency stop](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/02-safety/emergency-stop/)) |
| **An E-stop**, a normally closed button on the base | the [BOM](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/build/bill-of-materials/) names one; any NC switch works |
| **A USB cable**, type B, to the PC | |
| **An ST-Link programmer and the programming adapter**, to upload the firmware once | the [programming adapter](https://source-robotics.com/products/parol6-programming-adapter) in the shop |
| **A PC** with Windows, Linux or macOS | see the [minimum PC](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/01-overview/what-you-need/#the-pc) |

Read in more detail: [What you need](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/01-overview/what-you-need/).

## 2. Anchor the robot

Bolt the base to the table through its six holes, or clamp it to the edge. A free-standing PAROL6 tips over when
it extends.

!!! success "Check"
    Push the top of the base sideways, firmly: it must not lift or slide.

Read in more detail: [Mounting the robot](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/04-installation/mounting/).

## 3. Install Python and Git, and open a terminal

The PC software is written in Python, and Git downloads it. A **terminal** is the window where you type commands:
type one line, press Enter, wait until it finishes.

=== "Windows"
    1. Download **Python 3.11.9** from [python.org](https://www.python.org/downloads/release/python-3119/): the
       "Windows installer (64-bit)". 3.11.9 is the last 3.11 release with an installer.
    2. Run it. On its first screen tick **Add python.exe to PATH**, then press **Install Now**.
    3. Download **Git** from [git-scm.com](https://git-scm.com/downloads/win) and install it with the settings it
       proposes.
    4. Open a terminal: press the Windows key, type `cmd` and press Enter. A black window opens.
    5. Type `python --version` and press Enter, then `git --version`.

    The commands on this page start with `cd %USERPROFILE%\Documents`, which takes the terminal to your Documents
    folder. If Windows answers that it cannot find the path, your Documents folder is kept in OneDrive: type
    `cd %USERPROFILE%\OneDrive\Documents` instead. To open a terminal in any folder, open the folder in File
    Explorer, click the address bar, type `cmd` and press Enter.

=== "Linux"
    1. Open a terminal: Ctrl+Alt+T on Ubuntu, or Terminal in the applications menu.
    2. Install Git: `sudo apt install git` (it asks for your password).
    3. The software needs **Python 3.11**: the commander runs on 3.10 or 3.11 only, the Python API on 3.11 or
       newer. Ubuntu's own Python is 3.10 on Ubuntu 22.04 and 3.12 on Ubuntu 24.04, so install 3.11 next to it,
       with its virtual environments and its window toolkit:
       ```
       sudo add-apt-repository ppa:deadsnakes/ppa
       sudo apt install python3.11 python3.11-venv python3.11-tk
       ```
    4. Type `python3.11 --version` and press Enter, then `git --version`. Each program below gets its own
       virtual environment made with Python 3.11; inside it, `python` is that Python 3.11.

=== "macOS"
    1. Download **Python 3.11.9** from [python.org](https://www.python.org/downloads/release/python-3119/): the
       "macOS 64-bit universal2 installer". Run it.
    2. Open a terminal: press Cmd+Space, type `Terminal` and press Enter.
    3. Install Git with the Xcode command line tools: type `xcode-select --install`, press Enter and confirm the
       window that opens.
    4. Type `python3.11 --version` and press Enter, then `git --version`. Each program below gets its own
       virtual environment made with Python 3.11; inside it, `python` is that Python 3.11.

!!! success "Check"
    The terminal answers `Python 3.11` and a number, and `git version` and a number. If it says a command is not
    found, install that program again (on Windows, tick **Add python.exe to PATH**), then open a new terminal.

## 4. Upload the main firmware

A control board from the shop comes with the **test firmware**, which turns all six motors as soon as the board
starts. Put the **main firmware** on it before you switch on the assembled robot. You do this once.

1. Download the [robot repository](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/PAROL6-Desktop-robot-arm) into your
   Documents folder:
   ```
   cd %USERPROFILE%\Documents
   git clone https://github.com/Source-Robotics/PAROL6-Desktop-robot-arm.git
   ```
   On Linux and macOS, the first line is `cd ~/Documents`.
2. Install [VS Code](https://code.visualstudio.com/). Open it, click the **Extensions** icon on the left, search
   for **PlatformIO IDE** and install it. Restart VS Code when it asks.
3. On Windows, install the ST-Link driver: in File Explorer, open `PAROL6-Desktop-robot-arm` in your Documents
   folder, right-click `en.stsw-link009.zip`, choose **Extract All**, and run `dpinst_amd64.exe` from the
   extracted folder.
4. **Unplug the 24 V supply** from the robot. Plug the programming adapter onto the 2×5 header next to the USB
   port, and the ST-Link into the PC. The adapter powers the board's microcontroller, not the motors.
5. In VS Code: **File**, **Open Folder**, and choose `PAROL6 control board main software` inside
   `PAROL6-Desktop-robot-arm`. The first time, PlatformIO downloads its tools for a few minutes: wait until the bar
   at the bottom is quiet.
6. Click the **→** arrow (Upload) in the bar at the bottom of VS Code.
7. When it has finished, unplug the programming adapter.

!!! success "Check"
    The terminal at the bottom of VS Code ends with `SUCCESS`. If not, see the [Firmware](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/board/08-firmware/)
    page and [Control board troubleshooting](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/board/11-troubleshooting/).

Read in more detail: [Firmware](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/board/08-firmware/) · [Firmware and first run](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/build/firmware-and-first-run/).

## 5. Install the robot software

Choose one, or install both: the **commander software** is a window with buttons, a program editor and a 3D
simulator; the **Python API** drives the robot from Python programs you write. Each one goes into its own folder
with its own **virtual environment** (`.venv`), a private copy of Python for that program: the two need different
versions of the same packages, so they cannot share one.

=== "Commander software"
    In the terminal, download the [commander software](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/PAROL-commander-software),
    make its virtual environment and install what it needs (a few minutes):

    ```
    cd %USERPROFILE%\Documents
    git clone https://github.com/Source-Robotics/PAROL-commander-software.git
    cd PAROL-commander-software
    python -m venv .venv
    .venv\Scripts\activate
    python -m pip install -r requirements.txt
    ```

    On Linux and macOS:

    ```
    cd ~/Documents
    git clone https://github.com/Source-Robotics/PAROL-commander-software.git
    cd PAROL-commander-software
    python3.11 -m venv .venv
    source .venv/bin/activate
    python -m pip install -r requirements.txt
    ```

    After the activate line the prompt starts with `(.venv)`.

=== "Python API"
    In the terminal, download the [Python API](https://github.com/PCrnjak/PAROL6-python-API), switch to version
    0.9.1, make its virtual environment and install it (a few minutes):

    ```
    cd %USERPROFILE%\Documents
    git clone https://github.com/PCrnjak/PAROL6-python-API.git
    cd PAROL6-python-API
    git checkout v0.9.1
    python -m venv .venv
    .venv\Scripts\activate
    python -m pip install .
    ```

    On Linux and macOS:

    ```
    cd ~/Documents
    git clone https://github.com/PCrnjak/PAROL6-python-API.git
    cd PAROL6-python-API
    git checkout v0.9.1
    python3.11 -m venv .venv
    source .venv/bin/activate
    python -m pip install .
    ```

    After the activate line the prompt starts with `(.venv)`. Git reports a "detached HEAD" after the checkout:
    that is expected.

!!! success "Check"
    The install ends without an `ERROR` line. If one appears, see [Commander installation](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/gui/commander/installation/)
    or [Python API installation](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/programming/02-python-api/installation/).

## 6. Connect

1. The E-stop to the two E-stop terminals on the base. Without it the robot will not run.
2. The USB cable to the PC.
3. The 24 V supply to the power connector, and the supply's mains plug into the switched socket strip, or behind
   the mains switch, within your reach. Nothing happens yet: the board is off until the button is pressed.

Read in more detail: [Connecting](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/04-installation/connecting/).

## 7. Switch on

Hold the arm by the forearm and press the power button on the base. The motors energise, you hear six clicks,
and the arm holds its position. Let go.

!!! success "Check"
    Six drivers initialise and the arm supports itself before you let go. If it does not, use
    [First power-on: if nothing happens](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/04-installation/first-power-on/#if-nothing-happens).

Read in more detail: [First power-on](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/04-installation/first-power-on/) · [Switching on and off](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/05-operation/switching-on-off/).

## 8. Start the software

First find the robot's **serial port**, the name the PC gives the USB connection:

- **Windows**: open Device Manager (right-click the Start button), then **Ports (COM & LPT)**: the robot is a "USB
  Serial Device" with a number, for example `COM5`.
- **Linux**: `ls /dev/ttyACM*` in the terminal, usually `/dev/ttyACM0`. If the software later reports
  "permission denied", run `sudo usermod -aG dialout $USER`, then log out and in again.
- **macOS**: `ls /dev/cu.usbmodem*` in the terminal.

=== "Commander software"
    For the first run, write the port into the program. Open
    `PAROL-commander-software/GUI/files/Serial_sender_good_latest.py` in a text editor (VS Code: **File**,
    **Open File**) and find these lines near the top:
    ```python
    if my_os == "Windows": 
        STARTING_PORT = 8 # COM3
    else:   
        STARTING_PORT = 0
    ```
    On Windows, replace `8` with the number of your port, `5` for `COM5`. On Linux, `0` is `/dev/ttyACM0`; change
    it if yours has another number. Save the file. Then start the program in the terminal:
    ```
    cd %USERPROFILE%\Documents\PAROL-commander-software
    .venv\Scripts\activate
    cd GUI\files
    python Serial_sender_good_latest.py
    ```
    On Linux and macOS:
    ```
    cd ~/Documents/PAROL-commander-software
    source .venv/bin/activate
    cd GUI/files
    python Serial_sender_good_latest.py
    ```
    Two windows open: the commander and the simulator. At the bottom of the commander, type the serial port in
    the port field (`COM5` on Windows, `ttyACM0` on Linux) and press **Connect**, more than once if the first try
    fails.

=== "Python API"
    1. Start the **controller**, the program that talks to the robot, with your port, and leave its terminal open:
       ```
       cd %USERPROFILE%\Documents\PAROL6-python-API
       .venv\Scripts\activate
       parol6-server --serial COM5
       ```
       On Linux and macOS: `cd ~/Documents/PAROL6-python-API`, then `source .venv/bin/activate`, then
       `parol6-server --serial /dev/ttyACM0` (macOS: the `/dev/cu.usbmodem…` name).
    2. Open a **second** terminal and activate the same virtual environment in it:
       ```
       cd %USERPROFILE%\Documents\PAROL6-python-API
       .venv\Scripts\activate
       python
       ```
       (Linux and macOS: `cd ~/Documents/PAROL6-python-API`, `source .venv/bin/activate`, `python`.) The prompt
       changes to `>>>`: Python now runs each line you type. Type these three lines:
       ```python
       from parol6 import RobotClient
       rbt = RobotClient()
       rbt.ping()
       ```
    Keep this second terminal open: the next steps type into it.

Read in more detail: [The commander software](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/gui/commander/) · [The Python API](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/programming/02-python-api/).

!!! success "Check"
    The commander's response log shows the robot's data, or `ping()` answers with `hardware_connected=True`. If
    it does not, use [Communication troubleshooting](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/08-troubleshooting/communication/).

## 9. Jog each joint

Before homing, check that every joint turns the way the software thinks it does: each one briefly, a few degrees.
The figure shows each joint's positive direction, in colour, over the pose in grey.

![Each joint turned 30 degrees in its positive direction, in colour, over the pose in grey](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/assets/kinematics/parol6_joint_directions.webp){ width="900" }
![Each joint turned 30 degrees in its positive direction, in colour, over the pose in grey](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/assets/kinematics/parol6_joint_directions_dark.webp){ width="900" }

Before homing, both programs check each jog against the joint limits with a position count that starts at 0
when the board is switched on. That count puts joint 2 past its positive limit and joints 3 and 6 at or below
their negative limits. So, until the robot is homed:

- **Joint 2** jogs only in its **negative** direction. Check that it turns opposite to the figure.
- **Joints 3 and 6** jog only in their positive direction, which is the one to check.
- **Joints 1, 4 and 5** jog both ways.

A refused jog does not move: the commander logs `Error: Robot jog -> Position out of range`, the Python API
stops the joint before it starts.

=== "Commander software"
    In the **Joint jog** menu, press the left arrow (positive) of joints 1 and 3 to 6 briefly, and the right arrow
    (negative) of joint 2.

=== "Python API"
    ```python
    rbt.jog_j(0, speed=0.2, duration=0.5)     # joint 1, positive, half a second
    rbt.jog_j(1, speed=-0.2, duration=0.5)    # joint 2, negative
    ```
    The first number is the joint: `0` is joint 1, `5` is joint 6. A negative `speed` jogs the negative way.

A joint that turns the wrong way is fixed in the firmware, not by trial:
[Firmware and first run](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/build/firmware-and-first-run/#a-joint-turns-the-wrong-way).

Read in more detail: [Jogging](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/05-operation/jogging/) · [Joint limits and directions](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/03-technical-data/joint-limits/).

!!! success "Check"
    Joints 1 and 3 to 6 turned the way the figure shows, and joint 2 turned the opposite way on its negative jog.
    If one did not, fix it before you home:
    [A joint turns the wrong way](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/build/firmware-and-first-run/#a-joint-turns-the-wrong-way).

## 10. Home

Homing finds each joint's reference at its limit switch or sensor. Joints 1, 2 and 3 move to their switches
together, then 4, then 6, then 5, and the arm ends in the after-homing pose: the standby pose turned 90° about
joint 1. Stay at the E-stop: a joint that grinds at its end stop has a switch that does not trigger.

Before you press Home:

- **Joint 6** stands so that it finds its sensor within one turn in the negative direction, with the tool's
  cables and tubes not wound up. The figure shows the pose: the gripper as drawn, the sensor (blue) and the homing
  pin (red); joint 6 turns along the green arrow.
- **The tool** is mounted, and the firmware's joint 5 homing offset matches it. Joint 5 homes against a feature
  of the tool holder; `j5_homing_offset` in `main.cpp` is 8900 for the pneumatic gripper holder (as shipped) and
  8035 for the SSG-48. If you change it, upload the firmware again as in step 4
  ([Joint 5 and the tool](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/05-operation/mastering/#joint-5-and-the-tool)).

![Joint 6 before homing: the sensor, the homing pin and the direction of rotation](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/assets/J6_home.webp){ width="700" }

=== "Commander software"
    Press **Home**.

=== "Python API"
    ```python
    rbt.home(wait=True)
    ```

Read in more detail: [Homing](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/05-operation/homing/) · [Homing failures](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/08-troubleshooting/homing-failures/).

!!! success "Check"
    Homing finishes, the physical arm matches the simulator, and the pin passes through the witness marks of each
    joint, which line up in the after-homing pose ([Witness marks](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/05-operation/mastering/#witness-marks)). If a
    joint keeps travelling or the pose is wrong, stop and use [Homing failures](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/08-troubleshooting/homing-failures/).

## 11. Move it

The robot now knows where it is. Three simple moves: bend the arm a little, turn the base, and come back. The
Python API adds a short straight line down and up from the bent pose.

=== "Commander software"
    Paste this program into the program window and press **Start**; **Stop** halts it.
    ```
    Begin()
    MoveJoint(90,-70,160,0,30,180,t=3)
    Delay(1)
    MoveJoint(60,-70,160,0,30,180,t=3)
    Delay(1)
    MoveJoint(90,-90,180,0,0,180,t=3)
    End()
    ```
    `MoveJoint` takes the six joint angles in degrees; `t=3` makes the move take three seconds. Jogging in the
    Cartesian jog menu moves the tool in straight lines instead.

=== "Python API"
    Type these lines at the `>>>` prompt, one at a time; each waits until its move is done:
    ```python
    rbt.move_j([90, -70, 160, 0, 30, 180], speed=0.3)       # bend the arm: six joint angles in degrees
    rbt.move_l([0, 0, -30, 0, 0, 0], rel=True, speed=0.3)   # a straight line 30 mm down
    rbt.move_l([0, 0, 30, 0, 0, 0], rel=True, speed=0.3)    # and 30 mm back up
    rbt.move_j([60, -70, 160, 0, 30, 180], speed=0.3)       # turn the base
    rbt.move_j([90, -90, 180, 0, 0, 180], speed=0.3)        # back to the after-homing pose
    ```
    `speed` is a fraction of the maximum: 0.3 is gentle. With `rel=True`, `move_l` takes a change from where the
    tool is: x, y and z in mm in the world frame, then three rotations in degrees.

Read in more detail: [RBTscript](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/programming/03-commander/rbtscript/) · [The Python API](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/programming/02-python-api/).

## 12. Switch off

Bring the arm to the **parked pose** first, folded in over the base, so that it has the least distance to fall:

=== "Commander software"
    Press **Park**: it writes a three-line program into the program window. Press **Start** to run it.

=== "Python API"
    ```python
    rbt.move_j([90, -144.683, 108.171, 2.222, 25.003, 180], speed=0.3)   # the commander's park pose
    ```
    Type `exit()` to leave Python.

Then hold the forearm and press the power button. The arm goes limp the moment the motors lose power.

## 13. Where to go next

| You want to | Read |
|---|---|
| attach a gripper | [End effectors](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/end-effectors/) |
| write programs | [Programming](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/programming/), [RBTscript](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/programming/03-commander/rbtscript/), [The Python API](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/programming/02-python-api/) |
| use inputs, outputs, pneumatics | [Peripherals](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/06-peripherals/) |

| fix something | [Troubleshooting](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/08-troubleshooting/) |

# About this manual

## Scope and audience

The PAROL6 Robot Manual covers the PAROL6 desktop robotic arm from the box, or the printer, to a robot that runs
programs: what the robot is, how to install it safely, how it is switched on, homed, jogged and run, which tools
and grippers it takes, its inputs, outputs and pneumatics, how it is maintained and what to do when something
fails. The Build guide, part of the same document, covers building one from the published files. Four more
documents live on this site: the [Control Board Manual](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/board/), for the electronics inside the base; the
[End Effectors Guide](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/end-effectors/), for the grippers and tools on the flange; the
[GUI Guide](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/gui/), for the graphical programs; and the [Programming Guide](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/programming/) with its
[API reference](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/reference/), for everyone who writes programs for the robot. The list under *Related
documents* gives their numbers.

The manual is written for someone who has a PAROL6 or is building one: a maker, a student, a teacher or an engineer
who can run a Python script and tighten a belt. It does not assume robotics training; the concepts the robot's
software uses are explained in the [Theory corner](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/theory/), which
anyone can read first. Read the [Safety](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/02-safety/) chapter before you power anything. The
[Quick start](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/quick-start/) is the first day on one page; the chapters are in the order you need them and go
deeper.

## Finding your way

The header has seven tabs. **PAROL6 Robot Manual** is the document you read from the start: the quick start, then
safety, technical data, installation, operation, peripherals, maintenance and troubleshooting, in numbered
chapters, followed by the build guide. **Control Board** is the manual of the electronics inside the base: the
connectors, the stepper drivers, the I/O wiring, the firmware, the serial protocol. **End effectors** is what goes
on the flange: the pneumatic and vacuum grippers, the SSG-48 and MSG electric grippers, a tool of your own, and
how each is mounted, connected and driven. **GUI interfaces** covers the graphical programs: the commander
software, Waldo Commander, Motor GUI. **Programming** is for everyone who writes programs for the robot: the
interfaces, the concepts, the Python API, RBTscript, ROS 2, and the reference where you look things up: every
method of the Python API, read from its source, the RBTscript commands, the serial protocol byte by byte, the
firmware parameters. **Theory corner** explains the robotics behind the software, from joint numbering and
units to kinematics, singularities and motion profiles, for anyone who wants to read first. **Support** says where
to get help and how to report a problem.

The whole site describes one PAROL6 release. The dropdown next to the site name switches between releases, and a
page from an older release says so in a bar at the top. The repository card on the right of the header opens the
repository the page belongs to; every page ends with a link to edit it and one to report a problem with it.
## Warnings and notes

Three kinds of warnings and notes appear in this documentation. Read every Danger and Notice before you act on
the step it belongs to. A green **Check** box after a setup step says what you should see when the step worked,
and where to go when it did not.

!!! note "Note"
    Points out something that is easy to miss or that changes what follows: a default, a limit, a side effect.

!!! warning "Notice"
    The robot, the tool, or data on the control board or the PC can be damaged or lost if this is ignored. Nobody is
    at risk.

!!! danger "Danger"
    Someone can be injured if this is ignored. Stop and read the whole box before acting on the step it belongs to.

# 1. Overview

PAROL6 is a 3D-printed six-axis desktop robotic arm with a 408 mm reach and a 1 kg payload, built to work like an
industrial arm in its mechanics, its control software and the way you use it. Everything about it is open source:
the printable parts, the bill of materials, the control board's firmware, the commander software and the Python
API. You can buy it [assembled](https://source-robotics.com/products/parol6-robotic-arm), as the [full kit](https://source-robotics.com/products/parol6-robotic-arm-kit) or as the [partial kit](https://source-robotics.com/products/parol6-partial-kit) of
the hard-to-find parts, or print and build one from the published files: the [Build guide](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/build/)
compares them.

## In this chapter

- [The robot system](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/01-overview/robot-system/): the arm, the control board, the PC software, and how they divide the work
- [What you get](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/01-overview/what-you-get/): what is in the box of an assembled robot or a kit
- [What you need](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/01-overview/what-you-need/): the power supply, the PC, the tools and the knowledge the robot asks of you


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/01-overview/robot-system/ -->

# The robot system

A working PAROL6 is three things: the arm, the control board inside its base, and a PC running the high-level
software. Each does a part of the job.

![PAROL6 with the connections on its base](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/assets/Connectors.webp){ width="700" }

## The arm

Six revolute joints, driven by NEMA 17 stepper motors through planetary gearboxes and belts, in PETG printed links.
Joints 1, 2 and 3 position the wrist; joints 4, 5 and 6 form a spherical wrist that orients the tool. Joint 6
ends in the flange the tool mounts on. The tool connections are on the forearm: an M8 connector for an electric
gripper and two push-in fittings for pneumatic lines. Each joint has a limit switch or an inductive sensor that
gives it a reference when the robot homes.

<div class="grid side-list" markdown>

![PAROL6 with the pneumatic gripper, its parts numbered](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/assets/figures/parol6_parts.webp){ width="760" }
![PAROL6 with the pneumatic gripper, its parts numbered](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/assets/figures/parol6_parts_dark.webp){ width="760" }

1. Base, with the control board inside
2. Joint 1 motor
3. Shoulder, turned by joint 1
4. Joint 2 motor
5. Upper arm
6. Joint 3 motor
7. Elbow
8. Forearm, also called the lower arm, turned by joint 4
9. Wrist, turned by joint 5
10. Flange, turned by joint 6
11. Air fittings for a pneumatic tool
12. Gripper, here the standard pneumatic gripper

</div>

The arm has no brakes and no joint encoders. The motors hold the arm while they are powered; the position is
counted in steps from the homing reference. Both facts shape how the robot is used, and the
[Safety](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/02-safety/) chapter returns to them.

## The control board

The [PAROL6 control board](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/board/) sits in the base: an STM32F446 microcontroller, six TMC5160 stepper
drivers, two isolated inputs and two isolated outputs, the E-stop input, a CAN bus for electric grippers, and USB
to the PC. Its firmware generates the step pulses, runs the homing sequence, reads the switches and the inputs,
drives the outputs and the gripper, and exchanges a packet with the PC at 100 Hz. It does not plan motion: it
executes the joint speeds and positions the PC sends it, 100 times a second.

## The PC software

The PC does the thinking: kinematics, trajectory planning, the simulator, the program interpreter, the interface.
There are two first-party programs, and others:

| | What it is | For |
|---|---|---|
| [Commander software](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/gui/commander/) | A desktop GUI with jogging, a 3D simulator, a program editor for RBTscript, I/O and gripper tabs | Using the robot by hand, teaching points, simple programs |
| [Python API](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/programming/02-python-api/) | A controller process that talks to the board, and a Python client library with blocking and asynchronous calls, planned and streamed motion, tools, collision checking | Programs, integrations, research, teleoperation, AI agents |
| [ROS 2 and MoveIt](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/programming/04-ros2/) | A MoveIt configuration and a `ros2_control` hardware interface that drive the Python API's controller | ROS users |
| [Community interfaces](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/programming/05-other-interfaces/) | Web GUIs, alternative firmware, vision demos | |

All of them speak the same [serial protocol](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/board/10-serial-protocol/) to the control board, so a board with
the main firmware works with any of them.

## How a move happens

1. You press a jog button, run a program line or call `move_j`.
2. The PC software computes the trajectory: the joint angles over time, with the speed profile you chose, within
   the joint limits.
3. One hundred times a second it sends the control board a packet with the target position and speed of each
   joint, the output states and the gripper command.
4. The board sets the stepper speeds and runs the steps; the drivers turn the motors.
5. The board answers with the actual position and speed of each joint, the switch and input states, the errors and
   the gripper's status, which the PC software shows and uses for the next cycle.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant PC as PC software
    participant B as Control board
    participant M as Motors
    Note over PC: a jog button, a program line, move_j: the trajectory is planned
    loop every 10 ms
        PC->>B: targets: joint positions and speeds, outputs, gripper
        B->>M: step pulses at the commanded speeds
        B-->>PC: actual positions and speeds, switches, inputs, errors
    end
```

| | |
|---|---|
| Mechanical files, BOM, building instructions, control board firmware, URDF | [PAROL6-Desktop-robot-arm](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/PAROL6-Desktop-robot-arm) |
| Commander software | [PAROL-commander-software](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/PAROL-commander-software) |
| Python API | [PAROL6-python-API](https://github.com/PCrnjak/PAROL6-python-API) |
| ROS 2 MoveIt configuration | [PAROL6-ROS2-MOVEIT](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/PAROL6-ROS2-MOVEIT) |
| This documentation | [PAROL-docs](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/PAROL-docs) |
| Shop, videos, community | [source-robotics.com](https://source-robotics.com/), [YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/@source-robotics), [Discord](https://discord.gg/prjUvjmGpZ) |

The full list is on [Downloads and files](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/cad-files/).

# What you get

## An assembled robot

A PAROL6 [from the shop](https://source-robotics.com/products/parol6-robotic-arm) comes assembled, wired and tested, with the control board in the base running the main
firmware, the E-stop button, the pneumatic gripper holder, and the robot homed once on the bench. Check the
contents against the order; the power supply, grippers and the programming adapter are separate items unless the
order includes them.

## A kit

The [full kit](https://source-robotics.com/products/parol6-robotic-arm-kit) contains every part of the [BOM](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/build/bill-of-materials/) except the printed parts
and the power supply. The [partial kit](https://source-robotics.com/products/parol6-partial-kit) contains the hard-to-find parts: the board, the drivers, the
bearings, belts, pulleys, connectors, sensors, switches and the pneumatics; you add the gearboxes, the motors,
the power supply and the printed parts. The [Build guide](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/build/#kits) lists every kit. You assemble
a kit with the Build guide and the assembly manual. The control board in a kit carries the test firmware, as
every control board from the shop does: it turns all six motors as soon as it starts. Upload the main firmware
before you switch on the assembled robot ([Firmware and first run](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/build/firmware-and-first-run/)).

## A control board on its own

Every control board is tested end to end before it ships and comes with the **test firmware**, which exercises
the drivers, the switches and the I/O from a serial terminal. Upload the main firmware before you use it with the
commander software or the Python API: [Firmware](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/board/08-firmware/).

## The files

Everything else you get is on GitHub: the STL and STEP files, the BOM with purchase links, the building
instructions PDF and the video playlist, the firmware sources, the software. [Downloads and files](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/cad-files/)
lists them.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/01-overview/what-you-need/ -->

# What you need

## Power

A 24 V DC supply of at least 5 A. The [BOM](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/build/bill-of-materials/) names a Mean Well 120 W DIN-rail unit;
any regulated 24 V 5 A supply with the robot's GX16 power connector wired to it does. The control board accepts
18 to 24 V; below 24 V the motors lose torque and speed. The robot draws about 40 W in typical use and more when
all six motors accelerate at once.

Plug the supply in through a **mains switch within reach**, a switched socket strip for example. It is the stop
that still works when the PC software has frozen ([Emergency stop](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/02-safety/emergency-stop/)), and the
switch you reach for when the E-stop has no effect.

## The E-stop

A normally closed emergency stop button, wired to the two E-stop terminals of the control board. The robot does
not run without it. The kit's button mounts on the base in the printed holder; any NC switch works for a bench
setup ([Emergency stop](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/02-safety/emergency-stop/)).

## The PC

The PC runs the kinematics and the planner and must send a packet to the robot every 10 ms without hiccups. A
machine that falls behind makes the robot stutter. Tested systems and the minimum are in the commander
repository's [confirmed working systems](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/PAROL-commander-software/blob/main/confirmed_working_systems.md):
at least an Intel i5 six-core processor of 2017 or newer, or an AMD equivalent. The tested systems include two
Windows 10 PCs with six-core AMD Ryzen processors, a Radxa ROCK 5B on Linux and a six-core MacBook Pro.

| | Commander software | Python API |
|---|---|---|
| Operating system | Windows, Linux, macOS | Windows, Linux (x86-64 and ARM64), macOS (ARM64) |
| Python | 3.10 or 3.11 | 3.11 or newer |
| Connection | USB (a serial port, 3 Mbaud) | USB on the PC that runs the controller; clients anywhere on the network |

A USB type B cable connects the robot to the PC. USB does not power the board.

## Tools

For an assembled robot: hex keys (2, 2.5, 3 mm) for the mounting screws and the gripper, a small screwdriver for
the terminal blocks. For a build, the [Build guide](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/build/) lists the rest, down to the blue
threadlocker and the thermal cement.

## Knowledge

You should be able to use a hex key. Python and the terminal you can learn on the way: the
[Quick start](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/quick-start/) gives every command to type, for someone who has never used either. The
[Theory corner](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/theory/) explains the robotics vocabulary the software uses, from
joint numbering to singularities, in the order you meet it.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/02-safety/ -->

# 2. Safety

PAROL6 is a desktop robot, light enough to lift with one hand, and it can still hurt you: it pinches, it moves
fast, it moves by itself when it homes, and it falls when it loses power. This chapter is short. Read all of it
before the first power-on, and have everyone who works at the robot read it.

!!! danger
    The project's [Safety Warning and Disclaimer](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/PAROL6-Desktop-robot-arm/blob/main/SAFETY_WARNING_AND_DISCLAIMER.md)
    applies to everything on this site: the hardware, the firmware, the software and this documentation are
    under development, and you build, modify and operate the robot at your own risk.

## In this chapter

- [Intended use](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/02-safety/intended-use/): what the robot is for, and what it is not
- [Hazards](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/02-safety/hazards/): pinch points, the fall on power loss, induced voltage, hot motors, the tool
- [Emergency stop](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/02-safety/emergency-stop/): what the E-stop does, and what it does not
- [Moving the robot by hand](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/02-safety/moving-by-hand/): when it is allowed and the two things never to do
- [What the robot protects against, and what not](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/02-safety/safety-functions/)
- [Planning the cell](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/02-safety/planning-the-cell/): the person, the guarding, the program


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/02-safety/intended-use/ -->

# Intended use

PAROL6 is made for education, research, hobby robotics and light automation on a bench: pick-and-place of light
objects, camera and sensor experiments, teaching robot programming, prototyping a task before buying an
industrial arm. It is an open-source, 3D-printed machine assembled by its owner or by a small workshop, and it is
not a certified industrial robot.

**Use it**

- on a bench or frame it is bolted to, in a dry room
- with a payload within its rating: 1 kg near the base, 0.5 kg at full reach, tool included
- with the E-stop connected and within reach
- with the person who runs it able to see the whole arm

**Do not use it**

- around people who do not know it is a robot: children, visitors, a crowded desk
- for anything that must not fail: it has no brakes and no joint position feedback, and a lost step is silent
- with tools that cut, heat or spray without your own guarding and risk assessment
- in wet, dusty or hot places, or outdoors

A self-built robot is the builder's responsibility from the first screw: the currents, the wiring, the limit
switches and the mechanical stops are all yours to get right, and the [Build guide](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/build/) says where
the mistakes are made.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/02-safety/hazards/ -->

# Hazards

## Pinch and crush points

Every joint is a pinch point, and the elbow and wrist fold against the upper arm and forearm. The motors are
geared: a finger between two links when a joint closes is crushed, not pushed away. Keep hands, cables and tubes
out of the arm's path while it is enabled, and never reach into the workspace of a running program. Under the
elbow, the belt that drives joint 3 runs onto its pulley: a finger or a loose cable there is drawn in.

![The pinch points of PAROL6, after homing: the wrist, the elbow, the belt and pulley under the elbow, the shoulder and the base](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/assets/figures/parol6_pinch_points.webp){ width="550" }
![The pinch points of PAROL6, after homing: the wrist, the elbow, the belt and pulley under the elbow, the shoulder and the base](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/assets/figures/parol6_pinch_points_dark.webp){ width="550" }

## Clothing, hair and eyes

A joint that closes catches more than fingers: its belts and pulleys pull in hair, loose sleeves, scarves,
lanyards and jewellery. Tie back long hair and take those off before you work at a powered robot, and keep them
out of the arm's reach while it moves. Wear safety glasses with a pneumatic gripper, with a sharp or pointed
tool, and whenever the robot can drop or throw a part.

## The arm falls when the power goes

PAROL6 has no brakes. The moment the motors lose power, from the button, the supply, a blown fuse or a pulled
cable, the arm goes limp and falls under its own weight, with whatever it carries. The gearing slows the fall of
joints 2 and 3 a little; it does not stop it.

- Never switch the robot off while it is extended or carrying something: bring it to the parked pose first,
  folded in over the base, where it has the least distance to fall ([Switching on and off](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/05-operation/switching-on-off/#switching-off)).
- Hold the forearm when you press the power button.
- Keep hands out from under the arm.
- Expect the fall during any power failure, and place nothing fragile under the arm.

## Motion you did not command

- **Homing moves every joint**, at speed, toward its limit switch, as soon as Home is pressed. The arm must be
  free to move and the switches must work ([Homing](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/05-operation/homing/)).
- **A program restarts** where you told it to, and `Loop()` restarts it forever.
- **A lost step** makes the arm move to a different place than the one on the screen. After a collision or a
  stall, stop and home again.
- **A wrong joint direction** on a new build sends a joint the wrong way on the first jog, into its stop. Jog
  slowly and briefly the first time ([Firmware and first run](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/build/firmware-and-first-run/)).

## Stepper-induced voltage

A stepper motor turned by hand is a generator. Moving the arm quickly while the supply is connected and the
board off can power the board on and energise the motors, with the arm wherever you left it. Move an unpowered
robot slowly, and only toward the parked pose or into its box.

## Hot motors

After hours of motion the wrist motors reach 70 °C ([Currents and temperatures](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/03-technical-data/operating-temperatures/)).
That is hot to the touch and close to the limit of the plastic around them.

## Electricity

The robot runs on 24 V, which is safe to touch. The power supply you plug it into is connected to the mains:
use a closed, approved supply, never an open-frame one on the desk. The control board has no reverse-polarity
protection on its power input.

## The tool

A pneumatic gripper closes with the force of the compressed air behind it, whatever is between its fingers; the
electric grippers close with up to 80 N. A vacuum gripper drops its load the moment the air stops. Treat the tool
as part of the robot in every rule above.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/02-safety/emergency-stop/ -->

# Emergency stop

The E-stop is the red button on the base, a normally closed contact wired to the control board's E-stop input.
It must be connected for the robot to run.

![E-stop wiring to the control board](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/assets/ESTOP_CON.webp){ width="800" }

## What pressing it does

The control board reads the E-stop input in every command cycle and reports it to the PC in every packet. The PC
software acts on it:

- the **commander software** disables the robot: it sends the disable command, the firmware stops accepting
  motion commands, and the log shows *Robot disable; button or estop*. A running program is stopped. The motors
  stay energised and hold the arm. Release the button and press **Enable** to continue; **Start** runs a program
  again from its first line.
- the **Python API's controller** cancels the move in progress and the queue, sends the disable command to the
  firmware, and refuses every motion command with `SYS_ESTOP_ACTIVE` while the button is pressed. When the button
  is released, the controller clears that error by itself and accepts commands again, but the firmware stays
  disabled and the arm does not move until `reset()` sends the enable command. Call `reset()` after every
  E-stop, before the next move.

!!! danger "The E-stop is a software stop"
    The control board's firmware (release 1) reports the E-stop and does not itself cut the motor power or the
    step pulses: the PC software stops the motion. A PC that has crashed, a program that has frozen, or a USB
    cable that has fallen out leaves the E-stop without effect, and the firmware keeps executing the last packet
    it received: a joint that was jogging in the commander keeps turning until it reaches its blocker. For those
    cases the hard stop is the **power supply**: a switch on the supply's mains side within reach, and the
    knowledge that the arm will fall when you use it.

## What it does not do

- It does not cut power to the motors, so the arm does not fall when it is pressed.
- It does not stop the gripper: an electric gripper keeps its grip, a pneumatic one stays where the valve left it.
- It does not stop a Python script of your own: the script keeps running. Its commands are refused while the
  button is pressed and accepted again after the release, before the arm can move. Stop the script before you
  release the button, then call `reset()`.

## If someone is caught by the arm

!!! danger "The E-stop does not free anyone"
    Pressed, the E-stop leaves the motors holding the arm where it is, and a joint cannot be pushed back by hand
    against a holding motor. To free a trapped hand or finger, either release the E-stop, enable the robot and
    jog that joint away slowly, the smallest step at a time; or support the arm with one hand and switch off the
    power supply with the other, knowing that the arm goes limp and falls. Decide which before you need it, and
    keep the supply's switch within reach ([Planning the cell](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/02-safety/planning-the-cell/)).

## The contact

Normally closed, so that a cut wire, a loose terminal or an unplugged button is read as a stop. A normally open
button does not work. The control board has two E-stop connectors on the same input: a second button can be
wired in series, or a safety relay's contact. [Inputs, outputs and E-stop](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/board/06-io-and-estop/) has the
wiring.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/02-safety/moving-by-hand/ -->

# Moving the robot by hand

An unpowered PAROL6 can be moved by hand: the joints turn against the friction of their gearboxes and belts, and
the arm has no brakes to release. This is how you pose it for packing and how you lift it. Two rules:

!!! danger "Never more than one turn, except joint 6"
    **No joint may ever be turned more than one full turn**, by hand or by software. Cables and pneumatic tubes
    run through the joints, and a second turn wraps and tears them. The one exception is **joint 6**: with the
    bare flange it can turn without limit; with a gripper or a tool, the tool's cables and tubes wrap as it
    turns, and they set how far it may go. Joints 1 to 5 have printed blockers that stop them; on a build
    without them, the rule is yours to keep.

![Joint 5 at its lower and upper limit, -120 and +120 degrees, over the standby pose in grey. A gripper can reach the forearm before that: check the clearance with a slow jog](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/assets/figures/parol6_j5_range.webp){ width="860" }
![Joint 5 at its lower and upper limit, -120 and +120 degrees, over the standby pose in grey. A gripper can reach the forearm before that: check the clearance with a slow jog](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/assets/figures/parol6_j5_range_dark.webp){ width="860" }

!!! danger "Not while the supply is connected"
    A stepper turned by hand generates voltage, and a quick move can switch the board on with the arm in your
    hands. Unplug the power supply, or move slowly, and only toward the parked pose.

## When the robot is powered

Do not force a powered joint. The motor holds it with its full holding current; what gives is a belt, a set
screw or a printed part, and afterwards the position the software reports is wrong. To move a powered robot,
jog it.

## After moving by hand

The robot does not know it was moved: the firmware counts steps and sees none. **Home again** before any program
or Cartesian move. The commander's position display and the simulator are wrong until you do.

## Lifting

Bring the arm to the parked pose, joints 2 and 3 toward their limit switches so that the arm folds over the base,
then lift by the base, not by the arm. [Transport and storage](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/09-transport/) has the packing.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/02-safety/safety-functions/ -->

# What the robot protects against, and what not

Know what the hardware and the software catch, and what they do not, before you decide how the robot is guarded.

## What is protected

| Against | How | Where |
|---|---|---|
| A target outside the joint limits | The planner refuses it; a jog stops at the limit. Firmware 1, the commander and the Python API check the earlier, partly wider limits ([Joint limits](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/03-technical-data/joint-limits/#limits)) | Commander, Python API |
| A speed or acceleration above the limits | Clamped to the robot model's limits | Commander, Python API |
| A move through a singularity (Cartesian) | The commander stops the move; the API's IK fails and refuses the command | Commander, Python API |
| A pose the arm cannot reach | The IK fails and the command is refused | Commander, Python API |
| Self-collision and collision with declared obstacles | Collision checking of planned moves and jogs against the robot's meshes and your keep-out shapes | Python API ([set_shapes](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/reference/python/configuration/)) |
| The E-stop pressed | Reported by the board, acted on by the PC software ([Emergency stop](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/02-safety/emergency-stop/)) | Commander, Python API |
| A driver overheating | The TMC5160 shuts its outputs down when it gets too hot; the fan keeps it far below that. The joint then goes limp, and firmware 1 does not tell the PC | Control board |
| A short on a motor output | The TMC5160 switches the output off. Firmware 1 reads the driver's short and open-load flags once at start-up and does not report them | Control board |

## What is not protected

| Not against | Why | What you do instead |
|---|---|---|
| **A collision with something the software does not know** | There are no joint encoders and no force sensing: the stepper pushes until it stalls, then loses steps silently | Keep the workspace clear; check programs in the simulator first; declare obstacles to the Python API's collision checker |
| **Lost steps** | Open-loop motors; the position is counted, not measured | After a stall or a collision, home again; keep speeds and payloads within the limits |
| **A fall on power loss** | No brakes | Switch off only in the parked pose; keep hands and objects out from under the arm |
| **A frozen PC** | The E-stop acts through the PC software; the firmware does not stop on its own | A mains switch on the power supply within reach |
| **Lost communication with the PC** | The firmware has no timeout: it keeps executing the last packet until the next one arrives. After a move to a position (programs, the Python API) the joint stops near that target. After a jog in the commander the joint keeps turning at the jog speed until it reaches its blocker | Keep the mains switch within reach; a short, direct USB cable |
| **Motor temperature** | Only the drivers are measured, not the motors | Reduce the current for long runs ([Currents and temperatures](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/03-technical-data/operating-temperatures/)) |
| **The tool** | The robot does not know what the tool does | Guard the tool as you would the robot |
| **A wrong joint direction on a new build** | The firmware trusts its configuration | Jog each joint briefly before homing |

The commander's safety functions are described in [Errors and recovery](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/05-operation/errors-and-recovery/);
the Python API's in [Errors](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/programming/02-python-api/errors/).


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/02-safety/planning-the-cell/ -->

# Planning the cell

A robot cell is the robot, what it works on, and the people around it. For a PAROL6 on a bench the plan fits on
a page, and it is worth writing.

## The person

One person runs the robot and sees all of it. Nobody else reaches into the workspace while it is enabled. The
E-stop is within that person's reach, and so is the power supply's switch.

## The space

- The arm's reach, 408 mm from the axis of joint 1 to the flange, plus the tool, and a margin for the elbow, which
  swings behind the base when the arm folds: a sphere of about half a metre.
- Nothing fragile inside it, and nothing that the arm could knock onto the floor.
- The cables and tubes outside the sweep, or fixed so the arm cannot catch them.
- For a robot that runs unattended or near others, an enclosure: acrylic panels on the profile frame are enough
  to keep hands out; the robot cannot break them.

## The program

- Run every new program in the simulator first, at full speed, and watch for the arm folding into the base or
  the table.
- Start on the real robot at low speed: in the commander, low `v=` or long `t=` in the moves (the speed slider
  only scales jogging); in the Python API, the `speed` fraction of each move.
- Make the first move of a program go from the after-homing pose to a known pose, so that a program started
  right after homing always begins safely.
- Use `Delay()` and the inputs to wait for the world, rather than assuming it.

## The tool and the parts

- The payload includes the tool. A gripper and a camera together can be most of the 0.5 kg the arm carries at
  full reach.
- A pneumatic gripper needs 5 to 7 bar (check your gripper's rating) and a valve wired to an output; the
  valve's two tubes decide whether it is normally open or closed ([Pneumatics](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/06-peripherals/pneumatics/)).
- Know what the gripper does at an E-stop and at a power loss. The E-stop leaves the gripper as it is: an
  electric gripper keeps its grip, and a pneumatic or vacuum gripper stays where the valve left it. When the
  power or the air goes, the vacuum gripper drops its part.

## When something changes

Changing the tool, the base, the table height or the fixture changes the kinematics and the clearances. Update
the tool in the software, check the limits with a slow jog, and run the programs in the simulator again.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/03-technical-data/ -->

# 3. Technical data

The numbers of PAROL6 V1: the specifications, the joint limits and their directions, the dimensions and the
kinematic model, the drives with their ratios and resolutions, and the motor currents with the temperatures they
lead to.

## In this chapter

- [Specifications](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/03-technical-data/specifications/)
- [Joint limits and directions](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/03-technical-data/joint-limits/)
- [Dimensions and kinematics](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/03-technical-data/kinematics/)
- [Drives, ratios and resolution](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/03-technical-data/drives-and-ratios/)
- [Currents and temperatures](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/03-technical-data/operating-temperatures/)

The control board's own specifications are in the [Control Board Manual](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/board/03-technical-data/).


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/03-technical-data/specifications/ -->

# Specifications

| Parameter | Value |
|---|---|
| Degrees of freedom | 6 revolute joints |
| Reach | 408 mm to the flange, 434 mm to the standard pneumatic gripper's TCP, from the axis of joint 1 |
| Payload | 1 kg near the base, 0.5 kg across the full workspace |
| Repeatability | 0.1 mm |
| Weight | 5.5 kg |
| Material | 3D-printed PETG, steel shafts and bearings |
| Motors | NEMA 17 stepper motors, one per joint |
| Gearing | Planetary gearboxes (joints 2, 3, 6) and HTD3 belts (joints 1, 3, 4, 5) |
| Position reference | Limit switches (joints 2, 3, 5) and inductive sensors (joints 1, 4, 6); no joint encoders |
| Brakes | None: the arm falls when the motors lose power |
| Power supply | 24 V DC, 5 A, recommended for optimal robot performance (18 V minimum) |
| Power consumption | About 40 W typical |
| Control | PAROL6 control board (STM32F446, six TMC5160 drivers) in the base |
| PC connection | USB, serial at 3 Mbaud, 100 Hz command cycle |
| Inputs and outputs | 2 isolated inputs, 2 isolated outputs, E-stop input |
| Buses | 1 CAN bus for electric grippers (a second is on the board, not populated) |
| Tool connections | M8 4-pin gripper connector (24 V, CAN) at the forearm; 2 pneumatic lines, 4 mm tube, base to forearm |
| Mounting | 6 holes in the base, spaced for 30×30 mm aluminium profiles; clamps |
| Operating temperature | Room temperature; the printed parts limit the motor temperatures ([Currents and temperatures](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/03-technical-data/operating-temperatures/)) |

## Joint ranges

| Joint | Range |
|---|---|
| Joint 1 | 194.8° (±97.4°) |
| Joint 2 | 113.4° |
| Joint 3 | 189.1° |
| Joint 4 | 229.2° (±114.6°) |
| Joint 5 | 240.6° (±120.3°) |
| Joint 6 | 360° in software; mechanically unlimited, but see [Moving the robot by hand](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/02-safety/moving-by-hand/) |

The ranges are those of the robot's model (robot_descriptions 2.15.1); the exact limits are on
[Joint limits and directions](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/03-technical-data/joint-limits/).

## Speeds

The speed limits are set in the PC software, not in the firmware, and the two programs differ: the commander
allows less on joints 1, 2, 3 and 6 and on the tool, and more on joints 4 and 5.

| Joint | Python API: maximum speed | Python API: acceleration | Commander: maximum speed |
|---|---|---|---|
| Joint 1 | 132 °/s (15000 steps/s) | 395 °/s² | 57 °/s (6500 steps/s) |
| Joint 2 | 70 °/s (25000 steps/s) | 211 °/s² | 51 °/s (18000 steps/s) |
| Joint 3 | 99 °/s (32000 steps/s) | 298 °/s² | 62 °/s (20000 steps/s) |
| Joint 4 | 141 °/s (10000 steps/s) | 422 °/s² | 309 °/s (22000 steps/s) |
| Joint 5 | 141 °/s (10000 steps/s) | 422 °/s² | 309 °/s (22000 steps/s) |
| Joint 6 | 152 °/s (27000 steps/s) | 456 °/s² | 124 °/s (22000 steps/s) |
| Tool, linear | 200 mm/s | 550 mm/s² | 60 mm/s |
| Tool, angular | 100 °/s | 275 °/s² | 25 °/s |

The steps per second are converted with the ratios of [Drives, ratios and resolution](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/03-technical-data/drives-and-ratios/). In
the Python API a joint's acceleration is three times its speed, so a joint reaches full speed in a third of a
second, and jogging is limited to 80 % of the maxima. The commander jogs within lower limits of its own, which
its speed slider scales: 13 °/s on joint 1, 8 °/s on joint 2, 11 °/s on joint 3, 98 °/s on joints 4 and 5 and
101 °/s on joint 6 at 100 % (1500, 3000, 3600, 7000, 7000 and 18000 steps/s), and 60 mm/s for the tool. A joint
driven at its maximum with a reduced motor current or a heavy payload loses steps: lower the speed before you
lower the current.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/03-technical-data/joint-limits/ -->

# Joint limits and directions

## Joint numbering and positive directions

Joints are numbered from the base up. Joints 1, 2 and 3 are also called the base, shoulder and elbow joints, and
joints 4, 5 and 6 wrist 1, wrist 2 and wrist 3, the names the robot model and ROS use. Each picture shows one joint
turned 30° in its positive direction, in colour, over the pose in grey. The arrow at the joint points the same
way, and the commander software's left arrows jog in that direction.

![Each joint turned 30 degrees in its positive direction, in colour, over the pose in grey](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/assets/kinematics/parol6_joint_directions.webp){ width="900" }
![Each joint turned 30 degrees in its positive direction, in colour, over the pose in grey](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/assets/kinematics/parol6_joint_directions_dark.webp){ width="900" }

| Joint | Also called | Positive direction |
|---|---|---|
| J1 | base | counter-clockwise, seen from above |
| J2 | shoulder | leans the upper arm forward, the way the forearm points in the standby pose |
| J3 | elbow | raises the forearm |
| J4 | wrist 1 | clockwise, seen from the tool |
| J5 | wrist 2 | tips the tool up, in the standby pose |
| J6 | wrist 3 | clockwise, seen from the tool |

## Standby and after homing

The **standby pose** is the pose of the Denavit-Hartenberg table and the kinematics sheets, and the reference
for the limits below: the upper arm vertical, the forearm horizontal, the arm pointing away from the
electronics case at the back of the base. **After homing** the robot stands in the same pose turned 90° about joint 1, counter-clockwise
seen from above: the firmware sets joint 1 to +90° when it finishes homing.

| Pose | Joint 1 | Joint 2 | Joint 3 | Joint 4 | Joint 5 | Joint 6 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Standby | 0° | −90° | 180° | 0° | 0° | 180° |
| After homing | 90° | −90° | 180° | 0° | 0° | 180° |

The Python API calls the after-homing pose its standby (`STANDBY_ANGLES_DEG`), and a later `home()` moves
there; the commander software's standby is the standby pose above.

![The standby pose, from the front and from the side, with the joints marked](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/assets/figures/parol6_standby.webp){ width="900" }
![The standby pose, from the front and from the side, with the joints marked](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/assets/figures/parol6_standby_dark.webp){ width="900" }

## Limits

The joint limits of PAROL6's model in [robot_descriptions](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/robot_descriptions)
(version 2.15.1), in degrees, in the angles the software shows (the standby pose above).

| Joint | Negative limit | Standby | Positive limit | Range |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| J1 | −97.40° | 0° | +97.40° | 194.8° |
| J2 | −146.15° | −90° | −32.70° | 113.4° |
| J3 | 105.52° | 180° | 294.59° | 189.1° |
| J4 | −114.59° | 0° | +114.59° | 229.2° |
| J5 | −120.32° | 0° | +120.32° | 240.6° |
| J6 | none | 180° | none | no limit with the bare flange; with a tool, its cables and tubes set it |

![Each joint at both its limits, in its colour, over the standby pose in grey; the arc spans the range, in the angles the software shows. Joint 1 is seen from above, with the after-homing position marked; joint 4 is seen from the tool, with joint 5 at 90 degrees so that the tool's swing shows; joint 6 has no limit](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/assets/figures/parol6_joint_ranges.webp){ width="860" }
![Each joint at both its limits, in its colour, over the standby pose in grey; the arc spans the range, in the angles the software shows. Joint 1 is seen from above, with the after-homing position marked; joint 4 is seen from the tool, with joint 5 at 90 degrees so that the tool's swing shows; joint 6 has no limit](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/assets/figures/parol6_joint_ranges_dark.webp){ width="860" }

!!! note "The firmware and the software still use the earlier limits"
    Firmware 1, the commander software and the Python API (0.9.1) enforce the
    limits of the earlier model until they are updated: J1 ±123.05°, J2 −145.01° to −3.38°, J3 107.87° to
    287.87°, J4 ±105.47°, J5 ±90°, J6 0° to 360°. A target between the two is accepted by them; keep to the table
    above. Before homing they apply these limits to a position count that starts at 0 at power-up, so joint 2
    cannot be jogged in its positive direction, nor joints 3 and 6 in their negative one, until the robot is
    homed ([Jogging](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/05-operation/jogging/#jogging-a-robot-that-is-not-homed)).

Joints 1 to 5 are stopped at both ends by printed blocker parts, the mechanical stops a little past the limits
above. The limit switch or sensor that homes a joint sits near its blocker, so that it triggers just before the
joint reaches it. Joint 6 has no blocker: with the bare flange nothing stops it, and with a tool only the tool's
cables and tubes do.

!!! warning "Grippers and bases change the limits"
    A gripper changes where joint 5 can go without colliding with the forearm, and a riser under the base changes
    what joint 2 can reach. The software limits do not know about either: check the real clearances with a slow
    jog before you run a program near a limit.

!!! warning "The limits are not a safety function"
    The limits only stop the software from commanding a joint further. Inside them the arm can still hit a
    person, the table or itself, no safety-rated part checks them, and a wrong homing shifts them with it. They
    protect the robot's cables and parts, not the people near it ([Safety](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/02-safety/)).

!!! danger "Never more than one turn, except joint 6"
    **No joint may ever be turned more than one full turn**, by hand or by software: the cables and pneumatic
    tubes that pass through the joints wrap and tear. The one exception is **joint 6**: with the bare flange it
    can turn without limit; with a gripper or a tool, the tool's cables and tubes wrap as it turns, and they set
    how far it may go ([Moving the robot by hand](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/02-safety/moving-by-hand/)).


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/03-technical-data/kinematics/ -->
