    ![PAROL6 with the SSG-48 gripper, fin-ray jaws: dimensions and the DH table to the TCP](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/assets/kinematics/parol6_ssg48_stock.webp){ width="700" }
    ![PAROL6 with the SSG-48 gripper, fin-ray jaws: dimensions and the DH table to the TCP](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/assets/kinematics/parol6_ssg48_stock_dark.webp){ width="700" }

=== "MSG"

    ![PAROL6 with the MSG gripper, solid jaws: dimensions and the DH table to the TCP](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/assets/kinematics/parol6_msg.webp){ width="700" }
    ![PAROL6 with the MSG gripper, solid jaws: dimensions and the DH table to the TCP](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/assets/kinematics/parol6_msg_dark.webp){ width="700" }

=== "MSG soft jaws"

    ![PAROL6 with the MSG gripper, soft TPU jaws: dimensions and the DH table to the TCP](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/assets/kinematics/parol6_msg_tpu_glue.webp){ width="700" }
    ![PAROL6 with the MSG gripper, soft TPU jaws: dimensions and the DH table to the TCP](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/assets/kinematics/parol6_msg_tpu_glue_dark.webp){ width="700" }

| Dimension | What it is | Value |
|---|---|---|
| a1 | Base height: the floor to the joint 2 axis | 110.5 mm |
| a2 | Shoulder offset: the joint 1 axis to the joint 2 axis | 23.42 mm |
| a3 | Upper arm: joint 2 to joint 3 | 180 mm |
| a4 | Elbow offset | 43.5 mm |
| a5 | Forearm: the joint 3 axis to the wrist centre | 177 mm |
| a6 | The joint 6 centre to the TCP, along the tool axis | depends on the tool, below |
| a7 | Sideways offset of the TCP | depends on the tool, below |

| Tool | a6 | a7 |
|---|---|---|
| Flange only (the TCP is the flange face) | 50.5 mm | 0 |
| Pneumatic gripper | 62.3 mm | 45.25 mm |
| SSG-48, solid or fin-ray jaws | 134.3 mm | 0 |
| MSG, solid or soft jaws | 134.3 mm | 28.35 mm |

A riser under the base changes a1, and a tool of your own changes a6 and a7: tell the software about the tool
([Tools and the TCP](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/programming/02-python-api/tools-and-tcp/)), or the poses it reports will be wrong.

!!! note "The software still computes with the earlier model"
    These pages give the model's dimensions. Until the software is updated, the Python API (its built-in URDF) and
    the commander software compute with a5 = 176.35 mm, and the commander with a6 = 62.8 mm for the pneumatic
    gripper, so a pose they report can differ from these sheets by up to about 0.65 mm.

## Kinematic structure

The first three joints place the wrist centre; the axes of joints 4, 5 and 6 intersect in one point, a
spherical wrist, which is what makes the inverse kinematics tractable. The
[Theory corner](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/theory/kinematics/) explains forward and inverse kinematics, and
[Configurations and singularities](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/theory/configurations-and-singularities/) the eight ways the arm can
reach one pose.

## Denavit-Hartenberg parameters

Standard DH, each joint's transform being `A_i = Rz(theta_i) Tz(d_i) Tx(a_i) Rx(alpha_i)`, from the base to the
TCP. `q1` to `q6` are the model's joint angles (the URDF's), all 0 in the standby pose; the theta column already
contains the joint offsets, so do not add them twice. Theta is the angle the software shows: joint 2's software
angle is q2 − 90°, joint 3's is q3 + 180° and joint 6's is q6 + 180°, the others are equal. The sheets above give
the same table for each tool.

| Joint | Link | theta | alpha | a | d |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Base | q1 | -90° | a2 = 23.42 mm | a1 = 110.5 mm |
| 2 | Shoulder | q2 - 90° | 180° | a3 = 180 mm | 0 |
| 3 | Elbow | q3 + 180° | 90° | -a4 = -43.5 mm | 0 |
| 4 | Wrist 1 | q4 | -90° | 0 | -a5 = -177 mm |
| 5 | Wrist 2 | q5 | 90° | 0 | 0 |
| 6 | Wrist 3, to the TCP | q6 + 180° | 180° | -a7 | -a6 |

The models were checked at 128 poses including the joint limits: the DH table, the URDF and the MuJoCo model agree
to within 0.006 mm and 0.002°. The Python API does not use the table directly: it loads its URDF and computes the
kinematics numerically. The commander software uses a Robotics Toolbox DH model.

## Mounting holes

Six holes in the base, on a pattern made for 30×30 mm aluminium profiles. The mounting plates folder of the
repository has STEP drawings of a small and a big base plate: [Mounting the robot](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/04-installation/mounting/).


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/03-technical-data/drives-and-ratios/ -->

# Drives, ratios and resolution

## Motors and gearing

| Joint | Motor | Gearing | Ratio |
|---|---|---|---|
| Joint 1 | NEMA 17, 65 N·cm (60 mm) | HTD3 belt, 15-tooth pulley to a 96-tooth printed pulley | 6.4 : 1 |
| Joint 2 | NEMA 17, 65 N·cm (60 mm) | EG planetary gearbox | 20 : 1 |
| Joint 3 | NEMA 17, 45 N·cm (40 mm) | EG planetary gearbox 20 : 1, then a belt 38 : 42 | 18.095 : 1 |
| Joint 4 | NEMA 17, 45 N·cm (40 mm) | HTD3 belt, 12-tooth pulley to 48 teeth | 4 : 1 |
| Joint 5 | NEMA 17, 45 N·cm (40 mm) | HTD3 belt, 12-tooth pulley to 48 teeth | 4 : 1 |
| Joint 6 | NEMA 17, 16 N·cm (20 mm) | EG planetary gearbox | 10 : 1 |

The planetary gearboxes are the precision EG series with 15 to 20 arc-minutes of backlash; the cheaper MG series
fits and works, with more backlash. The belts are 6 mm wide HTD3, tensioned by small bearings; their lengths are
in the [BOM](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/build/bill-of-materials/).

## Steps and microsteps

The stepper motors have 200 full steps per turn. The control board runs the TMC5160 drivers at 32 microsteps, so
one motor turn is 6400 microsteps, and every position and speed the firmware and the PC exchange is in these
steps. Through the gearing, one step at the joint is:

| Joint | Steps per joint turn | Step size |
|---|---|---|
| Joint 1 | 40 960 | 0.00879° (0.000153 rad) |
| Joint 2 | 128 000 | 0.00281° (0.000049 rad) |
| Joint 3 | 115 810 | 0.00311° (0.000054 rad) |
| Joint 4 | 25 600 | 0.01406° (0.000245 rad) |
| Joint 5 | 25 600 | 0.01406° (0.000245 rad) |
| Joint 6 | 64 000 | 0.00563° (0.000098 rad) |

Conversions: degrees per step = 360 / (200 × 32) / ratio; the software's `DEG2STEPS` and `STEPS2DEG` do exactly
this. A microstep is not a guaranteed position: the motor's holding torque at a fraction of a full step is small,
so the real resolution under load is coarser than the table, which is why the repeatability is specified at
0.1 mm rather than at the step size.

## Try it

<div class="calc" data-steps-per-motor-turn="6400" markdown="0">
  <div class="calc__row calc__row--inline">
    <label for="jc-joint">Joint</label>
    <select id="jc-joint" name="joint">
      <option value="6.4">Joint 1, ratio 6.4</option>
      <option value="20" selected>Joint 2, ratio 20</option>
      <option value="18.095">Joint 3, ratio 18.095</option>
      <option value="4">Joint 4, ratio 4</option>
      <option value="4">Joint 5, ratio 4</option>
      <option value="10">Joint 6, ratio 10</option>
    </select>
    <label for="jc-deg">Joint angle, degrees</label>
    <input id="jc-deg" type="number" name="degrees" step="0.1" value="45">
    <label for="jc-speed">Joint speed, degrees per second</label>
    <input id="jc-speed" type="number" name="degps" step="1" value="30">
  </div>
  <p class="calc__result"><strong data-out="steps">16 000</strong> steps from the standby pose · one step is <strong data-out="stepdeg">0.00281°</strong> at the joint</p>
  <p class="calc__result"><strong data-out="stepsps">10 667</strong> steps per second · the motor turns at <strong data-out="rpm">100</strong> rpm</p>
</div>

The conversions of this page, with your numbers: 6400 microsteps per motor turn, through the joint's ratio.

## Why open loop works here

The motors are not fitted with encoders: the position is the count of steps commanded since homing. This works
because the planner never asks a motor for more than its torque at the commanded speed and acceleration, with
margin; a stepper that is not overloaded does not lose steps. If one is overloaded (a collision, a payload over
the limit, too high a speed with a reduced current) it loses steps silently, the arm is then not where the
software thinks it is, and the only cure is to home again. [Steppers, open loop and backlash](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/theory/steppers-and-open-loop/)
goes deeper.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/03-technical-data/operating-temperatures/ -->

# Currents and temperatures

## Motor currents

The control board sets each motor's running current in the firmware. The values are chosen for the motors of the
BOM and for the printed parts around them; joints 4 and 5 run below their motors' rating because their motors are
enclosed in the forearm.

| Joint | Maximum current (`constants.h`) | Current while moving | Holding current |
|---|---|---|---|
| Joint 1 | 2000 mA | 85 % of the maximum: 1700 mA | 70 % of that: 1190 mA |
| Joint 2 | 2000 mA | 1700 mA | 80 %: 1360 mA |
| Joint 3 | 1900 mA | 1615 mA | 80 %: 1292 mA |
| Joint 4 | 1700 mA | 1445 mA | 80 %: 1156 mA |
| Joint 5 | 1700 mA | 1445 mA | 80 %: 1156 mA |
| Joint 6 | 965 mA | 820 mA | 88 %: 722 mA |

The firmware calls `rms_current(MOTORx_MAX_CURRENT * 0.85, hold_multiplier)`; the hold multiplier is 0.7 for
joint 1, 0.8 for joints 2 to 5 and 0.88 for joint 6 (`motor_init.cpp`; [Firmware parameters](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/reference/firmware-parameters/)). Lower currents give
less torque, which means lower reachable speeds and accelerations and a higher chance of lost steps; higher
currents heat the motors and the plastic around them.

## Temperatures

Stepper motors are rated for 100 °C and more, but PAROL6 is plastic, and PETG softens around 80 °C. These are the
motor case temperatures measured on a robot at the default currents, at room temperature:

| Joint | Holding position for 5 h | Moving for 2 h |
|---|---|---|
| Joint 1 | 51 °C | 64 °C |
| Joint 2 | 54 °C | 64 °C |
| Joint 3 | 48 °C | 52 °C |
| Joint 4 | 60 °C | 73 °C |
| Joint 5 | 60 °C | 72 °C |
| Joint 6 | 61 °C | 65 °C |

Through a thermal camera, a powered PAROL6 shows where the heat is: the motors of joints 2 and 3 beside the
shoulder, the elbow (the hottest point in this picture, 50 °C) and the wrist motors in the forearm, and the control
board at the back of the base. The scale runs from 29.6 to 50.0 °C.

![A powered PAROL6 through a thermal camera: warm motors at the shoulder, the elbow and in the forearm, and the control board in the base](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/assets/thermal_image.webp){ width="420" }

!!! danger "Long runs"
    Joints 4 and 5 come within 10 °C of the plastic's limit after two hours of continuous motion. For a robot that
    runs for hours, reduce the currents in the firmware (`MOTORx_MAX_CURRENT` in `constants.h`, or the
    `hold_multiplier` in `motor_init.cpp`), lower the duty cycle, or let it rest in a pose that does not load the
    motors. A deformed forearm cannot be straightened: it has to be printed again.

The stepper drivers protect themselves: a TMC5160 that gets too hot shuts its outputs down, and its joint goes
limp. The fan in the base keeps them well below that ([Control board technical data](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/board/03-technical-data/)).
Firmware 1 does not tell the PC when a driver is hot: the joints' temperature error bits in its packet are
always 0. The
driver temperature is not the motor temperature.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/04-installation/ -->

# 4. Installation

Where to put the robot, how to fix it, what to connect, and the first power-on.

## In this chapter

- [Installation site](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/04-installation/installation-site/)
- [Mounting the robot](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/04-installation/mounting/)
- [Connecting](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/04-installation/connecting/)
- [First power-on](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/04-installation/first-power-on/)

Building the robot is the [Build guide](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/build/); wiring the control board inside the base is in the
[Control Board Manual](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/board/04-connectors/).


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/04-installation/installation-site/ -->

# Installation site

- **A rigid table or frame.** The arm accelerates its 5.5 kg quickly; a wobbly table shakes and spoils the
  repeatability. An aluminium profile frame or a solid bench is right.
- **Clearance.** The arm reaches 408 mm from the axis of joint 1 in every direction, plus the tool, and its elbow
  swings further back than the tool when it folds. Keep a free sphere of about 500 mm around the base, and nothing
  fragile in it. The simulator shows the sweep of a program before the robot runs it.
- **Room temperature, dry, dust-free.** The base draws air through its fan over the stepper drivers.
- **The E-stop within reach** of the person at the PC, and reachable from where someone would stand to load the
  robot.
- **Cables.** The power, USB and E-stop cables leave the base at the back; route them so that nothing pulls on
  them and so that the arm cannot sweep over them.
- **Pneumatics.** If you use the pneumatic gripper, a valve and an air supply at 5 to 7 bar near the base; check
  your gripper's rating ([Pneumatics](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/06-peripherals/pneumatics/)).
- **A mains switch within reach** on the power supply's mains side, a switched socket strip for example: the stop
  for when the PC software has frozen ([Emergency stop](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/02-safety/emergency-stop/)).

The [Planning the cell](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/02-safety/planning-the-cell/) page covers the safety side: who can reach the robot,
guarding, and what the software can and cannot stop.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/04-installation/mounting/ -->

# Mounting the robot

!!! danger "An unanchored robot falls over"
    When the arm extends, the centre of gravity leaves the base. Never run PAROL6 free-standing, not even for a
    test.

## The base holes

Six holes in the base, spaced for 30×30 mm aluminium profiles. Bolt the base to a plate or a profile frame with
M5 screws and T-nuts.

![The six holes in the base](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/assets/base2.webp){ width="600" }

## Clamps

For a desk, clamp the base to the edge with two screw clamps over the base's rim. Check that the clamps do not
interfere with the fan intake and the connectors at the back.

## A profile frame

The repository's [`STL/UTILITY`](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/PAROL6-Desktop-robot-arm/tree/main/STL/UTILITY)
folder has `connectors_4_alu_profiles.STL`, which prints a set of corner connectors for a frame of 30×30
profiles, as in the figure. You need M5 T-nuts, M5 × 12 mm screws for the connectors and M5 × 18 to 20 mm screws
for the base.

![PAROL6 on a 30×30 aluminium profile frame](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/assets/alu_profile.webp){ width="600" }

## Mounting plates

The `mounting plates` folder of the repository has STEP files of a small and a big base plate, with the hole
pattern, for a plate you have machined or cut.

## Orientation

PAROL6 is designed to stand upright on its base. Wall and ceiling mounting are not supported: the payload, the
motor currents and the speed limits are set for an upright arm, and with no brakes the arm would fall into the
mount when powered off.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/04-installation/connecting/ -->

# Connecting

The robot needs three connections to run. They are on the back of the base.

![The power (green), USB (blue) and E-stop (yellow and pink) connections, and the power button (red)](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/assets/Connectors.webp){ width="700" }

| Connection | Connector | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **24 V power** | GX16 2-pin | From the 24 V 5 A supply. Mind the polarity when you wire your own cable: the board has no reverse-polarity protection |
| **USB** | USB type B | To the PC. USB does not power the board |
| **E-stop** | Two screw terminals | A normally closed contact between them. Open means stop |

Plug the power supply into the mains through a switch within your reach, a switched socket strip for example: it
is the stop that still works when the PC software has frozen ([Emergency stop](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/02-safety/emergency-stop/)).

## The E-stop

The E-stop must be a normally closed contact: pressing it, unplugging it or cutting its wire opens the circuit,
and all of these stop the robot, which is what you want. A normally open button does not work. The control board
has two E-stop connectors on the same input, so a second button can be wired in series.

The kit's button comes with a printed housing and a PG7 cable gland. [Emergency stop](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/02-safety/emergency-stop/)
says what happens when it is pressed, and the [Control Board Manual](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/board/06-io-and-estop/) has the wiring
diagram.

## The gripper

An electric gripper (SSG-48, MSG) plugs into the M8 connector at the forearm, which carries 24 V and CAN:
[Electric grippers](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/end-effectors/). Pneumatic tubes from the valve go to the two push-in
fittings at the base: [Pneumatics](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/06-peripherals/pneumatics/).

## Inputs and outputs

The two inputs, two outputs and their supply terminals are on the side of the control board, reachable through
the base: [Inputs and outputs](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/06-peripherals/io/).

!!! warning "Nothing else on the programming port"
    The 2×5-pin programming header next to the USB port is for the ST-Link programming adapter only. An ST-Link
    connected with plain jumper wires without the adapter has destroyed boards. See [Firmware](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/board/08-firmware/).


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/04-installation/first-power-on/ -->

# First power-on

The first time, and every time after that:

1. **Check the E-stop is connected** and released.
2. **Hold the arm by the forearm.** The motors energise with a jolt, and until they do the arm is limp.
3. **Press the power button** on the base. The 24 V stage switches on, each driver initialises with a click, six
   clicks, and the arm holds its position.
4. Let go. The robot is now enabled, not homed, and waiting for the PC.

!!! success "Check"
    Six clicks, the fan runs, and the arm holds when you let go. If not: [If nothing happens](#if-nothing-happens).

Nothing moves until the PC software commands it. Start the [commander software](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/gui/commander/)
or the [Python API's controller](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/programming/02-python-api/controller/), connect, check the jog directions
and home: the [Quick start](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/quick-start/) walks through it.

## What the button does

The button is not a switch in the power line: it tells the firmware to turn the 24 V stage on, and the firmware
keeps it on. A short press while the robot is on turns it off. The board stays powered, and turns itself on, as
long as 3.3 V is present on the programming header, which is why a connected ST-Link keeps the robot on and the
button useless: [Switching on and off](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/05-operation/switching-on-off/).

## If nothing happens

- No clicks, no fan: no 24 V. Check the supply, the GX16 cable and its polarity.
- Clicks, but the PC software does not connect: the serial port name, or the board runs the test firmware. See
  [Communication](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/08-troubleshooting/communication/).
- The board turned on by itself when the supply was plugged in: something supplies 3.3 V to the programming
  header, or the arm was moved while unpowered ([Hazards](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/02-safety/hazards/#stepper-induced-voltage)).


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/05-operation/ -->

# 5. Operation

How the robot is switched on and off, homed, jogged and run, what happens when something goes wrong, and how it
is mastered.

## In this chapter

- [Switching on and off](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/05-operation/switching-on-off/)
- [Homing](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/05-operation/homing/)
- [Jogging](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/05-operation/jogging/)
- [Running programs](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/05-operation/running-programs/)
- [Errors and recovery](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/05-operation/errors-and-recovery/)
- [Mastering](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/05-operation/mastering/)

Each page says what to do in the commander software and in the Python API; the details of either are in the
[Programming Guide](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/programming/).


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/05-operation/switching-on-off/ -->

# Switching on and off

## Switching on

1. E-stop connected and released; power supply on; USB to the PC.
2. Hold the arm by the forearm.
3. Press the power button on the base. The fan starts, the six drivers initialise with a click each, and the
   motors hold the arm.
4. Start the PC software and connect. The robot is enabled and not homed; nothing moves until you command it.

The firmware energises the motors at the moment the 24 V stage comes up, whether or not a PC is connected, and
holds them with the holding current from then on.

## Switching off

!!! danger "Not while it moves"
    Never switch the robot off while it is running a program or carrying something. If it behaves unexpectedly,
    press the E-stop; if the E-stop has no effect, switch off the power supply. The power button is the last
    resort, and only with the arm held.

1. Stop the program and bring the arm to the **parked pose**, folded in over the base, where it has the least
   distance to fall. In the commander, **Park** writes a three-line program into the program window that moves
   there; press **Start** to run it. In the Python API,
   `rbt.move_j([90, -144.683, 108.171, 2.222, 25.003, 180], speed=0.3)` moves to the same pose.
2. Disconnect in the software, or stop the controller.
3. Hold the forearm.
4. Press the power button. The motors release at once and the arm goes limp in your hand.

## The button and the programming adapter

The button does not switch the power line: it tells the firmware to turn the 24 V stage on and off. The
microcontroller itself runs from 3.3 V derived from that stage, or from the programming header. **While an
ST-Link or the programming adapter is connected, the board has 3.3 V, turns on by itself when the supply is
plugged in, and cannot be switched off with the button.** Upload firmware with the 24 V supply disconnected, then
unplug the adapter, then plug the supply in and press the button ([Firmware](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/board/08-firmware/)).

## After a power failure

The arm has fallen. Check that nothing is damaged and nothing is trapped under it, switch on as above, and home
before anything else: the position is lost.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/05-operation/homing/ -->

# Homing

After power-up the robot does not know where its joints are: the motors count steps, and the count starts at
zero wherever the arm happens to stand. Homing gives each joint a reference by driving it to its limit switch or
sensor, then moving a known number of steps to the after-homing pose. It must be done after every power-up, and again
after a collision, a stall or any move by hand.

## Before you press Home

- The arm can move freely to every limit: nothing on the table in the way, no cable caught.
- The tool is mounted: joint 5 homes against the tool's feature on the SSG-48 and the pneumatic gripper, and
  the homing offset in the firmware matches the tool ([Joint 5 and the tool](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/05-operation/mastering/#joint-5-and-the-tool),
  [SSG-48](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/end-effectors/ssg-48/)).
- Joint 6 stands so that it finds its sensor within one turn in the negative direction, with the cables and
  tubes not already wound up. The figure shows the pose: the gripper as drawn, the sensor (blue) and the homing
  pin (red); joint 6 turns along the green arrow.
- You are at the E-stop.

![Joint 6 before homing: the sensor, the homing pin and the direction of rotation](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/assets/J6_home.webp){ width="700" }

## The sequence

The firmware runs the sequence; the PC only starts it and watches.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    S([Home]) --> A[Joints 1, 2 and 3 drive together to their sensor and switches]
    A --> B[Each backs off about a thousand steps and approaches again slowly:<br>the second trigger is the reference]
    B --> C[Joints 1, 2 and 3 move to their after-homing positions]
    C --> D[Joint 4: the same against its inductive sensor, then its after-homing position]
    D --> E[Joint 6 turns in the negative direction until its sensor sees the pin,<br>backs off, re-approaches, moves on so that joint 5 can home]
    E --> F[Joint 5 homes against its switch]
    F --> G[Joints 5 and 6 move to their after-homing positions together]
    G --> H([Every counter set to its after-homing value: six joints homed])
```

1. **Joints 1, 2 and 3 move together** toward their switches: joint 1 to its inductive sensor, joints 2 and 3 to
   their limit switches. Each stops when it triggers.
2. Each backs off, 850 steps on joint 1 and 1050 on joints 2 and 3, and approaches again slowly, and the position
   where it triggers the second time is the reference: the first hit may have pressed the switch too far.
3. Joints 1, 2 and 3 move from the reference to their after-homing positions (13500, 19588 and 23020 steps away).
4. **Joint 4** does the same against its inductive sensor (backing off 1550 steps) and moves to its after-homing
   position.
5. **Joint 6** turns in the negative direction until its sensor sees the homing pin, backs off, re-approaches,
   and moves on to the position from which joint 5 can home.
6. **Joint 5** homes against its switch, and joints 5 and 6 move to their after-homing positions together:
   joint 5 by `j5_homing_offset`, joint 6 back to the point where its sensor triggered.
7. The firmware sets every joint's counter to its after-homing value (`standby_position` in the firmware), and
   reports all six joints as homed.

A video of a correct homing: [Homing reference](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OCCQkIWPWwo). It takes about half
a minute. The result is the after-homing pose: the standby pose turned 90° about joint 1, with joint 1 at +90°
([Joint limits and directions](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/03-technical-data/joint-limits/#standby-and-after-homing)).

=== "Commander software"
    Press **Home**. The response log reports the joints as they home; the position display and the simulator are
    right once all six are homed.

=== "Python API"
    ```python
    rbt.home(wait=True)
    ```
    The first `home()` after power-up runs the referencing sequence. A later `home()` on a referenced robot is a
    planned, collision-checked joint move back to the after-homing pose; `home(calibrate=True)` runs the sequence again.
    Planned motion is refused with `MOTN_NOT_HOMED` until the robot is referenced.

## If it goes wrong

Press the E-stop when a joint grinds at its end without stopping: its switch does not trigger. Joints 1, 4 and 6
use inductive sensors whose LED lights when they see metal; a sensor that does not light needs its trigger screw
adjusted. If joint 6 keeps turning, its homing pin is not where the sensor looks. [Homing failures](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/08-troubleshooting/homing-failures/)
has the cases.

## Mastering

A homed robot stands within a few steps of the after-homing pose. The exact number of steps from each switch to the
witness marks differs between builds; [Mastering](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/05-operation/mastering/) says how to measure and set it.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/05-operation/jogging/ -->

# Jogging

Jogging moves one joint, or the tool along one axis, for as long as you hold a button or repeat a command. It is
how you check a new robot, teach a pose and get out of trouble.

## Joint jog

Each joint has a pair of arrows in the commander's **Joint jog** menu: the **left arrow is the positive**
direction, the right arrow negative, as in [Joint limits and directions](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/03-technical-data/joint-limits/).
The speed slider sets the speed as a percentage of the commander's jog maximum, which is lower than the speed a
program may use ([Speeds](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/03-technical-data/specifications/#speeds)). A jog stops at the joint limit.

=== "Python API"
    ```python
    rbt.jog_j(0, speed=0.3, duration=0.5)               # joint index 0 = J1, 30 % speed, 0.5 s
    rbt.jog_j(joints=[1, 2], speeds=[0.2, -0.2], duration=1.0)
    ```
    A jog command runs for `duration` and the arm brakes to rest when no newer jog arrives; a GUI repeats it while
    the button is held. Joints are indexed from 0 in the API.

## Cartesian jog

The tool moves along X, Y or Z, or rotates about them, in the **world frame** (WRF, fixed to the base) or the
**tool frame** (TRF, fixed to the tool). The commander's **Cartesian jog** menu has the six pairs of arrows and
the WRF/TRF switch; a jog in the tool frame moves the tool along its own axes, which is the natural way to
approach a part.

=== "Python API"
    ```python
    rbt.jog_l("WRF", "X", speed=0.2, duration=0.5)
    rbt.jog_l("TRF", axes=["Z", "RZ"], speeds_list=[0.2, 0.1], duration=0.5)
    ```

A Cartesian jog needs a homed robot, and it can run into a singularity, where the planner cannot find joint
speeds for the tool's motion: the commander stops the jog, and the Python API refuses it. Jog a joint away from
the singular pose and continue ([Configurations and singularities](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/theory/configurations-and-singularities/)).

## Jogging a robot that is not homed

Joint jog works before homing: it is how you check the directions on a new build. The positions shown are
meaningless until the robot is homed, and a Cartesian jog is refused.

Both programs still check each jog against the joint limits, with a position count that starts at 0 when the
board is switched on. That count puts joint 2 past its positive limit and joints 3 and 6 at or below their
negative limits, so until the robot is homed:

- **joint 2** jogs only in its negative direction (the right arrow);
- **joints 3 and 6** jog only in their positive direction (the left arrow);
- **joints 1, 4 and 5** jog both ways.

A refused jog does not move: the commander logs `Error: Robot jog -> Position out of range`, the Python API stops
the joint before it starts.

!!! warning
    Before homing, the limits are checked against a count that does not match the arm, so they do not protect
    the joint: nothing stops it at its real limit except the printed blocker. Jog briefly and slowly.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/05-operation/running-programs/ -->

# Running programs

A program is a list of moves, delays, I/O and gripper commands. PAROL6 runs programs in two ways.

## RBTscript in the commander software

The commander's **Program** window takes an RBTscript program: one command per line, `MoveJoint`, `MoveCart`,
`MoveCartRelTRF`, `Delay`, `Output`, `Gripper`, with `Begin()` and `End()` or `Loop()` around it. The command
list next to the window inserts a command with the robot's current pose as its arguments, which is how you teach
points: jog to the pose, click the command. **Start** runs the program, **Stop** halts it.

```
Begin()
MoveJoint(90,-90,180,0,0,180,t=3)
MoveCart(0,263,242,90,0,90,t=2)
Output(1,HIGH)
Delay(1)
Output(1,LOW)
End()
```

[RBTscript](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/programming/03-commander/rbtscript/) has the language and [Examples](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/programming/03-commander/examples/)
has programs to start from. Programs are plain text files you can keep and share.

## Python with the Python API

A Python script that calls the client is a program: every motion call queues a move on the controller, and the
script waits for it or not, as you choose.

```python
from parol6 import RobotClient

with RobotClient() as rbt:
    rbt.home(wait=True)
    rbt.select_tool("SSG-48")
    rbt.tool.calibrate()
    rbt.delay(2)                  # the SSG-48 needs about 3 s; calibrate() waits only 2 s
    rbt.move_j([90, -90, 180, 0, 0, 180], speed=0.5)
    rbt.move_l([0, 263, 200, 90, 0, 90], speed=0.3)
    rbt.tool.close(speed=0.5, current=0.4)
    rbt.move_l([0, 263, 242, 90, 0, 90], speed=0.3)
    rbt.tool.open()
```

The Python API also runs programs written for other tools, and from other machines: the controller accepts
commands over the network from any client, so a program can run on a laptop while the controller runs on the PC
at the robot. [The Python API](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/programming/02-python-api/) is the guide.

## Simulate first

Both programs have a simulator. The commander opens its 3D window with the GUI and mirrors the robot; the Python
API's controller runs with `simulator(True)` or the `DryRunRobotClient` without hardware, through the same
kinematics and collision checks. Run a new program in the simulator at full speed, then on the robot at low speed.

## Speed

The commander's speed slider scales jogging only; a program's speed is in its moves, `v=` and `a=` or `t=`. The Python API takes a `speed` fraction per move and
`set_execution_speed()` scales the queue while it runs; `pause()` and `resume()` hold and continue it.

## Stopping a program

- **Stop** in the commander, or `stop()` in the API: the current move is cancelled, the queue cleared, the robot
  stays enabled and holding.
- The **E-stop**: the robot is disabled and the program or the queue is stopped; in the Python API, call
  `reset()` after releasing it ([Emergency stop](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/02-safety/emergency-stop/)).
- Closing the software: stop the program first. The firmware has no timeout: it keeps executing the last packet
  it received until the next one arrives. After a move to a position the joints stop near that target and hold.

!!! danger "When the PC stops sending during a jog"
    If the commander closes, crashes or loses the USB connection while a joint jogs (in joint or Cartesian
    jog), the firmware keeps that joint turning at its jog speed until it reaches its blocker. Programs that use
    speed tracking (`speed` as the last argument of a move) behave the same way. Use the mains switch of the power
    supply ([Emergency stop](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/02-safety/emergency-stop/)).


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/05-operation/errors-and-recovery/ -->

# Errors and recovery

## What the robot reports

Every 10 ms the control board sends the PC the joints' positions and speeds, which joints are homed, the state of
the inputs, outputs and E-stop, the gripper's status, and two error bytes reserved for the drivers' temperature
and position flags. The PC software adds its own: inverse kinematics failures, limit violations, timing problems.

## The commander software

The **response log** shows what the robot and the program are doing and why a command was refused. The common
entries:

| Log | Meaning | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| *Robot disable; button or estop* | The E-stop is open, or Disable was pressed | Release the E-stop; press **Enable** |
| An inverse kinematics error | The target pose has no solution, or lies past a singularity | Change the pose or the approach; move in joint space to get near it |
| A joint limit error | The move would leave a joint's range | Choose a reachable target |
| Jogging stops in Cartesian mode | A singularity | Jog a joint away from it |
| The time between commands rises above 10 ms | The PC cannot keep the 100 Hz loop | Close other programs; a faster PC ([Communication](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/08-troubleshooting/communication/)) |

**Enable** clears the errors and enables the robot; **Clear error** resets the homing state but does not re-enable
a disabled robot; **Disable** stops the firmware from accepting motion commands while the motors keep holding.

## The Python API

A refused command raises `MotionError` with a code, a cause and a remedy, from the controller's error catalog:
`IK_TARGET_UNREACHABLE`, `MOTN_NOT_HOMED`, `SYS_ESTOP_ACTIVE`, `SYS_SELF_COLLISION`, `MOTN_CANCELLED` and the
others on [Errors](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/reference/python/errors/). `error()` returns the current error, `activity()` what the
robot is doing. After an E-stop is released, call `reset()`: it enables the firmware again, and until then the arm
does not move. After `stop()` nothing needs clearing.

## After a collision or a stall

The motors have lost steps and the arm is not where the software says. Stop the program, move the arm clear if
it is trapped (disable it, or switch off with the forearm held), check the belts and the printed parts, and
**home again** before anything else.

## After the arm fell

Power was lost with the arm extended. Check every joint by hand for free movement, look at the belts and the
couplers, switch on with the forearm held, and home.

## A joint moves the wrong way

On a new build or after work on the wiring: stop at once. The direction is set per joint in the firmware
([Firmware and first run](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/build/firmware-and-first-run/#a-joint-turns-the-wrong-way)); do not try to home
until every joint jogs in the right direction.

## The gripper reports an error

The electric grippers report their own errors through the robot: not calibrated, E-stop, timeout. The commander's
**Gripper** tab has **Clear gripper error** and **Calibrate gripper**: clear the error first, then calibrate,
and wait until the calibration has finished before the first move. The Python API's `tool.calibrate()`
calibrates but has no clear ([SSG-48](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/end-effectors/ssg-48/), [MSG](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/end-effectors/msg/)). The gripper
manuals explain each error.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/05-operation/mastering/ -->

# Mastering

Homing brings each joint to its switch and then a fixed number of steps to the after-homing pose. That number is in
the firmware, measured on the reference robot. Printers and parts differ, so on your robot the homed pose may be
off by a fraction of a degree per joint. Mastering measures the difference and corrects the number, so that a
homed robot stands exactly at its witness marks.

## Witness marks

Holes in neighbouring links that line up when the joint stands where homing should leave it, in the
after-homing pose (90°, −90°, 180°, 0°, 0°, 180°): a pin pushed through them proves the pose. PAROL6 has them on
every joint.

![Witness marks of PAROL6](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/assets/parolw.webp){ width="800" }

## The procedure

1. Home the robot.
2. For each joint, jog it in small steps until the pin fits through its witness marks. Jog at the lowest speed
   and read the joint's position from the commander's position display or `rbt.angles()`.
3. Convert the angle you jogged by to motor steps with the joint's ratio ([Drives, ratios and resolution](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/03-technical-data/drives-and-ratios/)),
   or read the step count from the firmware's telemetry.
4. For joints 1 to 4: in `motor_init.cpp`, add that number of steps to the joint's `homed_position` (subtract if
   you jogged in the negative direction), upload the firmware, and home again. The pin should now fit without
   jogging. Joints 5 and 6 work differently, below.

```cpp
/// @brief Number of steps from when the limit switch is hit to the standby position
Joint__->homed_position = 13500;   // joint 1: raise or lower by the steps you measured
```

The values of the reference robot are on [Firmware parameters](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/reference/firmware-parameters/).

## Joint 5 and the tool

Joint 5 homes against a feature of the tool, so its number depends on the tool: 8900 steps with the pneumatic
gripper holder and 8035 with the SSG-48, set as `j5_homing_offset` in `main.cpp`. Master joint 5 by changing that
value, not its `homed_position`. A custom tool needs its own value, found the same way.

## Joint 6

Joint 6 has no offset to master in firmware 1. Its `homed_position` (15900) is only the position from which
joint 5 homes: when joint 5 is done, joint 6 turns back to the point where its sensor saw the homing pin, and that
point is its after-homing position. If joint 6 does not line up with its witness marks after homing, move its
sensor or its homing pin.

## When to master again

After replacing a belt, a switch, a sensor or a printed part of a joint, or when the robot's absolute accuracy
matters more than its repeatability. The repeatability does not depend on mastering: a homed robot returns to
the same place every time, whether or not that place is exactly the witness mark.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/06-peripherals/ -->

# 6. Peripherals

Everything the robot talks to besides the PC and the tool: switches and sensors on its inputs, valves and lamps on
its outputs, the air for the pneumatic gripper, and the CAN bus for the electric grippers.

![The control board's connections to the outside world](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/assets/IMG1.webp){ width="800" }

## In this chapter

- [Inputs and outputs](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/06-peripherals/io/)
- [Pneumatics](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/06-peripherals/pneumatics/)
- [CAN bus](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/06-peripherals/can-bus/)

The electrical details of the connectors are in the [Control Board Manual](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/board/06-io-and-estop/).


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/06-peripherals/io/ -->

# Inputs and outputs

The control board has two isolated inputs and two isolated outputs on screw terminals at the side of the board,
reachable through the base. They are isolated from the robot's electronics through optocouplers, and they share
a supply that you choose.

## The supply

- **Isolated**: connect an external supply's negative to **GND_SEL** and positive to **HV_SEL**. The inputs and
  outputs then work at that voltage, 12 or 24 V (the inputs need at least 12 V), and a fault on them cannot reach
  the robot.
- **Not isolated**: link the robot's own 24 V and GND to HV_SEL and GND_SEL. Simpler, and the valve of the
  pneumatic gripper is usually wired this way. A 2 A fuse protects the outputs in this mode.

![Isolated supply wiring](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/assets/Ext_supply.webp){ width="650" }

![Non-isolated wiring from the robot's 24 V](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/assets/Internal_24V.webp){ width="650" }

The E-stop is not part of this: it is wired to the robot's own supply whichever option you choose.

## Inputs

Switches, push buttons, light barriers and sensors. A switch goes between **HV_SEL** and **IN1** or **IN2**; a
three-wire sensor takes HV_SEL and GND_SEL for its supply and gives its signal to the input. Input voltage 12 to
50 V, 24 V nominal.

The robot reports the inputs in every packet: the commander's **IO** tab shows them, and the Python API's `io()`
returns `[in1, in2, out1, out2, estop]`. RBTscript's `Input()` has no action yet: a program stops on it
([Known issues](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/08-troubleshooting/known-issues/)).

## Outputs

Relays, valves, lamps, small actuators, up to 0.5 A each (1 A peak), 48 V maximum. A load goes between
**GND_SEL** and **OUT1** or **OUT2**; the output switches it to the supply. An inductive load, a valve or a relay
coil, gets a flyback diode across it.

=== "RBTscript"
    ```
    Output(1,HIGH)
    Output(1,LOW)
    ```

    Only output 1: in the current commander version `Output(2,...)` is refused by a bug in its check and stops
    the program ([RBTscript](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/programming/03-commander/rbtscript/)).

=== "Python API"
    ```python
    rbt.write_io(0, 1)       # output 1 high (logical index 0)
    rbt.write_io(1, 0)
    ```

The commander's **IO** tab switches the outputs by hand.

![The IO tab of the commander software](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/assets/IO_tab.PNG){ width="700" }


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/06-peripherals/pneumatics/ -->

# Pneumatics

Two 4 mm tubes run inside the arm from the push-in fittings at the base to the forearm, where the pneumatic or
vacuum gripper connects. A 5/2 solenoid valve at the base, driven by an output, switches the air.

## Pressure

5 to 7 bar; check your gripper's rating, and stay below the lowest rating of the gripper, the valve and the
fittings. The tubes and fittings are standard 4 mm pneumatic parts.

## The valve

A 5/2 valve, 24 V coil, 4 mm ports: one port from the compressor, two to the base fittings, the exhausts open.
The coil goes between **GND_SEL** and **OUTPUT1** ([Inputs and outputs](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/06-peripherals/io/)). Which of the two outputs is
pressurised when the coil is off decides whether the gripper is normally open or normally closed: swap the two
tubes to change it.

![Valve, tubes and gripper](../assets/pneumatic connection_edit.webp){ width="700" }

## Routing

The arm's tubes run inside it from the base to the push-in fittings on the forearm; they are one reason for the
one-turn rule of the joints. From the forearm fittings, the gripper's own tubes cross joints 5 and 6 outside the
arm, like an electric gripper's cable: give them enough slack for the range you use, since they, not the flange,
limit joint 6. Outside the base, give the tubes a loop so the arm cannot pull them.

## A vacuum gripper

Needs one line only: block the valve's second port ([Vacuum gripper](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/end-effectors/vacuum-gripper/)).

In the Python API, a pneumatic or vacuum tool's `open()` switches output 1 high and `close()` switches it low,
whatever the tubing does: lay the tubes so the two match ([Pneumatic gripper](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/end-effectors/pneumatic-gripper/)).


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/06-peripherals/can-bus/ -->

# CAN bus

The control board has a CAN bus for the electric grippers, wired to the M8 connector at the forearm. The board
is the master: it sends the gripper the command from the PC's packet every cycle (a move, a calibrate, a clear
error, or an empty status poll when nothing changed) and relays the gripper's answer back to the PC.

- **Bit rate**: 1 Mbit/s, the grippers' rate.
- **Node ID**: the gripper's CAN ID, 0 as shipped; the PC packet carries the ID the board addresses, so a gripper
  with another ID works if the software is told.
- **Termination**: 120 Ω at each end of the bus. At the board end, the **CAN1 JUMPER** connects the board's
  120 Ω resistor when it is on; at the other end, the gripper has its own termination switch, on as shipped
  ([CAN bus](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/board/07-can/)).

A second CAN controller is on the board, but its transceiver is not populated: CAN 2 is for your own
experiments. More axes on the bus, a seventh axis or a second gripper, are not supported by the firmware or the
software yet; the protocol the grippers speak is documented in the [STEPFOC](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/)
and [Spectral Micro](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/) references for anyone who wants to
extend it.

The electrical side is in [CAN bus](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/board/07-can/) of the Control Board Manual.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/07-maintenance/ -->

# 7. Maintenance

PAROL6 needs little: belts that stay tight, set screws that stay put, switches that trigger. Check them at the
intervals below and after any collision.

| Interval | What |
|---|---|
| Before each session | The E-stop works (press it with the robot enabled); nothing in the workspace; the cables and tubes free |
| Monthly, or every 50 hours | [Inspection](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/07-maintenance/inspection/): belts, couplers, switches, fan, printed parts |
| After a collision, a fall or a lost step | Inspection, then [Checking the homing](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/07-maintenance/homing-check/) |
| When a belt slips or a joint is loose | [Belts](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/07-maintenance/belts/), [Couplers and threadlocker](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/07-maintenance/couplers/) |

Before any work inside the base, unplug the supply and touch earthed metal: static electricity damages the
control board and its drivers.

## In this chapter

- [Inspection](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/07-maintenance/inspection/)
- [Belts](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/07-maintenance/belts/)
- [Couplers and threadlocker](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/07-maintenance/couplers/)
- [Checking the homing](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/07-maintenance/homing-check/)


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/07-maintenance/inspection/ -->

# Inspection

With the robot switched off and the supply unplugged:

- **Belts** (joints 1, 3, 4, 5): press each with a finger through its cover opening; it should give a little and
  spring back. A belt that sags or that you can push against the pulley needs tensioning ([Belts](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/07-maintenance/belts/)).
  Look for frayed edges and missing teeth.
- **Couplers and set screws**: hold the output of each joint and try to turn the motor side; any play that is not
  the gearbox's backlash is a loose set screw ([Couplers and threadlocker](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/07-maintenance/couplers/)).
- **Limit switches and sensors**: press each switch lever; it should click. The inductive sensors' LEDs light
  when a screw head comes near.
- **Printed parts**: cracks at screw bosses and bearing seats, especially on the elbow and the upper arm, and
  any warping of the forearm from heat.
- **Cables and tubes**: chafing where the arm's cables pass through the joints, and where the gripper's cable
  and tubes cross joints 5 and 6 from the forearm; the gripper cable's connector tight.
- **The fan**: turning when the robot is on, and the intake free of dust. A stopped fan overheats the drivers.
- **The base**: the mounting bolts tight, the E-stop button firm in its housing.

Then switch on, home, and watch the homing: each joint should back off and re-approach its switch cleanly, and
the pose at the end should match the witness marks ([Checking the homing](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/07-maintenance/homing-check/)).

## Cleaning

Clean the robot switched off and unplugged. Wipe the printed parts with a dry or slightly damp cloth; use no
solvents on them, and never spray anything into the base, where the control board and the fan are open to it.
Clear dust from the fan intake with a soft brush or a vacuum cleaner, not with compressed air, which drives the
dust into the board.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/07-maintenance/belts/ -->

# Belts

Belts drive joints 1, 3, 4 and 5. Over time they stretch a little and the joint loses stiffness; a belt that slips
a tooth loses the robot's position.

## Tension

The reference is the [belt tension video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=v0PYfEoIr3k): in it, maximum hand force
is applied to the belt, and that is the tension to aim for on joints 3 and 5. Joints 1 and 4 take slightly less.
A belt is tensioned by adding or moving the small tension bearings (3 × 8 × 4 mm and 3 × 10 × 4 mm) that press
on its back; if a belt is not tight enough, add another bearing as in the photos. You may or may not need a
tensioner on a given joint: it depends on your belts and printed parts, so fit one only where the belt is not
tight enough without it.

### Joint 5 belt

![Joint 5 belt and tensioner](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/assets/belt1.webp){ width="550" }

### Joint 4 belt

![Joint 4 belt and tensioner](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/assets/belt2.webp){ width="450" }

### Joint 3 belt

![Joint 3 belt and tensioner](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/assets/belt3.webp){ width="450" }

### Joint 1 belt

![Joint 1 belt and tensioner](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/assets/belt4.webp){ width="550" }

## Grease

A thin film of grease on the belts' teeth reduces noise and wear. Reapply when it dries out.

## Replacement

| Joint | Belt |
|---|---|
| Joint 1 | HTD3 396 mm, 6 mm wide |
| Joint 3 | HTD3 342 mm |
| Joint 4 | HTD3 201 mm |
| Joint 5 | HTD3 246 mm |

Replacing a belt means opening the joint as in the assembly manual; afterwards home the robot and check the
witness marks, and master if they do not line up.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/07-maintenance/couplers/ -->

# Couplers and threadlocker

The motor shafts, the gearbox outputs and the joint 6 shaft are joined by couplers and pulleys with set screws on
flats or keys. Vibration loosens set screws; a loose one lets the motor turn without the joint, and the robot
loses its position without noticing.

- If a joint starts to slip, or its position drifts between homings, find the set screw, tighten it, and apply
  **blue (medium) threadlocker**. Do not move the robot for 24 hours while it cures.
- Put a screw on the key as well as on the flat where the part has both.
- Apply threadlocker to every metal-to-metal screw joint on the robot: the motor mounts, the gearbox flanges,
  the bearing clamps. Printed parts and brass inserts do not need it, and the solvent in some threadlockers
  attacks plastic: keep it on the metal.
- Never use red (permanent) threadlocker; the parts cannot be taken apart again without heat.

After tightening a coupler, home the robot and check the witness marks.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/07-maintenance/homing-check/ -->

# Checking the homing

Homing is the robot's only position reference, so check it after any mechanical work, after a collision, and
whenever the robot's accuracy seems off.

1. Home the robot and watch each joint: it must reach its switch, back off, re-approach slowly, and move on. A
   joint that grinds at a stop, or re-approaches at full speed, has a switch problem ([Homing failures](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/08-troubleshooting/homing-failures/)).
2. At the end, try the pin at the witness marks of each joint ([Mastering](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/05-operation/mastering/)). It
   should slide in, or nearly. A joint that is off by more than a degree was knocked, slipped, or its switch
   moved.
3. Home three times in a row and compare the witness marks each time. The pose should repeat exactly: if it
   does not, the switch or the sensor triggers inconsistently, or something in the joint moves.
4. Jog to a taught pose from a program and check that the tool is where it was taught.

A joint that homes repeatably but to the wrong place is mastered; a joint that does not repeat is repaired.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/08-troubleshooting/ -->

# 8. Troubleshooting

- [By symptom](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/08-troubleshooting/by-symptom/): the robot does not turn on, does not connect, moves wrong, stops, makes noise
- [Homing failures](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/08-troubleshooting/homing-failures/)
- [Communication](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/08-troubleshooting/communication/): serial ports, the 100 Hz loop, slow PCs
- [Known issues](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/08-troubleshooting/known-issues/): the faults in the firmware and software that are known and not yet fixed, and
  what to do until they are

For the control board itself, see the [Control Board Manual's troubleshooting](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/board/11-troubleshooting/);
for the software, [Programming troubleshooting](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/programming/06-troubleshooting/). When you ask for help,
[Report a problem](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/support/report-a-problem/) says what to include.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/08-troubleshooting/by-symptom/ -->

# By symptom

| Symptom | Likely cause | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| Nothing happens at the power button | No 24 V; polarity; the button cable | Check the supply's LED, the GX16 cable, the JST button cable on the board |
| The board turns on by itself when the supply is plugged in | 3.3 V on the programming header (an ST-Link or the adapter is connected); the arm was moved while unpowered | Unplug the adapter; move an unpowered robot slowly |
| The robot cannot be switched off with the button | The same 3.3 V | Unplug the programming adapter |
| Clicks on power-up, but the PC does not connect | Wrong serial port; the test firmware is on the board; Linux permissions | [Communication](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/08-troubleshooting/communication/) |
| A joint jogs the wrong way | Direction not set for that joint in the firmware; a motor's wires swapped | [A joint turns the wrong way](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/build/firmware-and-first-run/#a-joint-turns-the-wrong-way) |
| A joint does not move at all | Driver not seated or faulty; motor connector; the joint is at its blocker | The test firmware: its driver report at power-on, and whether the motor turns with the others ([The test firmware](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/board/09-test-firmware/)) |
| A joint grinds at its end during homing | Its switch or sensor does not trigger | E-stop; [Homing failures](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/08-troubleshooting/homing-failures/) |
| Joint 6 keeps spinning during homing | The homing pin is not where the sensor looks | E-stop; set the joint 6 pose as in [Homing](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/05-operation/homing/) |
| The pose after homing is off by a few degrees on one joint | A loose coupler, a slipped belt, a moved switch | [Couplers](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/07-maintenance/couplers/), [Belts](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/07-maintenance/belts/), then [Mastering](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/05-operation/mastering/) |
| The robot's position drifts during a program | Lost steps: too fast, too heavy, a collision, a reduced current | Lower the speed; check the payload; home again |
| A joint hums or squeals and does not hold | A driver in error, a lost phase | The test firmware's driver report at power-on (its fault flags); check the motor cable |
| Cartesian jogging stops by itself | A singularity | Jog a joint away ([Configurations and singularities](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/theory/configurations-and-singularities/)) |
| A pose from the GUI cannot be reached by MoveCart | The inverse kinematics finds no solution along the straight line | Move in joint space; choose another orientation |
| The robot stutters while moving | The PC misses the 10 ms cycle | [Communication](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/08-troubleshooting/communication/) |
| The forearm is hot | Hours of motion at the default currents | [Currents and temperatures](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/03-technical-data/operating-temperatures/) |
| The gripper does nothing | Not calibrated; an error latched; the cable | Calibrate, clear the error; the gripper's manual |
| The E-stop has no effect | The PC software is frozen | Switch off the power supply; see [Emergency stop](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/02-safety/emergency-stop/) |


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/08-troubleshooting/homing-failures/ -->

# Homing failures

Stop with the E-stop first; a joint driven against its stop strips a belt or cracks a part.

## A joint does not stop at its switch

- **Joints 2, 3, 5** use mechanical limit switches. Check that the lever is pressed by the moving part, that
  the switch clicks, and that it is wired to 24 V and its signal terminal (polarity does not matter). The test
  firmware's `#LIMIT` shows the state live.
- **Joints 1, 4, 6** use inductive sensors that detect a screw head. The sensor's LED lights when it sees metal.
  If it does not light as the joint passes, adjust the trigger screw closer; the 4 mm sensors see about 1 to 2
  mm. Wiring: brown 24 V, blue GND, black signal.
- A switch on the wrong joint's terminal: wire each switch and sensor to the terminal the
  [wiring diagram](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/build/electronics-and-wiring/#wiring-the-arm-to-the-board) shows for its joint; the test
  firmware's `#LIMIT` shows which input changes when you press a switch.

## A joint stops too early

The switch triggers before the joint reaches it: a wire shorted, a sensor too close to a screw it should not
see, or a switch lever caught. Also the reason a homed pose is far off on one joint.

## Joint 6 turns more than a turn

Its sensor never sees the homing pin. Before homing, turn joint 6 by hand so that the pin is just before the
sensor in the direction of rotation ([Homing](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/05-operation/homing/)), and check the sensor's gap.

## Joint 5 does not reach its switch

The tool's homing feature is missing or in the wrong place, or the firmware's `j5_homing_offset` is for another
tool ([Your own tool](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/end-effectors/custom-tools/)).

## The homed pose does not match the witness marks

By a fraction of a degree: master the joint. By more: the joint slipped, a belt or coupler, or the switch
moved. Inspect, then master.

## Homing never finishes in the software

The PC lost the packet stream, or the firmware is waiting for a joint that does not report. Check the log, press
Clear error or `reset()`, and home again.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/08-troubleshooting/communication/ -->

# Communication

## The serial port

The control board appears on the PC as a serial port over USB: `COMx` on Windows, `/dev/ttyACMx` on Linux and
`/dev/cu.usbmodem…` on macOS. The commander takes `COM5` or `ttyACM0` in its connection field; the Python API's controller takes
`--serial COM5` or `--serial /dev/ttyACM0`, or finds the port from `PAROL6_COM_PORT`.

- **Windows**: Device Manager, Ports, shows the number. If the board is missing, try another cable or port; the
  board enumerates only when it has power.
- **Linux**: `ls /dev/ttyACM*`. Permission denied: `sudo chmod 666 /dev/ttyACM0`, or add yourself to the
  `dialout` group and log in again.
- **Connect fails the first time** in the commander: press Connect again; two or three tries are normal.
- **The port is busy**: another program has it, often a previous instance of the controller.

## The test firmware answers, the main firmware does not

A board from the shop carries the test firmware, which talks in text. Upload the main firmware ([Firmware](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/board/08-firmware/)).

## The 100 Hz loop

The PC must send a packet every 10 ms. The commander prints `Time between 2 commands in ms` in its terminal
output; it should sit near 0.010. The number is in seconds, despite the label: 0.010 is 10 ms. If it is often
higher, the robot stutters and the position tracking suffers.

- Close browsers and other heavy programs; disable power saving on the USB port and the CPU.
- A faster PC: six cores from 2017 or newer ([What you need](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/01-overview/what-you-need/#the-pc)).
- The Python API's controller logs `loop overbudget by +N%` when its loop runs late, and shows the figures in
  `loop_stats()`; it also accepts a lower `PAROL6_CONTROL_RATE_HZ`, at the cost of smoothness, and runs worse
  with TRACE or DEBUG logging on.

## The connection drops

A USB cable without ferrite near the motors, a hub, or a long cable: use a short, shielded cable straight into
the PC. When packets stop, the firmware keeps executing the last one: after a move to a position the joints stop
near that target and hold, but a joint that was jogging in the commander keeps turning until it reaches its
blocker. Keep the mains switch of the power supply within reach ([Emergency stop](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/02-safety/emergency-stop/)).


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/08-troubleshooting/known-issues/ -->

# Known issues

The faults in PAROL6's firmware and software that are known and not yet fixed, and what to do until they are. The
pages that describe each part say the same where it matters; this page collects them in one place. Which versions
work together is in [Versions and compatibility](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/appendix/compatibility/).

### Control board firmware

Seen in: release 1.

| | What happens | What to do | More |
|---|---|---|---|
| KI-1 | Enforces the joint limits of the earlier robot model, which differ from those in these pages; a target between the two is accepted. | Keep to the limits in the Joint limits table. | [Joint limits](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/03-technical-data/joint-limits/#limits) |

### Control board test firmware

Seen in: release 1.

| | What happens | What to do | More |
|---|---|---|---|
| KI-8 | Enables all six drivers when it boots and turns every motor slowly, without a command, with no limits and no homing, until the power is switched off; no command stops them. | Run it with the arm free to move or the motors unmounted, never on a robot folded against its stops. | [The test firmware](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/board/09-test-firmware/) |
| KI-9 | Most command names the parser knows (`#STATUS`, `#STEP1` to `#STEP6`, `#FLASH`, `#CAN`) are answered with `Unknown command`: only `#IO`, `#LIMIT`, `#STOP` and `#start` do something. | Use the four commands that work; CAN has its own test program. | [Test firmware commands](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/board/09-test-firmware/#commands) |

### Commander software

Seen in: main branch, 2025-09-23.

| | What happens | What to do | More |
|---|---|---|---|
| KI-2 | Enforces the joint limits of the earlier robot model, and computes with its dimensions (a5 = 176.35 mm, the pneumatic gripper's a6 = 62.8 mm), so its Cartesian positions are off by up to about 0.65 mm. | Keep to the limits in the Joint limits table; teach the poses that need accuracy on the robot. | [Kinematics](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/03-technical-data/kinematics/) |
| KI-3 | `Output(2,HIGH)` and `Output(2,LOW)` are refused by a bug in the program check (`Invalid Output() command`), and the program stops. | Use output 1 in commander programs, or switch output 2 from the Python API. | [RBTscript, I/O](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/programming/03-commander/rbtscript/#io) |
| KI-4 | `SpeedJoint()`, `Input()` and `Home()` pass the program check but have no action: the program stops on that line until you press **Stop**. | Leave them out of programs; home with the **Home** button before you start a program. | [RBTscript, SpeedJoint and SpeedCart](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/programming/03-commander/rbtscript/#speedjoint-speedcart) |
| KI-5 | `SpeedCart()`, `Get_data` and `Timeouts` are in the command menu but fail the program check: a program that contains one is refused. | Leave them out of programs. | [RBTscript, SpeedJoint and SpeedCart](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/programming/03-commander/rbtscript/#speedjoint-speedcart) |
| KI-6 | A move's profile written in quotes (`"trap"`) or as `func=trap` is ignored without a message, and the move gets the default profile. | Write the bare word, `trap` or `poly`, as the last argument. | [RBTscript](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/programming/03-commander/rbtscript/) |
| KI-7 | The Cartesian rotation jog buttons do nothing in the world frame (WRF). | Rotate in the tool frame (TRF), the default. | [The GUI](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/gui/commander/the-gui/) |

### Python API (parol6)

Seen in: 0.9.1.

| | What happens | What to do | More |
|---|---|---|---|
| KI-10 | Enforces the joint limits of the earlier robot model, and computes with its dimensions (a5 = 176.35 mm), so its Cartesian positions are off by up to about 0.65 mm from the model these pages use. | Keep to the limits in the Joint limits table; teach the poses that need accuracy on the robot. | [Kinematics](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/03-technical-data/kinematics/) |

## Something that is not here

Check [By symptom](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/08-troubleshooting/by-symptom/) first. If it is still not explained, [Report a problem](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/support/report-a-problem/)
says what to include so it can be reproduced. A fixed issue stays on this page, under "Fixed", with the version
that fixes it.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/09-transport/ -->

# 9. Transport and storage

## Moving the robot

1. Home it, then bring it to the **parked pose**: joints 2 and 3 toward their limit switches so the arm folds
   over the base. The commander's **Park** button writes a program that moves there
   ([Switching off](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/05-operation/switching-on-off/#switching-off)). Or move it by hand once it is switched off
   ([Moving the robot by hand](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/02-safety/moving-by-hand/)).
2. Switch off with the forearm held; unplug the supply, the USB and the E-stop.
3. Carry it by the base, not by the arm.

![The parked pose: the arm folded in over the base](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/assets/figures/parol6_parked.webp){ width="420" }
![The parked pose: the arm folded in over the base](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/assets/figures/parol6_parked_dark.webp){ width="420" }

## Packing

Fold the arm as above, put foam under the joint 3 limit switch so that the forearm rests on it and not on the
switch, and tape the forearm to the upper arm so that the joints cannot swing. Pack the robot upright in a box
with foam around the base; the gripper and the E-stop separately.

## Storage

Dry, at room temperature, folded. The stepper motors and the drivers have no shelf-life issues; the PETG parts
should not be stored where it gets hot, in a car or near a radiator. Before the first use after storage, run the
[Inspection](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/07-maintenance/inspection/).


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/build/ -->

# Build guide

PAROL6 is open hardware: you can print the parts, buy the rest from the bill of materials and build the robot
yourself. This guide is the order to do it in, with the facts that are not in the assembly manual; the step by
step assembly is in the [building instructions PDF](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/PAROL6-Desktop-robot-arm/tree/main/Building%20instructions)
and the [video playlist](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLSueoDrBt5MMTL9O8qAWZiJrNIf8-29Qz).

!!! warning
    A self-built robot is yours to make safe: the motor currents, the wiring, the switches and the stops. Read the
    [Safety](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/02-safety/) chapter before the first power-on, as you would for a bought one.

## The steps

1. [Bill of materials](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/build/bill-of-materials/): what to buy
2. [Printing the parts](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/build/printing/): the material, the settings, the print table
3. [Mechanical assembly](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/build/mechanical-assembly/): the manual, the videos, the things to get right
4. [Electronics and wiring](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/build/electronics-and-wiring/): the control board, the drivers, the motors, the switches
5. [Firmware and first run](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/build/firmware-and-first-run/): the test firmware, the main firmware, directions, homing

## Kits

You do not have to source everything yourself. The [shop](https://source-robotics.com/collections/all) sells the
robot in every state between a bag of parts and a working arm:

| | What is in it | You add |
|---|---|---|
| [Assembled robot](https://source-robotics.com/products/parol6-robotic-arm) | the robot, built, tested and ready for the commander software | nothing |
| [Full kit](https://source-robotics.com/products/parol6-robotic-arm-kit) | every part of the BOM except the printed parts and the power supply | the printed parts, a 24 V 5 A supply |
| [Partial kit](https://source-robotics.com/products/parol6-partial-kit) | the hard-to-find parts: the board, the drivers, the bearings, belts, pulleys, connectors, sensors, switches, the pneumatics | the gearboxes, the stepper motors and the power supply, which are heavy to ship and cheaper from a supplier near you; the printed parts |
| [Printed parts kit](https://source-robotics.com/products/parol6-3d-printed-parts-kit) | every printed part, in PETG, in several colours | everything else |
| [Screw kit](https://source-robotics.com/products/parol6-screw-kit) | every screw and nut of the BOM, counted | everything else |
| [Control board](https://source-robotics.com/products/parol6-control-board), [programming adapter](https://source-robotics.com/products/parol6-programming-adapter) | the electronics alone | everything else |

The partial kit is the best value for a builder with a printer: it carries the parts that are hard to find or
easy to get wrong, and leaves out the three items a local supplier sells cheaper than we can ship them. A full
kit skips the bill of materials; a printed parts kit skips the printing.

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/build/bill-of-materials/ -->

# Bill of materials

!!! note "This is a copy"
    The original is [BOM/BOM.md](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/PAROL6-Desktop-robot-arm/blob/main/BOM/BOM.md) in the robot's repository; this page is that
    file as of 2026-11-01 (commit `9954df6`), with the reference images shown inline. If a link is broken or a part
    is wrong, [open an issue](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/PAROL6-Desktop-robot-arm/issues/new) there, and the fix lands here with the next sync. If you would
    rather not source the parts yourself, the shop's [kits](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/build/#kits) cover every part or the hard-to-find ones.

Most items have links where you can buy the item, and some of them are affiliate links. Items like screws, belts and bearings can be bought locally or from many other vendors.

!!! note
    If any product links are broken, unavailable, or no longer point to the correct item, please [open an issue](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/PAROL6-Desktop-robot-arm/issues/new). You can also use the reference images to find the same or an equivalent part from another supplier.

## Motors
