# Printing the parts

## Material

PETG. The motors run warm and the parts around them see 60 to 70 °C in long use, which PLA does not survive;
PETG softens around 80 °C, prints without an enclosure, and bonds layers well. ABS or ASA work with an enclosure.
The repository's [PETG notes](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/PAROL6-Desktop-robot-arm/blob/main/Building%20instructions/PETG_printing.md)
give the printing basics: hot end 220 to 250 °C, bed 60 to 90 °C with glue, a layer fan, and the warping is
small.

## The files

All parts are in the repository's [`STL`](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/PAROL6-Desktop-robot-arm/tree/main/STL) folder, grouped by link:
[`BASE`](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/PAROL6-Desktop-robot-arm/tree/main/STL/BASE), [`SHOULDER`](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/PAROL6-Desktop-robot-arm/tree/main/STL/SHOULDER), [`UPPER_ARM`](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/PAROL6-Desktop-robot-arm/tree/main/STL/UPPER_ARM), [`ELBOW`](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/PAROL6-Desktop-robot-arm/tree/main/STL/ELBOW), [`FOREARM`](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/PAROL6-Desktop-robot-arm/tree/main/STL/FOREARM), [`WRIST`](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/PAROL6-Desktop-robot-arm/tree/main/STL/WRIST), [`ESTOP`](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/PAROL6-Desktop-robot-arm/tree/main/STL/ESTOP), [`GRIPPER_ATTACHMENTS`](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/PAROL6-Desktop-robot-arm/tree/main/STL/GRIPPER_ATTACHMENTS), [`UTILITY`](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/PAROL6-Desktop-robot-arm/tree/main/STL/UTILITY), [`mounting plates`](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/PAROL6-Desktop-robot-arm/tree/main/STL/mounting%20plates),
and [`SMALL_PRINT_BED`](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/PAROL6-Desktop-robot-arm/tree/main/STL/SMALL_PRINT_BED) for the split versions of the two largest parts.
The print table below says how each was printed on the reference robots; it is a tested starting point, not a
rule.

## Print table

The print table from the robot's repository, as it is. Every printed part with the settings it was printed with
on the reference robots: supports, mass, infill, print time, cooling, layer height, top and bottom layers,
perimeters. Click the table to enlarge it. The same table is in the repository as a
[PDF](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/PAROL6-Desktop-robot-arm/blob/main/Print%20table/Print_table.pdf) and as an
[Excel file](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/PAROL6-Desktop-robot-arm/blob/main/Print%20table/PR_EXCEL.xlsx).

![The PAROL6 print table: part, position in the arm, supports, mass, infill type and percentage, print time, cooling, layer height, top and bottom layers, perimeters](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/assets/print_table.webp){ width="1000" }

Print the pulleys with high infill and slow outer walls: their teeth carry the load. Check the first printed
pulley against a belt before printing the rest.

## Tolerances

Bearing seats and shafts are designed for a well-calibrated printer; a seat that is too tight is reamed, one
that is too loose is shimmed with tape or a drop of epoxy. Test the fit of the tapered bearings in their seats
before assembling a joint.

## Inserts

Four M3 brass inserts are melted into their holes with a soldering iron; everything else screws directly into the
plastic.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/build/mechanical-assembly/ -->

# Mechanical assembly

The assembly is documented step by step in the
[Parol building instructions PDF](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/PAROL6-Desktop-robot-arm/blob/main/Building%20instructions/Parol%20building%20instructions.pdf)
and shown in the [video playlist](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLSueoDrBt5MMTL9O8qAWZiJrNIf8-29Qz).
Read the whole manual once before you start: some steps cannot be undone without taking the joint apart again.
This page lists what to get right.

## The building instructions

<object data="../../assets/pdf/PAROL6_building_instructions.pdf#view=FitH&amp;navpanes=0" type="application/pdf" width="100%" height="820">
  <p>Your browser does not show PDFs inline: <a href="../../assets/pdf/PAROL6_building_instructions.pdf">download the building instructions (PDF, 8 MB)</a>.</p>
</object>

[Download the building instructions (PDF, 8 MB)](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/assets/pdf/PAROL6_building_instructions.pdf)

## Things to get right

- **Bearings seated square**: the tapered roller bearings carry the joint; a bearing that sits crooked makes the
  joint stiff in one direction and loose in the other.
- **Belt tension** as in the [belt tension video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=v0PYfEoIr3k): maximum hand
  force for joints 3 and 5, slightly less for 1 and 4, with the tension bearings ([Belts](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/07-maintenance/belts/)).
- **Threadlocker** on every metal-to-metal screw, blue, and on all set screws ([Couplers and threadlocker](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/07-maintenance/couplers/)).
  The couplers between motors, gearboxes and shafts are where a loose screw costs the most.
- **The limit switches and sensors** positioned so that the moving part presses the lever, or passes the sensor
  within a millimetre or two, before the joint reaches its mechanical stop.
- **Joint 1's blockers** fitted: without them joint 1 can spin a full turn and tear its wires.
- **Wires and tubes** with enough slack through each joint for its full range, and fixed so that they cannot be
  pinched by the belts.
- **Wire markings**: the print table spreadsheet's *Wire_markings* sheet lists the colour code of the motor and
  sensor cables used on the reference robots, which helps when the base is wired.

## Small print beds

The J1 turret blocker and the upper arm come split in `STL/SMALL_PRINT_BED`, with a README. Join the halves with
the dowel pins and slow epoxy, clamp them straight, and let them cure before the joint is assembled.

## Custom couplers and flanges

The repository's `custom_couplers.md` is a work in progress on machined alternatives to the shaft couplers, with
a press-fit flange; use the BOM's couplers until it is finished.

## Before the electronics

Turn every joint by hand through its range. Everything should move smoothly against the gearbox's resistance,
with no clicks and no tight spots, and every switch should click as its joint reaches it.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/build/electronics-and-wiring/ -->

# Electronics and wiring

![Four ways to destroy the control board](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/assets/board_warning.svg){ width="1000" }

The control board goes into the base with its fan and its six driver modules; the motors, switches, sensors,
the gripper connector, the E-stop and the power connector are wired to it.

## The control board

Everything about the board itself is in the [Control Board Manual](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/board/): the connectors, the pin
map, the drivers. The two things that destroy boards, both on the [Stepper drivers](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/board/05-stepper-drivers/)
page: a driver module inserted the wrong way round, and a driver without its heatsink cemented on. Read that
page before you plug anything in.

## Wiring the arm to the board

![Wiring diagram: motors, switches, sensors and connectors to the control board](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/assets/parol6v2_connection.webp){ width="750" }

- **Motors**: one four-wire cable per joint, to the terminals marked with its joint number (`J1_A+` to `J6_B-`).
- **Limit switches** (joints 2, 3, 5): one lead to 24 V, the other to the LIMIT terminal the wiring diagram shows
  in that joint's group; polarity does not matter.
- **Inductive sensors** (joints 1, 4, 6): brown to 24 V, blue to GND, black (signal) to the LIMIT terminal the
  wiring diagram shows in that joint's group.
- **The gripper connector**: 24 V, GND, CAN H and CAN L from the board to the M8 socket at the forearm.
- **The E-stop**: the NC contact to the two E-stop terminals.
- **Power**: the GX16 socket on the base to the XT30 on the board, polarity checked twice.
- **The power button**: the JST PH cable to the button connector.
- **The fan**: 5 V, three-pin, on the fan header; not a PWM fan.

Wire each switch and sensor to the terminal the diagram shows for its joint, joints 1 and 6 included, and check
each one with the test firmware's `#LIMIT` before you close the base.

The finished base looks like this:

![The wired control board in the base](../assets/WIRING V2.webp){ width="700" }

![The connectors on the base](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/assets/CONNECT.webp){ width="700" }

## Test before you close the base

Power the board with the test firmware and check every driver, switch, sensor, input and output from the serial
terminal ([The test firmware](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/board/09-test-firmware/)). It is far easier now than with the base closed and
the arm on top. You can also test your motors here, before the arm is assembled, to see that each one works.

Every control board sold by Source Robotics comes with the test firmware preloaded. It is the firmware every
board was tested with: each board is fully tested, every part of it, at the end of the production line.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/build/firmware-and-first-run/ -->

# Firmware and first run

## 1. The test firmware

A control board from the shop ships with the test firmware. Use it, with the base open and the motors not yet
driving the arm, to check every driver, every switch and sensor, and the I/O from a serial terminal: on the bench
before the arm is assembled, as in [Electronics and wiring](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/build/electronics-and-wiring/#test-before-you-close-the-base).
At power-on it prints a report on
each driver (`joint N Connection is: GOOD` or `BAD`) and turns every motor slowly; `#LIMIT` then shows the
switches and `#IO` the E-stop, the inputs and the supply voltage. [The test firmware](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/board/09-test-firmware/)
has the commands and what good output looks like.

!!! danger
    The test firmware turns all six motors slowly from the moment it boots until the power is switched off; no
    command stops them. On an assembled arm joints 1 to 5 reach their blockers within about a minute and keep
    pushing. Use it with the motors free to turn, never on an assembled robot.

!!! success "Check"
    Six `Connection is: GOOD` lines in the report; `#LIMIT` names each switch while you press it; `#IO` follows
    the E-stop and the inputs and shows the supply near 24000 mV. If not:
    [Control board troubleshooting](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/board/11-troubleshooting/).

## 2. Upload the main firmware

The main firmware is in the repository under `PAROL6 control board main software`; it is a PlatformIO project
for VS Code. Install VS Code and the PlatformIO extension, open the folder, and upload with an ST-Link through the
programming adapter, with the 24 V supply disconnected: [Firmware](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/board/08-firmware/) has the procedure and
the warnings.

!!! success "Check"
    PlatformIO ends the upload with `SUCCESS`. If not: [Control board troubleshooting](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/board/11-troubleshooting/).

## 3. First power-on

Unplug the programming adapter, plug in the supply, hold the forearm and press the button. Six clicks, and the
arm holds. Start the commander software, connect, and open the joint jog menu.

!!! success "Check"
    Six clicks, the fan runs, the arm holds itself, and the commander shows the robot's data. If not:
    [First power-on: if nothing happens](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/04-installation/first-power-on/#if-nothing-happens).

## 4. A joint turns the wrong way 

Jog each joint briefly. The joint must turn as in the figure, which shows each joint's positive direction
([Joint limits and directions](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/03-technical-data/joint-limits/)). Before homing, the commander checks jogs
against the joint limits with a position count that starts at 0, so some directions are refused with
`Error: Robot jog -> Position out of range`:

- **Joint 2**: press its **right** arrow (negative). It must turn opposite to the figure; its left arrow does
  nothing until the robot is homed.
- **Joints 1, 3, 4, 5 and 6**: press the **left** arrow (positive). It must turn as in the figure.

![Each joint turned 30 degrees in its positive direction, in colour, over the pose in grey](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/assets/kinematics/parol6_joint_directions.webp){ width="900" }
![Each joint turned 30 degrees in its positive direction, in colour, over the pose in grey](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/assets/kinematics/parol6_joint_directions_dark.webp){ width="900" }

A joint that turns the other way is the most common first-run problem, and it is fixed in the firmware, not by
rewiring:

```cpp
// motor_init.cpp, in Init_Joint_N: switch between 0 and 1
Joint__->direction_reversed = 1;
```

Upload again and check again. Swapping one motor phase's wires has the same effect, if you prefer to open the
base.

!!! success "Check"
    The left arrows of joints 1 and 3 to 6 turn them as in the figure, and joint 2's right arrow turns it the
    opposite way.

## 5. Home

With every direction right, set joint 6 and check the tool's homing offset as in
[Before you press Home](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/05-operation/homing/#before-you-press-home), then press **Home** and stay at the
E-stop. The sequence is on [Homing](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/05-operation/homing/);
if a joint grinds at a stop, press the E-stop and see [Homing failures](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/08-troubleshooting/homing-failures/).

!!! success "Check"
    Homing finishes, the simulator matches the robot, and the pin passes through the witness marks of each joint,
    which line up in the after-homing pose ([Witness marks](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/05-operation/mastering/#witness-marks)).

## The commander's terminal output

While it runs, the commander prints the robot's data to its terminal: the positions, the homed and I/O bytes,
the errors, the gripper data, and `Time between 2 commands in ms`, which should be near 0.010 (the number is in
seconds, despite the label: 0.010 is 10 ms). Watch it for a few minutes while jogging: if it is often much higher,
the PC is too slow ([Communication](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/08-troubleshooting/communication/)).

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/appendix/release-notes/ -->

# Release notes

## PAROL6

### V1 — 2025-03-08

Stable version of the PAROL6 mechanical files, code, documentation and BOM: the first tagged release of the
[robot repository](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/PAROL6-Desktop-robot-arm/releases/tag/V1). The repository's
main branch continues with BOM updates, the small print bed variants and the community projects list; the
firmware is unchanged since.

## Python API

The releases of [PCrnjak/PAROL6-python-API](https://github.com/PCrnjak/PAROL6-python-API/releases), newest first,
as published on GitHub. The tags `v0.9.0` and `v0.9.1` have no release notes on GitHub; the reference on this
site describes v0.9.1.

### v0.8.1 — 2026-09-20

A patch on **v0.8.0**: PR #51, the Cartesian streaming executor. No API changes.

#### Fixes

- **MOVECART and SERVOL hold their straight line.** Ruckig's synchronization was never set, so it defaulted to `Time` — the six tangent components only *finish* together, each taking its own time-optimal route there, and the tangent bows. The executor now runs under `Phase`, one shared profile for all six.
- **A repeated target no longer costs that synchronization.** A servo stream sets the same target every tick, and each re-plan drops to time synchronization unless the current velocity and acceleration line up exactly with the fresh profile; once out of phase the state drifts further out and the next tick fails too. Setting a target Ruckig is already tracking is now a no-op. On a 160 mm diagonal: 4.7 mm off the line before, 0.000 mm after.
- **The speed ceilings are TCP speeds again.** Ruckig bounds each component on its own, so an isotropic envelope let a diagonal run the resultant up to sqrt(3) times the configured limit — 1.35x as measured. The per-component ceilings are now scaled by the motion direction's largest component over its norm, and the same move peaks at exactly the 0.160 m/s jog ceiling.

### v0.8.0 — 2026-09-19

Everything since **v0.7.0**: PRs #41–#48, the PAROL6 side of waldoctl v0.14.0's skill runtime, full TCP calibration, bounded I/O, execution speed, demonstration metadata, held-object geometry and supervised restart. Pre-1.0, so breaking changes bump the minor.

#### Breaking changes

- **The waldoctl pin moves v0.12.0 → v0.14.0.** `set_tcp_transform`/`tcp_transform` and `set_execution_speed`/`pause`/`resume` are required of every client there and implemented here.
- **Completion waits query the exact command result** (#47, #48), and client and controller must both speak the new query. A controller session change during a wait raises `ConnectionError`; unknown, cancelled and expired results stay unconfirmed instead of passing for success, and replies to timed-out queries are filtered by response type.
- **TCP queries fail explicitly when the controller does not answer** (#43) rather than returning a stale value.
- **Unconfirmed blocking motion completion raises `TimeoutError`** (#45); the queued motion stays until it completes or is stopped.

#### Skills

- **Python skills run on the connected client** (#41). Decorated skills go through the existing synchronous connection and event loop, can use the typed PAROL6 async client internally, compose nested calls, and run unchanged under Commander's stepping wrapper. Live and dry-run clients advertise their skill capabilities. Stopping a planned trajectory now clears the segment player's activity, so status no longer sits at EXECUTING after a cancel.
- **Gripper skills discover PAROL6 gripper support** on the live client and native preview (#42); the preview tool exposes its key and type as metadata, so a requirement check cannot dispatch a command. Streaming updates preserve unread configuration, query and stop packets across a polling batch boundary.

#### Setup and calibration

- **Full TCP transforms through planning and readback** (#43). Translation and intrinsic XYZ orientation are queued, applied and confirmed before use; earlier queued motion keeps its frame, cancelled corrections do not leak into planning, and a tool/variant change clears the correction. The XYZ API stays and clears user rotation. Tool status reports its applied variant, so a calibration cannot silently bind to different jaws.
- **Bounded digital I/O** (#44). Reads and writes take a per-call deadline covering endpoint setup and retries; a missing read returns `None`, an unconfirmed write raises `TimeoutError`, and neither is mistaken for cancellation. Both facades advertise `io.digital`; dry-run output writes use logical indices and report dispatch errors.

#### Motion

- **Queued execution speed and explicit pause/resume** (#45). `set_execution_speed(0.1..1.0)` retimes the planned joint path; `pause()` decelerates to a hold with the queue retained and `resume()` continues at the selected speed, and changing speed while paused keeps the hold. Rate changes are checked against acceleration derived from the emitted positions, with preallocated buffers in the control loop; queued dwell pauses, while jog and servo-stream timing stay separate. Preview retimes durations and reports paused operations as unresolved. Physical transition tuning is unverified.
- **Held-object geometry under the flange** (#47). Only declared contact pairs are exempt; attach/detach requires confirmed whole-world application and invalid contact names keep the previous geometry. Reference or controller-context changes invalidate declarations and gate arm motion until explicit reconciliation or removal. The controller retains 1024 successful indices, including every command consumed by a blend.

#### Status surface

- **Session and timing metadata on every status frame** (#46): a nonzero session id, publication sequence and monotonic snapshot timestamp, so a client can record observation cadence and detect a controller restart. Missing metadata is explicitly unavailable. The offline client's no-tool identity matches the native controller.
- **Queue readback includes accepted commands** still waiting for planning or paused (#48), and clears completed or cancelled indices, so a supervised restart can tell whether the controller still has pending work. Restart detection also watches status broadcasts when the command socket goes quiet after a peer reset.

#### Dependencies

- **interpolatepy is gone.** Both profiles it supplied were only ever asked for rest-to-rest motion, so the trapezoidal and quintic curves are now evaluated here in closed form, across a numpy array rather than one Python call per sample. Positions match the previous output to within a thousandth of a motor step. This also removes a compiled dependency that, as of its 3.3.0, ships no Windows or Python 3.14 wheels.

### v0.7.0 — 2026-09-04

Everything since **0.3.2**, the last release. Four tags landed in between without notes, so this collects them. Pre-1.0, so breaking changes bump the minor.

#### Breaking changes

- **`RobotError` comes from waldoctl** rather than being defined here. A frontend represents a refusal the same way whichever backend raised it. It is an exception now, not a frozen dataclass, so a client can raise it as-is; anything that built one positionally or called `dataclasses.replace` on it needs updating. Tool-error attribution rebuilds the error from its wire form for exactly that reason.
- **`stop`, `estop` and `reset` replace `halt` and `resume`**, and a stop cancels the whole motion pipeline rather than just the active command.
- **`home(calibrate=)` replaces the separate CALIBRATE command.** Unhomed, or with `calibrate=True`, the arm runs the full end-stop referencing sequence; already homed, it takes a planned collision-checked move back to standby.
- **Planned motion is refused while unhomed.** Jogging stays available.
- **The waldoctl pin moves v0.7.0 → v0.12.0**, which removes the `Plane` keep-out shape. Persisted worlds containing a plane now raise on load.

#### Status surface

- **The control loop broadcasts its own health.** The p99 period and the deadline-miss count ride every STATUS frame in a `loop_health` mapping, so a display no longer polls the loop-statistics query for them. `drive_health` sits beside it and stays empty on this backend: the drives report per-joint error flags, not analog registers, and empty distinguishes "no such sensor" from "all zero".
- **`StatusBuffer`, homing progress and loop statistics conform to waldoctl**, and homing progress now survives a cancel.
- **A hardware e-stop disables the controller**, rather than only halting motion.

#### Motion

- **Trajectory settling is gated on progress, not elapsed ticks.**
- **Fast-path home**: an already-referenced arm takes a planned return move instead of re-running the firmware seek.
- **Command indices stay monotonic across a reset.**
- **The dry-run snapshot carries the pending blend chain**, so a preview mid-blend matches what the runtime will execute.

#### Fixes and hygiene

- A system command's `Command_out` was clobbered in the same tick by the executor fallback.
- The MSG gripper is seated on the flange rather than inside the wrist, and its built-in camera mount is declared.
- Test fixes surfaced by loaded runners: the unreachable-client test takes a free port instead of adding to the live one, which overflowed past 65535; the loop-health comparison waits for a frame that has caught up instead of demanding two samples of a climbing counter be equal.
- Typing: scipy stubs pinned per Python version, stale suppressions dropped, sync tool wrappers typed as `SyncTool`.

### v0.2.7 — 2026-05-14

First release with `setuptools_scm`-managed versioning. `pip install git+...@v0.2.7` now resolves to the matching version directly (no auto-bump dance, no tag/metadata drift).

#### Changes since v0.2.6

- Switch to `setuptools_scm` for dynamic versioning. The git tag is now the source of truth for the package version; `pyproject.toml` no longer carries a static `version = "..."` line. Removes `[tool.tbump]` and the `release.yml` workflow that auto-bumped on tag publish.

---

*Release notes written by Claude on the author's behalf.*

### v0.2.6 — 2026-05-14

#### Bug fixes

- Electric-gripper stall detection: terminate on stall when grasping, ignore PID hunting on clamped jaws, keep `move_active` set so subsequent commands don't short-circuit.
- `SetTcpOffset` now routes through the motion-planner subprocess (was applied controller-side only, leaving the planner with stale IK seeds).
- Failed tool actions clear stale error state and `command_index` so subsequent commands aren't blocked.
- `RobotClient.async_client` property removed (cross-loop foot-gun). Async users construct `AsyncRobotClient` directly. Minor API break.

#### Kinematics / motion

- TOPP-RA trajectory shake: njit'd IK-outlier smoother (median-filters IK output), denser IK sampling, sim-dt jitter fix.
- IK `max_iter` bumped 10 → 20 to help wrist-near-singular targets converge.
- Deterministic wrist-flip restart for IK branches that converge outside joint limits.

#### Dependencies

- pinokin pin bumped v0.1.5 → v0.1.6.

*Release notes written by Claude on the author's behalf.*

# Versions and compatibility

| PAROL6 release | Released | Control board | Control board firmware | Python API (parol6) | Commander software | Grippers | Docs |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 2025-03-08 | v2.0 (pluggable terminal blocks); v1.2 (spring contacts) is functionally identical | 1 (VERSION 1 in constants.h), main branch | 0.2.6 to 0.9.1 (the reference describes 0.9.1); Python 3.11 or newer | main branch (Python 3.10 or 3.11) | SSG-48 (Spectral Micro firmware 101 or newer), MSG (STEPFOC firmware 103 or newer), pneumatic MHZ2-16D, vacuum | 1 |

## Reading the table

- **Control board** v2.0 has pluggable terminal blocks; v1.2 had spring-loaded contacts. They are functionally
  identical and run the same firmware.
- **Control board firmware** is released with the robot (`#define VERSION 1`). The serial protocol it speaks is
  the one every PC program on this site uses.
- **Python API**: the reference on this site is read from the version named on the Programming landing page.
  Older 0.x versions have fewer commands; the API is pre-1.0, so a minor version can change an interface, as the
  [release notes](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/appendix/release-notes/) say.
- **Commander software** has no releases; the main branch is what you clone. The `experimental_kinematics` branch
  fixes most Cartesian jogging errors but can make dangerous moves: main is the safe one.
- **Grippers**: the firmware's gripper protocol works with every released firmware of both grippers.

# Community projects

Software, hardware modifications and experiments built around PAROL6 by its community. They are third-party
projects, not maintained by Source Robotics: use them at your own risk and check each one's licence and
documentation. The list is kept in the robot repository's
[community_projects.md](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/PAROL6-Desktop-robot-arm/blob/main/community_projects.md),
where a pull request adds yours.

## Control software and GUIs

| Project | What it is |
|---|---|
| [Waldo Commander](https://github.com/Jepson2k/Waldo-Commander) | A browser-based commander: Python programs with an editor and debugger, 3D simulation, teach by demonstration, and an MCP server so that an LLM can drive the arm. Built on the Python API through the waldoctl abstraction |
| [Parol6_Better_Command](https://github.com/thousands-star/Parol6_Better_Command) | The commander software refactored for easier editing, with vision |
| [PAROL6 Pilot](https://github.com/jointAxis77/pilot) | A web GUI |
| [PAROL6_GUI](https://github.com/jakubgrzebien1234-creator/PAROL6_GUI) | An alternative desktop GUI |
| [parol6_commander](https://github.com/Lyczko0/parol6_commander) | A web GUI on NiceGUI, ROS 2 and MoveIt 2, for calibrating, jogging and programming |
| [Parol6-firmware](https://github.com/Lyczko0/Parol6-firmware) | Alternative motion firmware for a Teensy 4.1 with ROS 2 over micro-ROS |
| [parol6_ros2_control](https://github.com/grahas/parol6_ros2_control) | The `ros2_control` hardware interface and bridge used by the MoveIt configuration's real-robot launch |

## Vision and AI

| Project | What it is |
|---|---|
| [PAROL6-Python-API-Gemini-Vision](https://github.com/AlvarEhr/PAROL6-Python-API-Gemini-Vision-Public) | Controlling PAROL6 with the Gemini LLM and a camera |
| [Tic-Tac-Toe-Robot-Project-Parol6](https://github.com/lennardkiebler-cryptoii/Tic-Tac-Toe-Robot-Project-Parol6) | A vision-guided tic-tac-toe player |

## Hardware

| Project | What it is |
|---|---|
| [parol6-printed-eg17](https://github.com/Pixelgamer4k/parol6-printed-eg17) | A printed gearbox alternative |

## The legacy Python API

[PAROL6-python-API-Alvar](https://github.com/PCrnjak/PAROL6-python-API-Alvar) is the first Python API, a
headless commander with a text-over-UDP client, kept as it is for the projects built on it. New work should use
the [current Python API](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/programming/02-python-api/).

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/terminology/ -->

# Glossary

**After-homing pose**
:   Where homing leaves the robot: the standby pose turned 90° about joint 1, joints at 90°, −90°, 180°, 0°, 0°,
    180°. The firmware (`standby_position`) and the Python API (`STANDBY_ANGLES_DEG`) call this pose standby. The
    witness marks line up in it.

**Blending** (blend radius)
:   Passing through a waypoint without stopping: the path cuts the corner within the given radius. The Python
    API's `r` parameter.

**Commander software**
:   Source Robotics' desktop program for PAROL6: a GUI with jogging, a simulator, a program editor for RBTscript,
    I/O and gripper control, talking to the control board over USB.

**Control board**
:   The electronics inside the base: an STM32 microcontroller, six TMC5160 stepper drivers, the inputs, outputs,
    E-stop input, CAN and USB. It runs the low-level firmware; the PC runs the high-level software.

**Controller** (Python API)
:   The `parol6-server` process: it talks to the control board over serial at 100 Hz, plans the motion and accepts
    commands over UDP from any number of clients.

**Direction, positive**
:   The direction in which a joint's angle increases, shown in the figure on *Joint limits and directions*. The
    commander's left arrows jog positive.

**E-stop**
:   The normally closed button on the base. Pressing it, unplugging it or cutting its wire opens the circuit, and
    the robot stops. It must be connected for the robot to run.

**Firmware**
:   The program on the control board. The *main* firmware runs the robot with the PC software; the *test* firmware
    checks the board and the wiring from a serial terminal.

**Flange**
:   The mounting face at the end of joint 6, where the tool is screwed on. With nothing on it, the TCP is the
    flange face.

**Forearm** (lower arm)
:   The link from the elbow (joint 3) to the wrist. It carries joint 4. Forearm and lower arm mean the same link.

**Homing** (referencing)
:   Finding each joint's position after power-up by driving it to its limit switch or sensor, then moving a known
    number of steps to the after-homing pose. Needed after every power-up; the robot does not know where it is
    before.

**Jogging**
:   Moving a joint, or the tool along an axis, at a chosen speed for as long as a button is held or a command
    repeats.

**Joint names**
:   Joints 1 to 6 by number, from the base up. Other names for the same joints: base, shoulder and elbow for 1 to
    3, and wrist 1, wrist 2 and wrist 3 for 4 to 6, as in the robot model and ROS.

**Limit switch, inductive sensor**
:   The references for homing: mechanical switches on joints 2, 3 and 5, inductive sensors on joints 1, 4 and 6.

**Mastering**
:   Fine-tuning the number of steps from a joint's limit switch to its witness mark, so that a homed robot stands
    exactly in the after-homing pose.

**Motion profile**
:   The shape of the speed curve of a move: trapezoidal, polynomial, time-optimal, and so on. The Python API
    offers several; the commander uses trapezoidal and quintic polynomial.

**Parked pose**
:   The arm folded in over the base, joints 2 and 3 toward their limit switches: how the robot rests when it is
    off, and the pose to switch off in, since the arm has the least distance to fall from it. The commander's
    **Park** button writes a program that moves there (90°, −144.683°, 108.171°, 2.222°, 25.003°, 180°).

**Pose**
:   The position and the orientation of the tool together: six numbers, x, y, z in millimetres and three angles in
    degrees. The standby, after-homing and parked poses are poses of the whole arm, given as six joint angles.

**RBTscript**
:   The commander software's program language: one command per line, `MoveJoint`, `MoveCart`, `Delay`, `Gripper`
    and so on.

**Standby pose**
:   The pose of the Denavit-Hartenberg table and the reference of the joint angles: joints at 0°, −90°, 180°, 0°,
    0°, 180°, the upper arm vertical, the forearm horizontal, the arm pointing away from the electronics case at
    the back of the base.
    After homing the robot stands in it turned 90° about joint 1 (joint 1 at 90°): the after-homing pose,
    which the Python API calls its standby.

**Stepper motor**
:   The motors of PAROL6: open-loop motors that move in steps, 200 full steps per turn, 6400 with the 32
    microsteps the control board uses. The position is counted, not measured.

**Test firmware**
:   The firmware every control board from the shop carries when it ships. It reports each driver at power-on and
    answers a few text commands (`#LIMIT`, `#IO`) from a serial terminal, and it turns all six motors slowly from
    the moment it starts until the power is switched off. Replace it with the main firmware before the robot is
    used ([The test firmware](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/board/09-test-firmware/)).

**TCP** (tool center point)
:   The point on the tool the robot positions and the origin of the tool frame. Selecting a tool in the software
    sets it; an offset moves it.

**TRF, WRF**
:   The tool reference frame, fixed to the tool, and the world reference frame, fixed to the base. Cartesian jogs
    and relative moves can be made in either.

**Upper arm**
:   The link from the shoulder (joint 2) to the elbow (joint 3).

**Witness marks**
:   Holes in the printed parts of neighbouring links that line up, so that a pin passes through, when the joint
    stands exactly in the after-homing pose.

**Wrist 1, wrist 2, wrist 3**
:   Other names for joints 4, 5 and 6. See *Joint names*.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/cad-files/ -->

# Downloads and files

Everything to download for PAROL6, at the versions these pages describe. The versions come from one file,
`versions.yml`, so this page changes with them; which versions work together is in
[Versions and compatibility](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/appendix/compatibility/).

## Firmware and software

| What | Version | Download | How to install |
|---|---|---|---|
| Control board firmware, a PlatformIO project | [V1](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/PAROL6-Desktop-robot-arm/tree/V1) | [PAROL6 control board main software](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/PAROL6-Desktop-robot-arm/tree/V1/PAROL6%20control%20board%20main%20software) | [Firmware](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/board/08-firmware/) |
