# PAROL6 Control Board Manual

![The PAROL6 control board v2.0](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/assets/PAROL6V2.webp)

<div class="doc-meta" markdown>

**Document number:** SR-2002

**PAROL6 release:** 1

**Revision:** 2026.A

**Published:** 2026-11-03

**Applies to:** PAROL6 control board v2.0 and v1.2, PAROL6 release 1

*Original instructions*

</div>

The PAROL6 control board is the controller of the PAROL6 arm: a 32-bit microcontroller, six stepper drivers, the
inputs and outputs, the E-stop input, CAN and USB on a board the size of a pack of playing cards, which is what
lets PAROL6 run without a control cabinet. This manual covers the board itself: its specifications, connectors
and pinout, the stepper drivers and their installation, the I/O and E-stop wiring, the CAN bus, uploading the
firmware, the test firmware, and the serial protocol the PC software uses. How the robot is used is in the
[Robot Manual](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/); how it is programmed in the [Programming Guide](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/programming/).

<div class="grid cards" markdown>

-   :material-chip: **The board**

    ---

    [Overview](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/board/01-overview/), [Safety](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/board/02-safety/), [Technical data](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/board/03-technical-data/),
    [Connectors and pinout](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/board/04-connectors/), [Stepper drivers](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/board/05-stepper-drivers/).

-   :material-electric-switch: **Wiring**

    ---

    [Inputs, outputs and E-stop](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/board/06-io-and-estop/), [CAN bus](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/board/07-can/).

-   :material-upload: **Firmware**

    ---

    [Uploading the firmware](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/board/08-firmware/), [the test firmware](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/board/09-test-firmware/),
    [the serial protocol](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/board/10-serial-protocol/), [troubleshooting](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/board/11-troubleshooting/).

</div>


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/board/01-overview/ -->

# 1. Overview

The control board sits in the base of PAROL6 and does the low-level work: it generates the step pulses for six
stepper motors, runs the homing sequence, reads the limit switches, the inputs and the E-stop, switches the
outputs, drives an electric gripper over CAN, and exchanges a data packet with the PC over USB 100 times a
second. It plans nothing: the PC computes every trajectory and sends the board the joint speeds and positions
to execute, cycle by cycle.

![Features of the control board](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/assets/img_parol.webp){ width="750" }

It works out of the box with PAROL6 and the commander software or the Python API, and it drives any six-axis
stepper arm that is wired like PAROL6.

## Versions

| Version | Status | Difference |
|---|---|---|
| **v2.0** | Current, in the shop | Pluggable terminal block connectors |
| v1.2 | Discontinued | Spring-loaded Phoenix contacts |

The two are functionally identical and run the same firmware.

![Control board v2.0](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/assets/PAROL6V2.webp){ width="600" }

![Control board v1.2 (discontinued)](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/assets/PCB1.webp){ width="600" }

## Testing

Every board is tested end to end before it ships, and comes with the test firmware preloaded, so that you can
check the wiring of your robot before the main firmware goes on ([The test firmware](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/board/09-test-firmware/)).

## Where it is published

The firmware, main and test, is in the robot repository:
[PAROL6 control board main software](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/PAROL6-Desktop-robot-arm/tree/V1/PAROL6%20control%20board%20main%20software)
and [PAROL6 control board test code](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/PAROL6-Desktop-robot-arm/tree/V1/PAROL6%20control%20board%20test%20code).
The board is sold [in the shop](https://source-robotics.com/products/parol6-control-board).

The board schematics and PCB design are not available as open source materials due to licensing agreements and
confidentiality terms established with our development partners. These proprietary design elements are subject
to contractual obligations that restrict their public distribution.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/board/02-safety/ -->

# 2. Safety

![Four ways to destroy the control board](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/assets/board_warning.svg){ width="1000" }

!!! danger "Four ways to destroy the board"
    1. **A stepper driver module inserted the wrong way round.** Check the orientation against the DIAG pins
       before the first power-on ([Stepper drivers](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/board/05-stepper-drivers/)).
    2. **A driver without its heatsink cemented on.** The TMC5160 modules need the heatsink and the fan.
    3. **An ST-Link connected with jumper wires without the programming adapter.** Use the adapter, or only
       the four pins named on [Firmware](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/board/08-firmware/).
    4. **Reversed supply polarity.** The XT30 power input has no reverse-polarity protection.

- The board runs on 24 V, which is safe to touch; the power supply you connect it to is the mains device.
- The outputs switch up to 1 A at up to 48 V; the inputs take up to 50 V. The isolation between them and the
  robot holds only if you power them from an isolated supply ([Inputs, outputs and E-stop](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/board/06-io-and-estop/)).
- The E-stop input is read by the firmware and acted on by the PC software; it does not cut the motor power
  ([Emergency stop](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/02-safety/emergency-stop/) in the Robot Manual).
- With 3.3 V on the programming header the board turns on when the supply is connected and cannot be switched
  off with the button. Disconnect the 24 V supply before you connect the programmer.
- The drivers are hot after use; the fan must run whenever the motors are energised.
- Static electricity damages the microcontroller and the drivers. Unplug the supply and touch earthed metal
  before you handle the board or a driver module, and hold them by the edges.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/board/03-technical-data/ -->

# 3. Technical data

## Hardware

| | |
|---|---|
| Microcontroller | STM32F446RE: Arm Cortex-M4 with DSP and FPU, 180 MHz, 512 KB flash |
| Stepper drivers | 6 × TMC5160 modules, SPI configured, 10 to 35 V, with stall, short and temperature protection; currents below |
| Microstepping | 32 (set by the firmware) |
| Inputs | 2, isolated, 12 to 50 V, 24 V nominal |
| Outputs | 2, isolated, 48 V maximum, 0.5 A continuous, 1 A peak; 2 A fuse for the non-isolated mode |
| E-stop | One input on a dedicated pin, two connectors in parallel, normally closed contact |
| CAN | 2 controllers; CAN 1 with its transceiver, CAN 2 transceiver not populated |
| USB | USB 2.0 full speed, a virtual serial port; the PC software opens it at 3 000 000 baud, a setting USB ignores |
| Additional memory | W25Q64FV SPI flash, 64 Mbit |
| Programming | SWD through the 2×5-pin header (ST-Link with the programming adapter) |
| Fan | 5 V, 3-pin header, 0.3 A maximum, not PWM |
| Power button | Soft switch: the button tells the firmware to switch the 24 V stage on and off |
| Supply voltage | 18 V minimum, 24 V maximum; 24 V is recommended for optimal robot performance |
| Supply voltage sense | The firmware reads the supply voltage (VBUS) |
| Size | Three M3 mounting holes; dimensions in the drawing below |

## Operating limits

| | |
|---|---|
| Stepper driver rated current | 2.5 A per motor |
| Stepper driver maximum current | 3.6 A, short bursts or with extreme cooling only |
| Driver overtemperature | The driver shuts its outputs down and its joint goes limp; firmware 1 does not tell the PC |
| Isolated input voltage | 12 V minimum, 24 V nominal, 50 V maximum |
| Isolated output voltage | 48 V maximum |
| Isolated output current | 1 A maximum |
| Fan current | 0.3 A maximum; around 0.1 A recommended |

The PAROL6 firmware runs the motors well below the drivers' ratings: 0.8 to 1.7 A ([Currents and temperatures](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/03-technical-data/operating-temperatures/)).

## Dimensions

![PCB dimensions in millimetres](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/assets/PCB_dimensions.webp){ width="700" }

## Mounting and cooling

Three M3 holes. The drivers need active cooling: a 40 × 40 × 20 mm 5 V fan, a Noctua NF-A4x20 or any 5 V fan of
that size that is not PWM controlled, blowing over the heatsinks. In PAROL6 the fan sits in the base's fan cover.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/board/04-connectors/ -->

# 4. Connectors and pinout

![The connections of the control board](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/assets/img_parol3.webp){ width="750" }

## Connectors

| Connection | Connector |
|---|---|
| 24 V power | XT30 male |
| Cooling fan | 3-pin, 2.54 mm pitch, 5 V |
| Power button | JST PH 4-pin (B4B-PH-SM4-TB) |
| USB | USB type B |
| Programming | 2×5-pin, 2.54 mm pitch (SWD) |
| Motors | 6 × 4-pin terminal blocks, one per driver |
| Limit switches, inputs, outputs, E-stop, CAN, 24 V out, GND, HV_SEL, GND_SEL | Pluggable terminal blocks along the edges |
| CAN termination | Two jumpers, CAN1 JUMPER and CAN2 JUMPER: on, each connects a 120 Ω resistor across its bus ([CAN bus](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/board/07-can/)) |

## Pin definitions

The microcontroller pins as the firmware defines them (`iodefs.h`), for anyone who writes firmware or probes the
board:

```c
#define PUL1 PC6     // step, joint 1          #define DIR1 PB15    // direction, joint 1
#define PUL2 PA10    // step, joint 5          #define DIR2 PA1     // direction, joint 5
#define PUL3 PC0     // step, joint 6          #define DIR3 PC1     // direction, joint 6
#define PUL4 PC3     // step, joint 4          #define DIR4 PA0     // direction, joint 4
#define PUL5 PC9     // step, joint 3          #define DIR5 PA8     // direction, joint 3
#define PUL6 PC5     // step, joint 2          #define DIR6 PB1     // direction, joint 2

#define SELECT1 PC7  // SPI chip select of driver 1 (joint 1)
#define SELECT2 PA9  // driver 2 (joint 5)
#define SELECT3 PC15 // driver 3 (joint 6)
#define SELECT4 PC2  // driver 4 (joint 4)
#define SELECT5 PC8  // driver 5 (joint 3)
#define SELECT6 PC4  // driver 6 (joint 2)
#define GLOBAL_ENABLE PA3   // ENABLE of all drivers

#define LIMIT1 PC12  // limit input of joint 6      #define LIMIT4 PD2   // limit input of joint 4
#define LIMIT2 PB3   // limit input of joint 2      #define LIMIT5 PB4   // limit input of joint 5
#define LIMIT3 PA15  // limit input of joint 3      #define LIMIT6 PC11  // limit input of joint 1

#define MISO PA6, MOSI PA7, SCK PA5   // SPI to the six drivers and the flash
#define FLASH_SELECT PA4              // chip select of the flash memory

#define LED1 PB2, LED2 PB10           // the two LEDs
#define SUPPLY_ON_OFF PC10            // switches the 24 V power stage
#define SUPPLY_BUTTON_STATE PC14      // reads the power button
#define INPUT1 PB6, INPUT2 PB5        // IN1, IN2 terminals
#define OUTPUT1 PC13, OUTPUT2 PB7     // OUT1, OUT2 terminals
#define ESTOP PB14                    // E-stop terminals
#define VBUS PB0                      // supply voltage sense
#define USB_D_PLUS PA12, USB_D_MINUS PA11
#define CAN1TX PB9, CAN1RX PB8        // CAN 1 (the gripper bus)
#define CAN1TX PB13, CAN1RX PB12      // CAN 2's pins (transceiver not populated)
```

`iodefs.h` defines `CAN1TX` and `CAN1RX` twice, the second time with CAN 2's pins, PB13 and PB12. The CAN driver
does not use these names: `CANInit()` in `CAN.cpp` picks the pins itself.

## Wiring the robot

![Wiring diagram of the robot to the control board](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/assets/parol6v2_connection.webp){ width="750" }

Limit switches to 24 V and their LIMIT terminal; inductive sensors to 24 V, GND and the LIMIT terminal (brown,
blue, black). The gripper's M8 socket to 24 V, GND, CAN H and CAN L. The finished wiring in PAROL6's base:

![The wired board](../assets/WIRING V2.webp){ width="650" }

![The connectors at the base](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/assets/CONNECT.webp){ width="650" }


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/board/05-stepper-drivers/ -->

# 5. Stepper drivers

![Four ways to destroy the control board](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/assets/board_warning.svg){ width="1000" }

The board takes six TMC5160 driver modules in the StepStick format, configured over SPI by the firmware.

!!! danger "Orientation"
    A driver module inserted the wrong way round destroys the board the moment power is applied, permanently.
    The orientation is given by the two DIAG pins: they must point at the red arrows in the figure. Check all six
    before every power-on after the drivers were touched.

![Driver orientation: the DIAG pins at the red arrows](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/assets/img_parol2.webp){ width="800" }

## Which drivers

Only the TMC5160 modules listed in the [BOM](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/build/bill-of-materials/) are tested; a board bought with
drivers has them fitted. A module from elsewhere must have the pinout in the figure, and:

- **Remove the two DIAG pins** if they are soldered: the capacitors on the board are in their way and the
  module will not seat.
- **Cement the heatsink** to the driver with thermal cement (not paste, not tape); a driver without a bonded
  heatsink overheats and fails, and takes the board with it.

![The TMC5160 module pinout](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/assets/stick.webp){ width="450" }

## Current

The firmware sets each driver's running and holding current for its joint ([Currents and temperatures](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/03-technical-data/operating-temperatures/)
and [Firmware parameters](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/reference/firmware-parameters/)). The modules' potentiometer, if they have one, is
not used.

## Cooling

The fan over the heatsinks must run whenever the motors are energised. A driver that gets too hot shuts its outputs
down and its joint goes limp, and firmware 1 does not tell the PC; in PAROL6's base with the fan they stay far
below that.

## Checking a driver

The test firmware reads every driver over SPI about three seconds after power-on and prints whether it answers
(`joint N Connection is: GOOD` or `BAD`) with its currents and fault flags, then turns every motor slowly
([The test firmware](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/board/09-test-firmware/)). A driver that does not answer is not seated, dead, or in the wrong
slot.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/board/06-io-and-estop/ -->

# 6. Inputs, outputs and E-stop

## The isolated I/O

Two inputs and two outputs on optocouplers, with their own supply rails **HV_SEL** and **GND_SEL** on the terminal
blocks. You decide what feeds those rails:

=== "Isolated supply"
    An external supply's negative to GND_SEL, positive to HV_SEL. The I/O then runs at that voltage, 24 V nominal
    and at least 12 V for the inputs, and a short or a surge on a sensor cannot reach the robot's electronics.

    ![Isolated supply wiring](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/assets/Ext_supply.webp){ width="650" }

=== "The robot's 24 V"
    Link the board's 24 V and GND terminals to HV_SEL and GND_SEL. The I/O shares the robot's supply, with a 2 A
    fuse protecting the outputs. Simpler, and enough for a pneumatic valve.

    ![Non-isolated wiring](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/assets/Internal_24V.webp){ width="650" }

The E-stop is on the robot's own supply in both cases.

### Inputs

Between HV_SEL and IN1 or IN2: a switch, a push button, a relay contact, or the signal of a sensor fed from HV_SEL
and GND_SEL. 12 to 50 V. The firmware reads them every cycle and reports them in the I/O byte of the packet.

### Outputs

Between GND_SEL and OUT1 or OUT2: a relay coil, a valve, a lamp. 0.5 A continuous, 1 A peak, 48 V maximum, with
a flyback diode across any coil. The firmware sets them from the I/O byte of the PC's packet.

## The E-stop

Two connectors on the same input, for a normally closed contact. The firmware reads the input every cycle and
reports it in the I/O byte; the PC software stops the robot when it sees the contact open ([Emergency stop](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/02-safety/emergency-stop/)).

![E-stop wiring](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/assets/ESTOP_CON.webp){ width="800" }

- The contact must be **normally closed**: an open circuit means stop, so an unplugged button or a cut wire stops
  the robot too. A normally open button does not work.
- Both connectors share one microcontroller pin: a second button goes in series on the other connector.
- Any NC switch works for a bench setup. The BOM's 19 mm E-stop and the printed housing go on the base.

## The power button

A momentary push button with an LED, on the JST PH connector. A press switches the 24 V stage on; a press while
on switches it off. The LED is fed from the button connector. The firmware reads the button on every pass of
its main loop.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/board/07-can/ -->

# 7. CAN bus

| | |
|---|---|
| CAN 1 | Transceiver fitted; terminals CAN H and CAN L; the gripper bus in PAROL6 |
| CAN 2 | Controller on the microcontroller, transceiver not populated |
| Bit rate | 1 Mbit/s, set by the firmware |
| Termination | One jumper per bus, **CAN1 JUMPER** and **CAN2 JUMPER**: with the jumper on, a 120 Ω resistor is connected between CAN H and CAN L; with it off, the bus is not terminated on the board |

In PAROL6, CAN 1 runs with 24 V and GND to the M8 socket at the forearm. The firmware addresses one gripper at the
CAN ID the PC's packet names (0 as the grippers ship), sends it a move, a calibrate, a clear-error or an empty
status frame every cycle, and relays its answer to the PC: [CAN bus](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/06-peripherals/can-bus/) in the Robot
Manual, and the gripper manuals for the messages themselves.

A CAN bus is terminated at both of its ends, 120 Ω at each. In PAROL6 the ends are the board, with its
CAN1 jumper, and the gripper, with its own termination switch. Nodes in the middle of a longer bus stay
unterminated. The jumpers are on the board figure in [Connectors and pinout](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/board/04-connectors/).


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/board/08-firmware/ -->

# 8. Firmware

Two firmware programs exist for the board, both in the robot repository as PlatformIO projects:

| | Folder | For |
|---|---|---|
| **Main firmware** | `PAROL6 control board main software` | Running the robot with the commander software or the Python API |
| **Test firmware** | `PAROL6 control board test code` | Checking the board and the wiring from a serial terminal ([The test firmware](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/board/09-test-firmware/)) |

A board from the shop carries the test firmware. Upload the main firmware before you use the robot.

## Tools

1. [VS Code](https://code.visualstudio.com/) with the **PlatformIO** extension from its marketplace.
2. A clone of the [robot repository](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/PAROL6-Desktop-robot-arm).
3. An **ST-Link** programmer and the [PAROL6 programming adapter](https://source-robotics.com/products/parol6-programming-adapter),
   or an ST-Link whose cable carries exactly SWCLK, SWDIO, GND and 3V3 to the pins of the 2×5 header in the
   table below.
4. On Windows, the [ST-Link USB driver (STSW-LINK009)](https://www.st.com/en/development-tools/stsw-link009.html)
   if PlatformIO cannot find the programmer.

!!! danger
    Use the programming adapter, or the four named pins only. An ST-Link wired to the header with jumper wires
    without the adapter has destroyed boards: other pins of the header are not for it.

The 2×5 programming header, as labelled in the side view of the [connections figure](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/board/04-connectors/), left to
right, the header to the left of the USB port:

| Row | | | | | |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Top | RESET | BOOT0 | **SWDIO** | none | **3V3** |
| Bottom | **GND** | GND | **CLK** (SWCLK) | none | 3V3 |

An ST-Link needs four of them: SWDIO, CLK, GND and 3V3. Leave RESET and BOOT0 unconnected.

## Uploading

1. **Disconnect the 24 V supply** from the robot.
2. Connect the adapter to the 2×5 header next to the USB port, and the ST-Link to the PC. The adapter supplies
   3.3 V, which powers the microcontroller (not the motors) and turns the board on.
3. In VS Code, **Open Folder** on the firmware's folder. PlatformIO downloads the toolchain the first time.
4. Build and **Upload** (the arrow in PlatformIO's toolbar). The upload takes a few seconds.
5. Disconnect the adapter. With it connected, the board cannot be switched off with the button and turns on by
   itself when the supply is connected.
6. Reconnect the 24 V supply and press the power button.

!!! success "Check"
    PlatformIO ends the upload with `SUCCESS`, and after step 6 the drivers click and the PC software
    connects. If not: [Troubleshooting](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/board/11-troubleshooting/).

## Version

`#define VERSION 1` in `constants.h`. The firmware is released with the robot (tag V1) and has not changed since;
the protocol it speaks is on [The serial protocol](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/board/10-serial-protocol/).


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/board/09-test-firmware/ -->

# 9. The test firmware

The test firmware turns the board into a bench instrument. At power-on it checks the six stepper drivers over SPI
and prints the result, then turns all six motors slowly, blinks the LEDs and toggles the two outputs; on request it
prints the E-stop, the inputs, the supply voltage and the limit switches over USB. It is what every board ships
with, and the right tool for a freshly wired robot before the base is closed.

!!! danger "The motors turn as soon as it starts"
    The test firmware enables all six drivers when it boots and turns every motor slowly, at 1000 steps per second,
    without being asked, with no limits and no homing, until the power is switched off. No command stops them:
    `#STOP` only ends a printout. Use it with the arm free to move or the motors unmounted, never on a robot folded
    against its stops.

## Connecting

Upload the firmware if the board does not have it ([Firmware](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/board/08-firmware/)), then open a serial terminal on the
board's USB port: PlatformIO's monitor, PuTTY or `screen`. The board is a USB device, so the baud rate does not
matter; PlatformIO's monitor uses the 3000000 set in the project's `platformio.ini`. Make the terminal send a line
feed at the end of each line: the firmware acts on a command only when the line feed arrives, so a terminal that
sends only a carriage return on Enter gets no answer. Two ways to power the board for the test:

- the programming adapter's 3.3 V, with the 24 V supply disconnected: the board talks, but the drivers have no
  power and report errors;
- the 24 V supply: the board is off until you press the power button, or supply 3.3 V from the adapter as well.

## What it does by itself

- **About three seconds after power-on** it reads every driver over SPI and prints a report per joint: `joint N
  Connection is: GOOD` or `BAD`, then the driver's current, hold and run current settings and its fault flags.
- **From then on** all six motors turn slowly and keep turning.
- **Every second** the two LEDs blink and outputs 1 and 2 toggle.

## Commands

`#` followed by the name, case as written, and the line feed. Four commands do something:

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `#IO` | Prints, once a second, the E-stop input, input 1, input 2 and the supply voltage in millivolts |
| `#LIMIT` | Prints, once a second, `Joint N is pressed` for every limit switch that is triggered, numbered by joint |
| `#STOP` | Ends the `#IO` or `#LIMIT` printout; the motors keep turning |
| `#start` | Toggles the two LEDs |

Every other name, including `#STATUS`, `#STEP1` to `#STEP6`, `#FLASH` and `#CAN`, is answered with `Unknown
command`: the parser knows the names, but the firmware does nothing with them. [Test firmware
commands](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/reference/test-firmware/) is the reference list.

## Testing CAN

CAN has its own test, next to the test firmware in the repository's `PAROL6 control board test code` folder and not
part of its build: the sketch `can_12_12` sends a frame with ID 0x446 every 500 ms at 1 Mbit/s and prints every
frame it receives, and `can_parol6_test.py` is the PC side, a python-can script for a USB-CAN adapter (slcan, 1
Mbit/s; set its port, `COM44` in the file) that prints the frames it receives with their node and command IDs.

## What good looks like

All six drivers answering, in the report at power-on:

![Serial output with all drivers responding](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/assets/STEPPER_GOOD.PNG){ width="600" }

A driver missing or faulty:

![Serial output with a faulty driver](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/assets/BAD_STEPPER_DRIVER.PNG){ width="600" }

With good drivers and the 24 V on, the motors turn slowly at 200 to 300 mA. A triggered limit switch, with
`#LIMIT`:

![A limit switch triggered](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/assets/LIMIT_GOOD.PNG){ width="550" }

The I/O report, with `#IO`; change the E-stop or an input and the values follow:

![The IO report](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/assets/GOOD_IO.PNG){ width="550" }

Outputs 1 and 2 toggle every second, and the two LEDs blink.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/board/10-serial-protocol/ -->

# 10. The serial protocol

The PC and the board exchange one packet each per control cycle over USB, a virtual serial port (the PC software
opens it at 3 000 000 baud, a setting USB ignores). The PC sends a command packet at 100 Hz; the board answers each
valid packet with a telemetry packet. Both are binary, framed with start bytes, a length byte, two end bytes and a
CRC byte, and together under 120 bytes. The byte-exact layout is on [The serial protocol](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/reference/serial-protocol/)
in the API reference; this page explains how it works.

![Packet structure](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/assets/bytes.webp){ width="700" }

## The cycle

```
loop:
    read the power button; run the active command (jog, go-to-position, home, idle)
    while serial data is available:
        read a byte; look for the three start bytes 0xFF 0xFF 0xFF
        the next byte is the length: that many bytes follow, including the CRC and the end bytes
        when the end bytes are 0x01 0x02: unpack the packet into the commanded positions, speeds, command,
            outputs, gripper fields; read the E-stop and inputs; write the outputs; send the gripper its frame;
            pack and send the telemetry packet
```

A valid packet starts one robot cycle: the firmware does nothing on its own between packets except run the
speeds it was last given. The PC must keep the packets coming; the time between the last two packets is measured
with a 703 125 Hz timer (90 MHz / 128, so 1.422 µs per tick: 10 ms is 7031 ticks) and returned in the telemetry
as `timing_data`, which is how the PC software checks that it keeps the 100 Hz loop.

## Commands

The command byte selects what the board does with the carrier data (the positions and speeds) in the same
packet:

| Command | Name | What the board does |
|---|---|---|
| 255 | Idle (dummy) | The joints stand still: it sets their speeds but steps none; it only continues a homing in progress. The default between moves |
| 123 | Jog | Runs each joint at its commanded speed (`runSpeed`) |
| 156 | Go to position with speed | Runs each joint at the average of its commanded speed and the speed that would close the position error in one cycle: the tracking the planners use |
| 100 | Home | Starts the homing sequence; idle packets continue it until done |
| 101 | Enable | Enables the robot and resets the homing state |
| 102 | Disable | Disables motion commands; the motors keep holding |
| 103 | Clear error | Resets the homing state |
| 69 | Repeatability test | A built-in two-pose cycle, for testing |

Motion commands (100, 123, 156) are ignored while the robot is disabled. A jog or go-to packet ends a homing in
progress; the homed bits in the telemetry change only by homing. The firmware does not check them before a move:
the PC decides when a move is allowed.

## Passive data

The I/O byte carries the two output states in every packet, and the gripper fields (ID, position, speed, current,
command bits, mode) are forwarded to the gripper over CAN every cycle: a move when they change, a calibrate for
mode 1, a clear-error for mode 2, and an empty status poll when nothing changed. They ride along with any command.

## Telemetry

The board returns the six positions and speeds in motor steps, which joints are homed, the inputs, outputs and
E-stop, two bytes of driver flags (temperature and position, reserved: the joint bits are cleared and the two
spare bits set), the timing, the last command byte it received, and the gripper's data. Of that, the gripper
reports only its position, current and status byte; the ID, speed and object-detection bytes are fixed values,
and the object detection is read from two bits of the status byte ([The serial protocol](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/reference/serial-protocol/)).

## Writing your own host

Anything that frames the packets as on the reference page and keeps the 100 Hz cadence can drive the board: the
commander software and the Python API are two such hosts, in Python. Start from the Python API's serial
transport rather than from scratch; the [Control ownership](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/theory/control-ownership/) page
says why two hosts must not talk to the board at once.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/board/11-troubleshooting/ -->

# 11. Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Cause | Remedy |
|---|---|---|
| No life at all with 24 V connected | The button; the supply; a reversed XT30 | Check the supply's output, the JST button cable, the XT30 polarity. A reversed supply has usually destroyed the board |
| The board is on but cannot be switched off | 3.3 V on the programming header | Unplug the ST-Link or adapter |
| The board turns on when the supply is connected | The same, or a motor was turned by hand | Unplug the programmer; move an unpowered robot slowly |
| The test firmware's report at power-on says `Connection is: BAD` for a joint | Not seated; dead; wrong orientation | Power off, check the orientation against the DIAG pins, reseat. A driver that was powered the wrong way round is dead, and the board may be too |
| A motor hums but does not turn | A phase open; a motor wire loose in the terminal | Check the four wires of that joint's cable |
| A motor turns the wrong way | Normal for a new build | Flip `direction_reversed` in the main firmware |
| A switch does not show in `#LIMIT` | Wiring; the switch; the wrong terminal | Check 24 V to the switch and the signal wire; try the other terminals to find which input changes |
| An inductive sensor never triggers | Gap; no 24 V; the sensor is PNP | NPN NO sensors only; brown 24 V, blue GND, black signal; gap of a millimetre or two |
| The E-stop reads pressed with the button released | Wiring open; the button is NO | NC contact between the E-stop terminals |
| The drivers are hot and shut down | The fan | The fan must run; 5 V, not PWM |
| No serial port on the PC | The board has no power; the cable; the driver (Windows) | The board enumerates only when powered; try another cable and port |
| The main firmware does not upload | ST-Link driver; the adapter; the target not powered | Install STSW-LINK009; check the adapter's 3.3 V; disconnect the 24 V supply |

For anything the firmware reports to the PC, the robot-side pages apply: [Troubleshooting](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/08-troubleshooting/)
in the Robot Manual.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/end-effectors/ -->

# PAROL6 End Effectors Guide

![The MSG gripper on PAROL6](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/assets/MSG_and_camera.webp)

<div class="doc-meta" markdown>

**Document number:** SR-3004

**PAROL6 release:** 1

**Python API (parol6):** v0.9.1

**PAROL6 commander software:** main

**Revision:** 2026.A

**Published:** 2026-11-03

**Applies to:** PAROL6 release 1, Python API (parol6) v0.9.1, PAROL6 commander software main

*Original instructions*

</div>

What goes on PAROL6's flange and how to set it up: the pneumatic and vacuum grippers from the robot's own files,
Source Robotics' SSG-48 and MSG electric grippers, and a tool of your own. Each page says how the end effector
mounts, how it connects, what to tell the firmware and the software, and how the commander software and the
Python API drive it. The electric grippers have manuals of their own; here is only what is PAROL6-specific.

| End effector | Driven by | Mounts with | Commander | Python API | Manual |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| [Pneumatic gripper](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/end-effectors/pneumatic-gripper/), SMC MHZ2-16D | a 5/2 valve on OUTPUT1, 5 to 7 bar | a printed holder on the joint 6 shaft coupler | `Output(1,HIGH)`, `Output(1,LOW)` | `select_tool("PNEUMATIC")` | this guide |
| [Vacuum gripper](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/end-effectors/vacuum-gripper/) | the same valve and an ejector | a printed holder | `Output(1,HIGH)`, `Output(1,LOW)` | `select_tool("VACUUM")` | this guide |
| [SSG-48](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/end-effectors/ssg-48/) adaptive electric gripper | CAN and 24 V through the M8 connector | `coupler_connector_PAROL6` | the Gripper tab, `Gripper()` | `select_tool("SSG-48")` | [SSG-48 manual](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/) |
| [MSG](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/end-effectors/msg/) compliant AI stepper gripper | CAN and 24 V through the M8 connector | `ring_cover-PAROL6` | the Gripper tab, `Gripper()` | `select_tool("MSG")` | [MSG manual](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/) |
| [Your own tool](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/end-effectors/custom-tools/) | 24 V and CAN, two air lines, two inputs and two outputs | the shaft coupler, or the coupler template | `Output(1,HIGH)`, `Output(1,LOW)`; the inputs in the IO tab | `set_tcp_offset()`, a `ToolConfig` | this guide |

## In this guide

- [The flange](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/end-effectors/flange/): the 8 mm shaft of joint 6, the connections at the forearm, the payload, the tool in
  the software
- [Pneumatic gripper](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/end-effectors/pneumatic-gripper/)
- [Vacuum gripper](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/end-effectors/vacuum-gripper/)
- [SSG-48](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/end-effectors/ssg-48/)
- [MSG](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/end-effectors/msg/)
- [Your own tool](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/end-effectors/custom-tools/)

Get the robot working before you attach a gripper: troubleshooting both at once is hard.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/end-effectors/flange/ -->

# The flange

Joint 6 ends in an 8 mm output shaft. Tools clamp onto it with a shaft coupler (8 mm bore, M4 set screws, three
in the BOM) that bolts to the tool's holder; the SSG-48 and MSG grippers use a printed coupler connector made for
this shaft. The coupler's set screws take blue threadlocker: joint 6 slipping on its shaft is the first thing to
check when a tool's orientation drifts ([Couplers and threadlocker](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/07-maintenance/couplers/)).

## Connections at the forearm

| | |
|---|---|
| **M8 4-pin connector** | 24 V, GND, CAN H, CAN L for an electric gripper; wired from the control board's CAN 1 and 24 V |
| **Two pneumatic tubes**, 4 mm | From the two push-in fittings at the base, through the arm, to the forearm |

The tubes and the gripper cable run through the arm and come out at the forearm. Joint 5 is held inside its
limits by its stops. Joint 6 has no limit with the bare flange; with a tool, the tool's cable and tubes run from
the forearm to the tool and wrap as joint 6 turns, so keep joint 6 within the turn they allow
([Joint limits and directions](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/03-technical-data/joint-limits/#limits)).

## The tool in the software

The software must know the tool to compute the pose of its tip. The commander's kinematic model is built for the
standard pneumatic gripper; the Python API has tool definitions with variants and a settable TCP offset
([Tools and the TCP](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/programming/02-python-api/tools-and-tcp/)):

```python
rbt.select_tool("PNEUMATIC")                       # default variant: vertical
rbt.select_tool("PNEUMATIC", variant_key="horizontal")
rbt.select_tool("SSG-48", variant_key="pinch")
rbt.select_tool("MSG", variant_key="150mm")
rbt.select_tool("VACUUM")
rbt.select_tool("NONE")                            # the bare flange
```

## Tool centre point

The tool centre point (TCP) is a6 = 50.5 mm from the joint 6 centre along the tool axis and a7 = 0 mm to the side.
With nothing on the flange, the TCP is the flange's reference point. The sheet is the robot's model from
[robot_descriptions](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/robot_descriptions) (version 2.15.1) with every joint at 0.
Tell the software about the tool ([Tools and the TCP](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/programming/02-python-api/tools-and-tcp/)); every tool
is compared on [Dimensions and kinematics](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/03-technical-data/kinematics/).

![PAROL6 with the flange only: dimensions to the TCP and the DH table](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/assets/kinematics/parol6_flange.webp){ width="600" }
![PAROL6 with the flange only: dimensions to the TCP and the DH table](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/assets/kinematics/parol6_flange_dark.webp){ width="600" }

## Homing and the tool

Joint 5 homes against a feature of the tool holder. The pneumatic gripper holder and the SSG-48's coupler
connector have it; a tool of your own needs it too, and the firmware's joint 5 homing offset must match the tool
([Your own tool](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/end-effectors/custom-tools/)).

## Payload

1 kg near the base, 0.5 kg at full reach, the tool included. A gripper with a camera and a cable can be most of
that. A short video shows the arm with a 1 kg payload:
[PAROL6 robot arm 1kg payload](https://www.youtube.com/shorts/3Co42vz91Tg).


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/end-effectors/pneumatic-gripper/ -->

# Pneumatic gripper

The standard tool: an SMC MHZ2-16D parallel gripper in a printed holder, driven by a 5/2 solenoid valve from one
of the control board's outputs.

## Parts

| | |
|---|---|
| Gripper | MHZ2-16D, two PC4-M5 push-in fittings |
| Holder | `GRIPPER_ATTACHMENTS/Pneumatic_gripper_holder.STL` (vertical) or `Pneumatic_gripper_holder_horizontal.stl`; `Gripper_ARMS.STL` for the fingers |
| Valve | 5/2 solenoid valve, 24 V, 4 mm tube ports |
| Tube | 4 × 2.5 mm pneumatic tube, 5 m |
| Air | 5 to 7 bar; stay below the lowest rating of the gripper, the valve and the fittings ([Pneumatics](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/06-peripherals/pneumatics/)) |

## Connections

The two tubes from the gripper leave the forearm and are joined to the two tubes that run through the arm to the
base; the valve's two outputs go to the two fittings at the base. **Swapping the two tubes swaps normally open
and normally closed**: choose the state the gripper should take without power.

![Pneumatic gripper tubing from the valve to the base and on to the gripper](../assets/pneumatic connection_edit.webp){ width="700" }

The valve's coil goes between **GND_SEL** and **OUTPUT1** on the control board, with the output supply set to the
robot's 24 V or an isolated one ([Inputs and outputs](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/06-peripherals/io/)).

## Tool centre point

The tool centre point (TCP) is a6 = 62.3 mm from the joint 6 centre along the tool axis and a7 = 45.25 mm to the
side. The TCP is the reference point of the original MHZ2-10D gripper, not a newly measured grasp centre. The sheet
is the robot's model from [robot_descriptions](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/robot_descriptions) (version
2.15.1) with every joint at 0. Tell the software about the tool ([Tools and the
TCP](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/programming/02-python-api/tools-and-tcp/)); every tool is compared on [Dimensions and
kinematics](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/03-technical-data/kinematics/).

![PAROL6 with the pneumatic gripper: dimensions to the TCP and the DH table](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/assets/kinematics/parol6_pneumatic.webp){ width="600" }
![PAROL6 with the pneumatic gripper: dimensions to the TCP and the DH table](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/assets/kinematics/parol6_pneumatic_dark.webp){ width="600" }

## Driving it

=== "RBTscript"
    ```
    Output(1,HIGH)    // the valve switches
    Delay(0.5)
    Output(1,LOW)     // and back
    ```

=== "Python API"
    ```python
    rbt.select_tool("PNEUMATIC")
    rbt.tool.close()              # output 1 low
    rbt.tool.open()               # output 1 high
    rbt.write_io(0, 1)            # the same as open(), as a plain output
    ```
    The tool's action lasts its estimated stroke, so a move queued after `close()` waits for the gripper.
    The API's `open()` switches output 1 high and `close()` switches it low: lay the tubes so that the gripper
    is open with the valve switched, or `open()` and `close()` come out the other way round.

## Orientation

The vertical holder puts the gripper along the axis of joint 6; the horizontal holder turns it 90°, which
reaches a table from the side. The Python API has a variant for each (`vertical`, `horizontal`); with the
commander, remember that the DH dimensions a6 and a7 assume the vertical holder.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/end-effectors/vacuum-gripper/ -->

# Vacuum gripper

A suction cup on a vacuum generator, fed by the same valve and tubes as the pneumatic gripper.

## Parts

The BOM's vacuum section: a suction cup gripper, a vacuum generator (ejector) and a 4 mm to 6 mm coupler. The
holder is `GRIPPER_ATTACHMENTS/vacuum_gripper_holder.STL`.

## Mounting

Print the holder and bolt the gripper to it. The gripper spins freely in the holder by default; to fix its
orientation, tie it with a zip tie to the screw shown in the figure.

![The vacuum gripper on the forearm](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/assets/vacuum_gripper.webp){ width="700" }

## Air

A vacuum generator needs one supply line, so one of the valve's two ports is blocked: a short piece of tube with
an M3 screw and threadlocker screwed into it does the job.

![One valve port blocked with a tube and an M3 screw](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/assets/vacuum_gripper2.webp){ width="700" }

## Driving it

The valve switches the air to the ejector, which pulls the vacuum: `Output(1,HIGH)` holds, `Output(1,LOW)`
drops. In the Python API, `select_tool("VACUUM")` gives `tool.open()`, which switches output 1 high, and
`tool.close()`, which switches it low. With the tubing above, `open()` holds the part and `close()` drops it;
`write_io(0, 1)` and `write_io(0, 0)` do the same.

!!! warning
    The part drops the moment the air stops, with the E-stop, a valve fault or a power failure. Do not carry
    anything over something it can damage.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/end-effectors/ssg-48/ -->

# SSG-48 adaptive electric gripper

![The SSG-48 gripper](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/assets/ssg48_hero.webp)

Source Robotics' 48 mm electric gripper: a Spectral Micro BLDC driver in gripper mode. It plugs into the M8
connector at the forearm and the control board drives it over CAN; the commander software and the Python API
both know it. Its own manual, [SSG48-gripper-docs](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/), covers
the gripper; this page covers PAROL6.

| | |
|---|---|
| Stroke | 48 mm |
| Grip force | about 54 N per ampere, 5 to 80 N; on PAROL6 up to about 54 N from the commander, 70 N from the Python API |
| Fingers | fin-ray or pinch, printed: `finger` and `pinch` in the Python API |
| Shop | [SSG-48](https://source-robotics.com/products/compliant-gripper) |

## Mounting

1. Fit `coupler_connector_PAROL6` from the gripper's repository to the gripper. It carries a shaft coupler with an
   8 mm bore and two M4 clamp screws for the joint 6 shaft, and the homing tab that joint 5 homes against: the
   tab goes on the same side as the gripper's cable connector, with an M3 × 12 screw in the marked hole, as the
   gripper's [assembly manual](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/SSG-48-adaptive-electric-gripper/blob/main/Assembly%20manual/Gripper_assembly_manual.pdf)
   shows on its last pages.
2. Slide the gripper onto the joint 6 shaft, orient it, and tighten the two clamp screws, one on each side, with
   blue threadlocker ([Couplers and threadlocker](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/07-maintenance/couplers/)).
3. Connect the [PAROL6 gripper cable](https://source-robotics.com/products/gripper-cable) between the gripper
   and the M8 connector at the forearm.

![The gripper connector at the forearm](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/assets/GRIP_CON.webp){ width="600" }

!!! danger "Only the PAROL6 cable"
    PAROL6 and PAR6 put the four signals on different pins. The PAR6 cable, or a self-made cable with a wrong
    pin, puts 24 V on the CAN pins and destroys the gripper's driver. The gripper manual's cable page has the
    pinout to check your own against.

Leave the gripper's CAN node ID at 0 and its termination switch on: it is the last node on the robot's bus
([CAN bus](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/06-peripherals/can-bus/)).

## Tool centre point

The tool centre point (TCP) is a6 = 134.3 mm from the joint 6 centre along the tool axis and a7 = 0 mm to the side.
The TCP lies on the joint 6 axis, with no sideways offset, for both jaw variants. The sheet is the robot's model
from [robot_descriptions](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/robot_descriptions) (version 2.15.1) with every joint
at 0. Tell the software about the tool ([Tools and the TCP](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/programming/02-python-api/tools-and-tcp/)); every
tool is compared on [Dimensions and kinematics](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/03-technical-data/kinematics/).

=== "Solid jaws"

    ![PAROL6 with the SSG-48, solid jaws: dimensions to the TCP and the DH table](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/assets/kinematics/parol6_ssg48.webp){ width="600" }
    ![PAROL6 with the SSG-48, solid jaws: dimensions to the TCP and the DH table](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/assets/kinematics/parol6_ssg48_dark.webp){ width="600" }

=== "Fin-ray jaws"

    ![PAROL6 with the SSG-48, fin-ray jaws: dimensions to the TCP and the DH table](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/assets/kinematics/parol6_ssg48_stock.webp){ width="600" }
    ![PAROL6 with the SSG-48, fin-ray jaws: dimensions to the TCP and the DH table](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/assets/kinematics/parol6_ssg48_stock_dark.webp){ width="600" }

## The joint 5 homing offset

Joint 5 homes against the tool, and the SSG-48's coupler sits differently from the pneumatic gripper holder. Set
`j5_homing_offset` to **8035** in `main.cpp` of the control board firmware (the default, 8900, is for the
pneumatic gripper) and upload ([Firmware](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/board/08-firmware/)). Check with the pin through the joint 5
witness marks after the first homing, and master if needed ([Mastering](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/05-operation/mastering/)).

## Driving it

The gripper must be calibrated after every power-up: it opens fully and closes fully to find its end stops, and
does not move before that. Clear any error first, then calibrate, then wait until the gripper reports itself
calibrated before the first move: about 3 s.

=== "Commander software"
    The **Gripper** tab: after homing the robot press **Clear gripper error**, then **Calibrate gripper**, and
    wait until the tab shows `Calibration status is: 1`. Then set position, speed and current with the sliders
    and press **Move GoTo**. The feedback section shows the current, the position and the status
    ([The GUI](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/gui/commander/the-gui/)). In RBTscript, after clearing the error in the tab:
    `Gripper_cal()`, `Delay(4)`, then `Gripper(position, speed, current)`
    ([RBTscript](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/programming/03-commander/rbtscript/#gripper)).

=== "Python API"
    ```python
    rbt.select_tool("SSG-48")                             # or add variant_key="pinch"
    rbt.tool.calibrate()                                   # queued; the API counts it done after 2 s
    rbt.delay(2)                                           # the rest of the calibration, with a margin
    rbt.tool.set_position(0.8, speed=0.5, current=0.4)     # fractions of the ranges; 0.4 is 580 mA
    rbt.tool.close(current=0.6)
    rbt.tool.open()
    rbt.tool.release()                                     # drop the grip, the jaws stay
    rbt.tool.stop()                                        # immediate: halt where the jaws are
    ```
    Tool actions are queued with the motion, so a move after `close()` waits for the grip; a `move` on a gripper
    that was never calibrated is refused when its turn comes. The API does not read the calibrated bit and has
    no clear-error action at this version: clear an error in the commander's Gripper tab or with Motor GUI
    ([Tools and the TCP](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/programming/02-python-api/tools-and-tcp/#calibrating),
    [Tools](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/reference/python/tools/)).

## Current and force

The current limit is the grip force, about 54 N per ampere: 300 mA is about 16 N, 1 A about 54 N. Start low
and raise it for a firmer grip; a high current with a high speed slams the jaws into the part. The gripper
manual's [Force and speed](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/latest/03-technical-data/force-and-speed/)
has the curve and the heat limits.

The commander takes the current in milliamps, 100 to 1000 mA, so its strongest grip is about 54 N. The Python
API takes it as a fraction of 100 to 1300 mA: `current=1.0` is 1.3 A, about 70 N.

## Status

The robot passes the gripper's status byte through: calibrated, in motion, object detected (while closing, while
opening, or none), and its error bits. The commander's Gripper tab shows the calibrated and E-stop error bits, and
the whole status byte as a number (labelled *Gripper object detection is*). The Python API's `tool.status()` gives
the jaw position and the current; its `engaged` and `part_detected` do not follow the status byte's bits at this
version ([Tool status](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/programming/02-python-api/tools-and-tcp/#tool-status)). The gripper manual's errors
page says what each error needs: [Errors and recovery](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/latest/06-operation/errors/).


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/end-effectors/msg/ -->

# MSG compliant AI stepper gripper

![The MSG gripper](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/assets/msg_hero.webp)

Source Robotics' modular stepper gripper: a STEPFOC driver in gripper mode, three rail lengths, three stepper
lengths and a camera mount. It plugs into the M8 connector at the forearm and the control board drives it over
CAN with the same commands as the SSG-48. Its own manual, [MSG-gripper-docs](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/),
covers the gripper; this page covers PAROL6.

| | |
|---|---|
| Stroke | 55, 105 or 155 mm, with the 100, 150 or 200 mm rail |
| Grip force | about 20, 25 or 36 N per ampere with the 21.5, 40 or 60 mm stepper; up to about 31, 50 or 76 N |
| Mass | about 380 g plus the camera: mind the [payload](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/end-effectors/flange/#payload) at full reach |
| Shop | [MSG gripper](https://source-robotics.com/products/msg-gripper) |

## Mounting

1. Replace the gripper's `ring_cover` with `ring_cover-PAROL6` from the repository's `Common parts`: it bolts to
   the robot's last joint, and the coupler plate's shaft coupler (8 mm bore, two M4 clamp screws) takes the
   joint 6 shaft ([Mounting on a robot](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/latest/04-installation/mounting/)).
2. Slide the gripper onto the shaft, orient it with the camera looking down between the jaws, and tighten the
   two clamp screws with blue threadlocker ([Couplers and threadlocker](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/07-maintenance/couplers/)).
3. Connect the [PAROL6 gripper cable](https://source-robotics.com/products/gripper-cable) between the gripper
   and the M8 connector at the forearm.
4. The camera is a plain USB camera with its own cable: route it outside the arm, with slack for joints 4, 5
   and 6, and fix it so the arm cannot catch it.

!!! danger "Only the PAROL6 cable"
    PAROL6 and PAR6 put the four signals on different pins. The PAR6 cable, or a self-made cable with a wrong
    pin, puts 24 V on the CAN pins and destroys the gripper's driver. The gripper manual's cable page has the
    pinout to check your own against.

Leave the gripper's CAN node ID at 0 and its termination switch, reachable through the stepper cover, on: it is
the last node on the robot's bus ([CAN bus](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/06-peripherals/can-bus/)).

## Tool centre point

The tool centre point (TCP) is a6 = 134.3 mm from the joint 6 centre along the tool axis and a7 = 28.35 mm to the
side. Both jaw variants share one TCP: an operating point, not a measured grasp centre. The sheet is the robot's
model from [robot_descriptions](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/robot_descriptions) (version 2.15.1) with every
joint at 0. Tell the software about the tool ([Tools and the TCP](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/programming/02-python-api/tools-and-tcp/));
every tool is compared on [Dimensions and kinematics](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/03-technical-data/kinematics/).

=== "Solid jaws"

    ![PAROL6 with the MSG, solid jaws: dimensions to the TCP and the DH table](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/assets/kinematics/parol6_msg.webp){ width="600" }
    ![PAROL6 with the MSG, solid jaws: dimensions to the TCP and the DH table](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/assets/kinematics/parol6_msg_dark.webp){ width="600" }

=== "Soft TPU jaws"

    ![PAROL6 with the MSG, soft TPU jaws: dimensions to the TCP and the DH table](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/assets/kinematics/parol6_msg_tpu_glue.webp){ width="600" }
    ![PAROL6 with the MSG, soft TPU jaws: dimensions to the TCP and the DH table](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/assets/kinematics/parol6_msg_tpu_glue_dark.webp){ width="600" }

## The joint 5 homing offset

Joint 5 homes against the tool, and the MSG's ring cover is not the pneumatic gripper holder that the firmware's
default offset (8900) assumes. After the first homing, check joint 5 with the pin through the witness marks; if
it is off, measure the offset and set `j5_homing_offset` in `main.cpp` as [Mastering](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/05-operation/mastering/)
describes.

## Driving it

The gripper must be calibrated after every power-up: it opens fully and closes fully to find its end stops, and
does not move before that. Clear any error first, then calibrate, then wait until the gripper reports itself
calibrated before the first move: about 5 to 6 s on the longer rails.

=== "Commander software"
    The **Gripper** tab: after homing the robot press **Clear gripper error**, then **Calibrate gripper**, and
    wait until the tab shows `Calibration status is: 1`. Then set position, speed and current with the sliders
    and press **Move GoTo**. The feedback section shows the current, the position and the status
    ([The GUI](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/gui/commander/the-gui/)). In RBTscript, after clearing the error in the tab:
    `Gripper_cal()`, `Delay(7)`, then `Gripper(position, speed, current)`
    ([RBTscript](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/programming/03-commander/rbtscript/#gripper)).

=== "Python API"
    ```python
    rbt.select_tool("MSG", variant_key="150mm")           # 100mm, 150mm or 200mm: the rail
    rbt.tool.calibrate()                                   # queued; the API counts it done after 2 s
    rbt.delay(5)                                           # the rest of the calibration, with a margin
    rbt.tool.set_position(0.8, speed=0.5, current=0.4)     # fractions of the ranges; 0.4 is 1180 mA
    rbt.tool.close(current=0.4)
    rbt.tool.open()
    rbt.tool.release()                                     # drop the grip, the jaws stay
    rbt.tool.stop()                                        # immediate: halt where the jaws are
    ```
    Tool actions are queued with the motion, so a move after `close()` waits for the grip; a `move` on a gripper
    that was never calibrated is refused when its turn comes. The API does not read the calibrated bit and has
    no clear-error action at this version: clear an error in the commander's Gripper tab or with Motor GUI
    ([Tools and the TCP](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/programming/02-python-api/tools-and-tcp/#calibrating),
    [Tools](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/reference/python/tools/)).

## Current and force

The current limit is the grip force, and the slope depends on the stepper: about 20 N per ampere with the
21.5 mm stepper, 25 with the 40 mm, 36 with the 60 mm. Stay within the stepper's maximum, 1.5 A, 2.0 A or 2.1 A.
The gripper manual's [Force and speed](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/latest/03-technical-data/force-and-speed/)
has the curves.

The commander takes the current in milliamps, 100 to 1000 mA, which is within every stepper's maximum. The
Python API takes it as a fraction of 100 to 2800 mA, a range above every stepper's maximum, so keep the fraction
at or below the value for your stepper:

| Stepper | Maximum current | Highest `current=` fraction |
|---|---|---|
| 21.5 mm | 1.5 A | 0.51 |
| 40 mm | 2.0 A | 0.70 |
| 60 mm | 2.1 A | 0.74 |

## Status

The robot passes the gripper's status byte through: calibrated, in motion, object detected (while closing, while
opening, or none), and its error bits. The commander's Gripper tab shows the calibrated and E-stop error
bits, and the whole status byte as a number (labelled *Gripper object detection is*). The Python API's `tool.status()` gives the jaw position and the current; its
`engaged` and `part_detected` do not follow the status byte's bits at this version
([Tool status](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/programming/02-python-api/tools-and-tcp/#tool-status)). The gripper manual's errors page says
what each error needs: [Errors and recovery](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/latest/06-operation/errors/).


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/end-effectors/custom-tools/ -->

# Your own tool

## Mounting

Clamp onto the 8 mm shaft of joint 6 with a shaft coupler from the BOM, or print a holder with a coupler
connector: the SSG-48 repository has a template, `STEPS/coupler_connector_generic_STEP.STEP` (and
`Gripper STL parts/connector_coupler_generic.STL`), and the `STL/WRIST/wrist.STL` in the robot's files shows the
mating geometry. Keep the tool within the payload and short: every millimetre past the
flange is leverage against joints 4 and 5.

## The joint 5 homing feature

Joint 5 finds its reference by driving the forearm's limit switch against a feature of the tool holder. Your
holder needs a surface in the same place as the pneumatic gripper holder's; compare with `Pneumatic_gripper_holder.STL`.
Then measure the homing offset: home, jog joint 5 until the pin fits the witness marks, and set
`j5_homing_offset` in `main.cpp` to the steps that gives ([Mastering](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/05-operation/mastering/)).

## Connections

Up to 24 V and CAN at the M8 connector, two air lines, and the control board's two inputs and two outputs at the
base. A tool that needs more, a camera's USB for instance, runs its cable outside the arm, with enough slack for
joints 4, 5 and 6 and fixed so the arm cannot catch it.

## The tool frame

The software positions the tool centre point. In the Python API, register the tool once with its transform from
the flange, or set an offset at run time:

```python
rbt.select_tool("NONE")
rbt.set_tcp_offset(0, 0, 120)                  # the tip, 120 mm along the tool's Z
index = rbt.set_tcp_transform(0, 0, 120, 0, 15, 0)   # with a rotation, intrinsic XYZ degrees
rbt.wait_command(index)
```

A permanent tool goes into the API's tool registry as a `ToolConfig` with its collision mesh, so that the
collision checker knows its shape ([Tools and the TCP](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/programming/02-python-api/tools-and-tcp/)). The
commander software has no tool setting: its poses are for the standard pneumatic gripper, and a different tool
means editing its robot model.

## Check before you run

Jog joint 5 and joint 6 through their ranges slowly with the tool mounted and watch for contact with the forearm:
the software's joint limits do not know the tool's shape.

# PAROL6 GUI Guide

![The commander window](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/assets/GUI2.webp)

<div class="doc-meta" markdown>

**PAROL6 commander software:** main

**Revision:** 2026.A

**Published:** 2026-11-03

**Applies to:** PAROL6 release 1, PAROL6 commander software main

*Original instructions*

</div>

The graphical programs for PAROL6 and its grippers: which one to open for which job, how to install it, and
what is on its screen. Programming the robot, in RBTscript or Python, is in the
[Programming Guide](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/programming/).

| | Commander software | Waldo Commander | Motor GUI |
|---|---|---|---|
| What it is | Source Robotics' desktop program: jogging, a 3D simulator, the RBTscript editor, the I/O and gripper tabs | A community browser interface on the Python API: a simulator, Python programs, teaching by demonstration, an MCP server for LLMs | Source Robotics' browser tool for the drivers inside the electric grippers |
| For | the first day, teaching poses, demos, simple sequences | remote use, programs in the browser, AI-driven control | setting up, testing and updating an SSG-48 or MSG gripper |
| Runs | on the PC at the robot, Python 3.10 or 3.11 | a server at the robot, any browser | any Chromium browser, with the CANvas adapter |
| Talks to | the control board over USB | the Python API's controller | the gripper's driver over CAN |

## In this guide

- The commander software: [Installation](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/gui/commander/installation/), [The GUI](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/gui/commander/the-gui/)
- [Waldo Commander](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/gui/waldo-commander/)
- [Motor GUI](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/gui/motor-gui/)

One program owns the control board at a time: the commander and the Python API's controller cannot be connected
together ([Control ownership](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/theory/control-ownership/)).
