<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/programming/04-ros2/ -->

# 4. ROS 2 and MoveIt

[PAROL6-ROS2-MOVEIT](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/PAROL6-ROS2-MOVEIT) is a MoveIt 2 configuration for
PAROL6 with the URDF, a simulation demo and launch files, tested on Ubuntu 22.04 with ROS 2 Humble.

## Simulation

```
sudo apt install ros-humble-desktop ros-humble-moveit
mkdir -p ~/ros2_ws/src && cd ~/ros2_ws/src
git clone https://github.com/Source-Robotics/PAROL6-ROS2-MOVEIT.git
cd ~/ros2_ws && colcon build
source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash && source install/setup.bash
LC_NUMERIC=en_US.UTF-8 ros2 launch parol6_moveit demo.launch.py
```

RViz opens with the robot, and MoveIt plans and executes on the mock hardware.

## The real robot

`real_robot.launch.py` brings up the same stack on `ros2_control`, with a hardware interface and a bridge that
talk to the Python API's controller, which must be running (`parol6-server --serial ...`, or its simulator mode).
The hardware interface lives in [parol6_ros2_control](https://github.com/grahas/parol6_ros2_control), a community
repository, cloned next to the MoveIt package:

```
cd ~/ros2_ws/src
git clone https://github.com/grahas/parol6_ros2_control.git
cd ~/ros2_ws && colcon build
ros2 launch parol6_moveit real_robot.launch.py bridge_python:=/path/to/venv/bin/python3
```

The `bridge_python` must have the `parol6` package installed. On Ubuntu 22.04 it does not install: the package
needs Python 3.11 or newer, and on Linux its kinematics backend ships wheels only for glibc 2.39 or newer
(Ubuntu 24.04), while 22.04 has Python 3.10 and glibc 2.35 ([Installation](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/programming/02-python-api/installation/)). The
interface's README gives the way round it: run `parol6-server` and the bridge on another machine, or under WSL2,
where `parol6` installs, and point the hardware interface's `bridge_host` parameter at it over the network.

## The URDF

The robot description, URDF and MuJoCo with meshes and a version per tool, is in
[robot_descriptions](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/robot_descriptions/tree/v2.15.1/guides/parol6.md), and an earlier URDF is inside the Python API (`parol6/urdf_model`). The gripper repositories have URDF and MJCF descriptions of the SSG-48 and MSG for
attaching to it.

## Other ROS 2 projects

[parol6_commander](https://github.com/Lyczko0/parol6_commander), a web GUI on ROS 2 and MoveIt 2, and
[Parol6-firmware](https://github.com/Lyczko0/Parol6-firmware), alternative firmware with micro-ROS, are community
projects ([Community projects](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/appendix/community/)).


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/programming/05-other-interfaces/ -->

# 5. Other interfaces

## Waldo Commander (web)

A community browser interface on the Python API, with a simulator, programs in the browser, teaching by
demonstration and an MCP server for LLMs: [Waldo Commander](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/gui/waldo-commander/) in the GUI Guide.

## The serial protocol directly

Anything that frames the packets of [the serial protocol](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/board/10-serial-protocol/) and keeps the 100 Hz
cadence can drive the control board from any language. The Python API's serial transport and the commander's
`Serial_sender_good_latest.py` are the two reference implementations.

## The legacy Python API

[PAROL6-python-API-Alvar](https://github.com/PCrnjak/PAROL6-python-API-Alvar) was the first Python API: a
headless commander (`headless_commander.py`) on the PC at the robot, listening for text commands over UDP on
port 5001, and a thin client (`robot_api.py`) with functions like `move_robot_joints`, `move_robot_pose`,
`control_electric_gripper`. It is frozen and kept for the projects built on it, including the Gemini vision
demo. New work belongs on the current API.

## AI agents

The current API's typed client, its dry-run preview and the MCP server in Waldo Commander are the paths for
LLM-driven control: an agent writes Python against the client, previews it dry, and runs it with a human at the
E-stop. The community list has examples ([Community projects](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/appendix/community/)).


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/programming/06-troubleshooting/ -->

# 6. Troubleshooting

## The Python API

| Symptom | Cause | Remedy |
|---|---|---|
| `ping()` returns `None` | No controller, wrong host or port, a firewall | Start `parol6-server`; check `--host`/`--port`; allow UDP 5001 |
| `ping()` says `hardware_connected=False` | No serial port given, or it failed to open | `--serial COM5`, or `connect_hardware("COM5")`; check the port is free |
| No status in `stream_status()` | Multicast blocked, or a different group | `PAROL6_STATUS_TRANSPORT=UNICAST` with `PAROL6_STATUS_UNICAST_HOST`; check `PAROL6_MCAST_IF` |
| `MotionError: MOTN_NOT_HOMED` | The robot is not referenced | `home(wait=True)` |
| `MotionError: SYS_ESTOP_ACTIVE` | The E-stop is pressed or a protective stop is latched | Release the button; `reset()` |
| `IK_TARGET_UNREACHABLE` on a pose that looks fine | Numerical IK, often around joint 4 | Change the orientation slightly; start from another posture; a joint move first |
| `COMM_VALIDATION_ERROR` or decode errors | Client and controller of different versions | The same version on both sides |
| `TimeoutError` on a blocking move | The move did not complete in `timeout` | Longer `timeout`; `stop()` to cancel the queued move |
| `loop overbudget by +N%` in the log | The PC cannot keep 100 Hz | Lower `PAROL6_CONTROL_RATE_HZ`; no DEBUG or TRACE logging; close other programs |
| Jittery motion | The same, or a long serial cable | As above; a short shielded USB cable |
| Motion refused with `SYS_SELF_COLLISION` where there is nothing | A declared shape, a held object, the tool's mesh | `shapes()`; the tool's variant; `PAROL6_COLLISION_CHECK=0` to confirm, then fix the world |
| A tool `move` fails with `MOTN_GRIPPER_*` | Not calibrated; no gripper answering on CAN | `tool.calibrate()`; the gripper's cable and manual |

## The commander software

| Symptom | Cause | Remedy |
|---|---|---|
| Connect does nothing | Wrong port; the port in use; Linux permissions | Try again; `COMx`/`ttyACMx`; `chmod 666` |
| The simulator shows a different pose | Not homed | Home |
| A command in the program does nothing | A typo in the name or the argument order; `End()` before it | The response log; the exact syntax on [RBTscript](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/programming/03-commander/rbtscript/) |
| `MoveCart` stops half way | A singularity | A joint move, or another orientation |
| `Gripper()` does nothing | Not calibrated; an error latched; a value out of range | Gripper tab: **Clear gripper error**, then **Calibrate gripper**; whole numbers, current 150 to 1000 mA |
| The program runs once and stops | No `Loop()` | Add it, or `End()` is where you want it |
| Import errors at start | Wrong Python or package versions | Python 3.10 or 3.11 and the pinned versions, in the commander's own virtual environment, activated ([Installation](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/gui/commander/installation/)) |
| `Time between 2 commands` far above 0.010 (seconds, despite the label) | The PC | [Communication](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/08-troubleshooting/communication/) |

## Both

The control board answers in text when you expected packets: it runs the test firmware; upload the main one
([Firmware](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/board/08-firmware/)). Two programs cannot share the port ([Control ownership](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/theory/control-ownership/)).


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/reference/ -->

# API reference

Where you look things up. The Python API pages are generated from the API's source at v0.9.1: the
signature and the docstring of every public method of `RobotClient`, the tool methods, the registered tools, the
error codes, the environment variables and the controller's options, with notes written around them. The build
fails when a page names a method the API no longer has, and the tests fail when a method is on no page.

<div class="grid cards" markdown>

-   :material-language-python: **Python API**

    ---

# Python API reference

The public methods of `RobotClient` (the sync client; the async client has the same methods, awaited, plus the
two status streams), generated from the API's source at v0.9.1. `rbt` in the signatures is a
client, `rbt = RobotClient()`.

The conventions, once: angles in degrees in order J1 to J6, poses as `[x, y, z, rx, ry, rz]` in millimetres and
degrees, `speed` and `accel` as fractions in (0, 1], `duration` in seconds, `r` a blend radius in millimetres,
joints indexed from 0 in jog calls. A motion call returns the command index (≥ 0), or −1 if no acknowledgement arrived; a
query returns `None` on a timeout; a refused or failed command raises `MotionError` ([Errors](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/reference/python/errors/)).

| `select_tool` | Configuration | [tools](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/reference/python/tools/#select_tool) |

# Motion

Planned moves: queued, run in order, each returning its command index. `wait=True` (the default) blocks until the
command completes and raises `MotionError` if it failed or was cancelled; `wait=False` returns at once for a later
`wait_command()`. Either `duration` or `speed` times a move, not both. [Motion](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/programming/02-python-api/motion/)
in the guide explains the choices.

### `home` 

```python
rbt.home(wait: bool = False, calibrate: bool = False, timeout: float = 60.0) -> int
```

Home the robot to its home position.

Uncalibrated (first home after power-on), this runs the full referencing sequence: each joint seeks its limit switch, then the robot moves to standby. Calibrated, it returns to standby with a normal planned, collision-checked joint move — unless `calibrate=True`, which re-runs the referencing sequence. The referencing sequence is firmware-driven and ignores the collision world, so clear keep-out geometry from the joints' sweep first.

Returns the command index (≥ 0) on success, -1 on failure.

```python
rbt.home()
```

| Parameter | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `wait` | If True, block until motion completes |
| `calibrate` | If True, always run the referencing sequence |
| `timeout` | Maximum time to wait in seconds (only used when wait=True) |

!!! note
    The referencing sequence is the firmware's ([Homing](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/05-operation/homing/)): it ignores the collision
    world, and it takes about half a minute. A later `home()` is a planned joint move to the API's standby, the after-homing pose.

### `move_j` 

```python
rbt.move_j(
    angles: list[float] | None = None,
    *,
    pose: list[float] | None = None,
    duration: float = 0.0,
    speed: float = 0.5,
    accel: float = 0.5,
    r: float = 0.0,
    rel: bool = False,
    wait: bool = True,
    timeout: float = 10.0,
) -> int
```

Joint-space move. Positional arg = joint angles; pose= kwarg = Cartesian target with IK.

Returns the command index (≥ 0) on success, -1 on failure.

```python
rbt.move_j([90, -90, 180, 0, 0, 180], speed=0.5)
```

| Parameter | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `angles` | 6 joint angles in degrees (ignored if pose= is set) |
| `pose` | If set, Cartesian target [x,y,z,rx,ry,rz] — dispatches to MOVEJ_POSE |
| `duration` | Motion duration in seconds; > 0 times the move and speed is unused |
| `speed` | Speed fraction in (0, 1], used when duration is 0 |
| `accel` | Acceleration fraction in (0, 1] |
| `r` | Blend radius in mm (0 = stop at target) |
| `rel` | If True, angles are relative to current position |
| `wait` | If True, block until motion completes |

### `move_l` 

```python
rbt.move_l(
    pose: list[float],
    *,
    frame: Frame = 'WRF',
    duration: float = 0.0,
    speed: float = 0.5,
    accel: float = 0.5,
    r: float = 0.0,
    rel: bool = False,
    wait: bool = True,
    timeout: float = 10.0,
) -> int
```

Linear Cartesian move to target pose.

Returns the command index (≥ 0) on success, -1 on failure.

```python
rbt.move_l([0, 263, 242, 90, 0, 90], speed=0.5)
```

| Parameter | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `pose` | Target [x,y,z,rx,ry,rz] in mm and degrees |
| `frame` | Reference frame ("WRF" or "TRF") |
| `duration` | Motion duration in seconds; > 0 times the move and speed is unused |
| `speed` | Speed fraction in (0, 1], used when duration is 0 |
| `accel` | Acceleration fraction in (0, 1] |
| `r` | Blend radius in mm |
| `rel` | If True, pose is relative delta |
| `wait` | If True, block until motion completes |

### `move_c` 

```python
rbt.move_c(
    via: list[float],
    end: list[float],
    *,
    frame: Frame = 'WRF',
    duration: float = 0.0,
    speed: float = 0.5,
    accel: float = 0.5,
    r: float = 0.0,
    wait: bool = True,
    timeout: float = 10.0,
) -> int
```

Circular arc through current position -> via -> end.

Returns the command index (≥ 0) on success, -1 on failure.

```python
rbt.move_c(via=[0, 250, 250, 90, 0, 90], end=[0, 263, 242, 90, 0, 90], speed=0.5)
```

| Parameter | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `via` | Via-point pose [x,y,z,rx,ry,rz] |
| `end` | End-point pose [x,y,z,rx,ry,rz] |
| `frame` | Reference frame |
| `duration` | Motion duration in seconds; > 0 times the move and speed is unused |
| `speed` | Speed fraction in (0, 1], used when duration is 0 |
| `accel` | Acceleration fraction in (0, 1] |
| `r` | Blend radius in mm |
| `wait` | If True, block until motion completes |

### `move_s` 

```python
rbt.move_s(
    waypoints: list[list[float]],
    *,
    frame: Frame = 'WRF',
    duration: float = 0.0,
    speed: float = 0.5,
    accel: float = 0.5,
    wait: bool = True,
    timeout: float = 10.0,
) -> int
```

Cubic spline through waypoints.

Returns the command index (≥ 0) on success, -1 on failure.

```python
rbt.move_s([[0, 263, 242, 90, 0, 90], [50, 250, 200, 90, 0, 90]], speed=0.5)
```

| Parameter | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `waypoints` | List of poses [[x,y,z,rx,ry,rz], ...] |
| `frame` | Reference frame |
| `duration` | Motion duration in seconds; > 0 times the move and speed is unused |
| `speed` | Speed fraction in (0, 1], used when duration is 0 |
| `accel` | Acceleration fraction in (0, 1] |
| `wait` | If True, block until motion completes |

### `move_p` 

```python
rbt.move_p(
    waypoints: list[list[float]],
    *,
    frame: Frame = 'WRF',
    duration: float = 0.0,
    speed: float = 0.5,
    accel: float = 0.5,
    wait: bool = True,
    timeout: float = 10.0,
) -> int
```

Process move — constant TCP speed with auto-blending at corners.

Returns the command index (≥ 0) on success, -1 on failure.

```python
rbt.move_p([[0, 263, 242, 90, 0, 90], [50, 250, 200, 90, 0, 90]], speed=0.5)
```

| Parameter | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `waypoints` | List of poses [[x,y,z,rx,ry,rz], ...] |
| `frame` | Reference frame |
| `duration` | Motion duration in seconds; > 0 times the move and speed is unused |
| `speed` | Speed fraction in (0, 1], used when duration is 0 |
| `accel` | Acceleration fraction in (0, 1] |
| `wait` | If True, block until motion completes |

# Jogging and servoing

Streamed motion: takes the arm at once and cancels the planned queue (`MOTN_CANCELLED` for every discarded
command). A jog ends when its `duration` runs out; a servo stream ends about 0.25 s after the last target. Then
the arm brakes to rest. Speeds are signed fractions in [−1, 1] for jogs and fractions in (0, 1] for servo
targets. `jog_j` works before homing; `jog_l` and the servo targets need a homed robot.
[Jogging and servoing](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/programming/02-python-api/streaming/) in the guide.

### `jog_j` 

```python
rbt.jog_j(
    joint: int | None = None,
    speed: float = 0.0,
    duration: float = 0.1,
    *,
    joints: list[int] | None = None,
    speeds: list[float] | None = None,
    accel: float = 0.5,
) -> int
```

Joint velocity jog. Single-joint or multi-joint.

Single joint:   jog_j(0, 0.5, 1.0) Multi joint:    jog_j(joints=[0,1], speeds=[0.5, -0.3], duration=1.0)

```python
rbt.jog_j(0, speed=0.5, duration=1.0)
```

| Parameter | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `joint` | Joint index (0-5) for single-joint jog |
| `speed` | Signed speed fraction for single-joint jog |
| `duration` | Jog duration in seconds |
| `joints` | List of joint indices for multi-joint jog |
| `speeds` | List of signed speed fractions for multi-joint jog |
| `accel` | Acceleration fraction 0-1 |

### `jog_l` 

```python
rbt.jog_l(
    frame: Frame,
    axis: Axis | None = None,
    speed: float = 0.0,
    duration: float = 0.1,
    *,
    axes: list[Axis] | None = None,
    speeds_list: list[float] | None = None,
    accel: float = 0.5,
) -> int
```

Cartesian velocity jog. Single-axis or multi-axis.

Single axis:  jog_l("WRF", "X", 0.5, 1.0) Multi axis:   jog_l("WRF", axes=["X","Y"], speeds_list=[0.5, -0.3], duration=1.0)

```python
rbt.jog_l("WRF", "X", speed=0.5, duration=1.0)
```

| Parameter | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `frame` | Reference frame ("WRF" or "TRF") |
| `axis` | Axis name for single-axis jog |
| `speed` | Signed speed fraction for single-axis jog |
| `duration` | Jog duration in seconds |
| `axes` | List of axis names for multi-axis jog |
| `speeds_list` | List of signed speed fractions for multi-axis jog |
| `accel` | Acceleration fraction 0-1 |

!!! note
    Axis names: `X`, `Y`, `Z`, `RX`, `RY`, `RZ`; frames `WRF` and `TRF`. Jogs are clamped to 80 % of the limits.

### `servo_j` 

```python
rbt.servo_j(
    angles: list[float] | None = None,
    *,
    pose: list[float] | None = None,
    speed: float = 0.5,
    accel: float = 0.5,
) -> int
```

Streaming joint position target. Fire-and-forget.

The stream stops about 0.25 s after the last target arrives: the arm brakes to rest and holds there.

```python
rbt.servo_j([90, -90, 180, 0, 0, 180])
```

| Parameter | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `angles` | 6 joint angles in degrees (ignored if pose= is set) |
| `pose` | If set, Cartesian target — dispatches to SERVOJ_POSE |
| `speed` | Speed fraction 0-1 |
| `accel` | Acceleration fraction 0-1 |

### `servo_l` 

```python
rbt.servo_l(pose: list[float], *, speed: float = 0.5, accel: float = 0.5) -> int
```

Streaming linear Cartesian position target. Fire-and-forget.

The stream stops about 0.25 s after the last target arrives: the tool brakes along its line to rest and holds there.

```python
rbt.servo_l([0, 263, 242, 90, 0, 90])
```

| Parameter | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `pose` | Target [x,y,z,rx,ry,rz] in mm and degrees |
| `speed` | Speed fraction 0-1 |
| `accel` | Acceleration fraction 0-1 |

### `stream_status` (async client only) 

```python
rbt.stream_status() -> AsyncIterator[StatusBuffer]
```

Async generator that yields status updates from multicast broadcasts.

```python
async for status in client.stream_status():
    print(f"Angles: {status.angles}")
```

This generator terminates automatically when `close` is called on the client, so callers do not need to manually cancel their consumer tasks.

Each yielded StatusBuffer is a copy - safe to store or process async. For zero-copy hot paths, use `stream_status_shared` instead.

Slow consumers automatically skip to the latest state (desired for real-time).

### `stream_status_shared` (async client only) 

```python
rbt.stream_status_shared() -> AsyncIterator[StatusBuffer]
```

Zero-copy async generator that yields the shared status buffer.

```python
async for status in client.stream_status_shared():
    # Process immediately - don't store references
    print(f"Angles: {status.angles}")
```

WARNING: The same buffer instance is yielded on every iteration. Do not store references to the yielded object - data will be overwritten on the next iteration. For safe storage, use `stream_status` or call status.copy().

This generator terminates automatically when `close` is called on the client.

Slow consumers automatically skip to the latest state (desired for real-time).


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/reference/python/control/ -->

# Control

Commands that change what the controller is doing: stops, the protective stop and its reset, pause and execution
speed, simulator mode, teleport, and the state reset. They are system commands: immediate, not queued, and
accepted also while the controller is disabled, except `teleport`, which is refused then. [Control ownership](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/theory/control-ownership/).

### `stop` 

```python
rbt.stop() -> int
```

Stop all motion — cancel the active move and clear the queue.

The controller stays enabled and holding position; the next motion command is accepted immediately.

```python
rbt.stop()
```

**Returns:** 1 if acknowledged, 0 on failure.

### `estop` 

```python
rbt.estop() -> int
```

Protective stop: stop all motion and latch the controller disabled until `reset()`.

```python
rbt.estop()
```

**Returns:** 1 if acknowledged, 0 on failure.

### `reset` 

```python
rbt.reset() -> int
```

Clear a latched protective stop, re-enabling motion.

```python
rbt.reset()
```

**Returns:** 1 if acknowledged, 0 on failure.

### `reset_state` 

```python
rbt.reset_state() -> int
```

Reset program state — world shapes, tool selection, errors, pause, motion profile and execution speed — and discard the queue, each discarded command failing with `MOTN_CANCELLED`.

The arm holds where it is. A protective stop stays latched (only `reset()` clears it), and homed state, digital outputs and the serial connection are kept.

```python
rbt.reset_state()
```

### `pause` 

```python
rbt.pause(*, timeout: float = 3.0) -> int
```

Request a controlled hold, retaining queued trajectory progress.

A confirmed request returns 1. Read `execution_speed().paused` to confirm the hold. Standalone Python completion timeouts continue.

```python
rbt.pause()
```

### `resume` 

```python
rbt.resume(*, timeout: float = 3.0) -> int
```

Resume the retained queue at its selected positive speed.

```python
rbt.resume()
```

### `set_execution_speed` 

```python
rbt.set_execution_speed(scale: float, *, timeout: float = 3.0) -> int
```

Select 10–100% of planned queued-motion speed, preserving pause.

```python
rbt.set_execution_speed(0.5)
```

### `simulator` 

```python
rbt.simulator(enabled: bool) -> int
```

Enable or disable simulator mode.

```python
rbt.simulator(True)
```

### `teleport` 

```python
rbt.teleport(angles_deg: list[float], tool_positions: list[float] | None = None) -> int
```

Instantly set joint angles and optional tool positions (simulator only).

The pose is exact, so the arm counts as homed afterwards and planned motion may follow. Whatever was driving the arm is cancelled with `MOTN_CANCELLED`.

```python
rbt.teleport([90, -90, 180, 0, 0, 180])
rbt.teleport([90, -90, 180, 0, 0, 180], tool_positions=[1.0])
```

**Returns:** 1 once the pose is applied, 0 when no reply arrives.

**Raises:**

- `ValueError`: for a non-finite angle, one outside the hard joint limits, or a tool position outside `[0, 1]`.
- `MotionError`: off the simulator (`SYS_NOT_SIMULATOR`), when the tool positions do not match the fitted tool's DOF count, or while the controller is disabled.

### `run_skill` 

```python
rbt.run_skill(invoke: Callable[[AsyncRobotClient], Coroutine[Any, Any, T]]) -> T
```

Execute a Python skill using this connection and its existing loop.

!!! note
    Skills are decorated Python functions from the waldoctl skill runtime, run on the connected client; Waldo
    Commander uses them. A plain script does not need them.

### `close` 

```python
rbt.close() -> None
```

Release UDP transport and background tasks.

Safe to call multiple times.

# Queries

Requests with a reply, immediate, returning `None` when no reply arrives in the client's timeout (the TCP queries
raise instead, see [Configuration](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/reference/python/configuration/)). [Status and waiting](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/programming/02-python-api/status-and-waiting/)
in the guide.

### `ping` 

```python
rbt.ping() -> PingResult | None
```

Return parsed ping result with hardware_connected status.

```python
rbt.ping()
```

### `angles` 

```python
rbt.angles() -> list[float] | None
```

Current joint angles in degrees [J1, J2, J3, J4, J5, J6].

```python
angles = rbt.angles()
```

```python
rbt.pose(frame: str = 'WRF') -> list[float] | None
```

Current TCP pose as [x, y, z, rx, ry, rz] in mm and degrees.

```python

```

### `joint_speeds` 


Current joint velocities in deg/s [J1, J2, J3, J4, J5, J6], the units of `StatusBuffer.speeds`.

```python

```

### `tcp_speed` 

```python

```

TCP linear velocity in mm/s.

```python

```

### `io` 

```python

```

Digital I/O status [in1, in2, out1, out2, estop].

`timeout` bounds setup, retries, and the reply; None uses client defaults.

```python

```

### `status` 

```python

```

Aggregate status snapshot (pose, angles, speeds, io, tool_status). Its `tool_status` is always a `ToolStatus`, key `"NONE"` when no tool is fitted.

```python
status = rbt.status()
```

### `activity`

What the robot is currently doing.

Returns state (idle/executing/error), current command name, parameters, and error description if applicable.

### `queue`

Queued command list.

### `error`

Current error state, or None if no error.

### `reachable`

Remaining freedom of movement per joint/axis before hitting limits.


### `is_estop_pressed`


Check if E-stop is pressed. Returns True if pressed.


### `is_robot_stopped` 

```python

```

Check if robot has stopped moving.

Prefer `wait_command()` for waiting on specific commands. This method polls raw joint speeds and is mainly useful for diagnostics or manual stopping logic.

```python
stopped = rbt.is_robot_stopped()
```

| Parameter | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `threshold_speed` | Speed threshold in deg/s |

**Returns:** True if all joints below threshold

### `is_simulator`

# Synchronization

Waiting for the controller, for a command, for a checkpoint or for the arm to come to rest; and the two queued
markers, delays and checkpoints. [Status and waiting](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/programming/02-python-api/status-and-waiting/) in the
guide says what "done" means.

### `wait_ready` 

```python
rbt.wait_ready(timeout: float = 5.0, interval: float = 0.05) -> bool
```

Poll ping() until server responds or timeout.

| Parameter | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `timeout` | Maximum time to wait for server to respond |
| `interval` | Polling interval between ping attempts |

**Returns:** True if server responded to PING, False on timeout

### `wait_command` 

```python
rbt.wait_command(command_index: int, timeout: float = 10.0) -> bool
```

Wait until a specific command index has been completed.

Queries exact success in the controller's last 1024 completions: a later command that finishes first — a jog, a `tool.stop()` — does not complete an unfinished one queued before it. Queued commands, tool actions among them, run in index order, so a wait on one covers everything queued ahead of it. Unknown or expired results are never inferred successful from the status high-water mark. A command that ended as a failure — cancelled by `stop()`/`estop()` (`MOTN_CANCELLED`) or failed by the pipeline — raises MotionError.

| Parameter | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `command_index` | The command index to wait for (returned by motion commands). |
| `timeout` | Maximum time to wait in seconds. |

**Returns:** True if the command completed within timeout, False otherwise.

**Raises:**

- `MotionError`: If the pipeline errored at or before command_index.

### `wait_motion` 

```python
rbt.wait_motion(
    timeout: float = 10.0,
    settle_window: float = 0.25,
    speed_threshold: float = 0.5,
    angle_threshold: float = 0.5,
) -> bool
```

Wait until the queue has run out and the arm has come to rest.

First waits for the latest command the controller has accepted — every command this client queued, and each newer one the status stream reports accepted — to end, then for the arm to hold still for `settle_window`. A command that failed or was cancelled ends the wait like one that completed; `wait_command()` tells which.

```python
rbt.wait_motion()
```

| Parameter | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `timeout` | Maximum time to wait in seconds |
| `settle_window` | How long robot must be stable to be considered stopped |
| `speed_threshold` | Max joint speed to be considered stopped (deg/s) |
| `angle_threshold` | Max angle change to be considered stopped (degrees) |

**Returns:** True if robot stopped, False if timeout

**Raises:**

- `ConnectionError`: If the controller session changes while a command is still being waited on.

### `wait_status` 

```python
rbt.wait_status(predicate: Callable[[StatusBuffer], bool], timeout: float = 5.0) -> bool
```

Wait until a multicast status satisfies predicate(status) within timeout.

### `checkpoint` 

```python
rbt.checkpoint(label: str) -> int
```

Insert a checkpoint marker in the motion queue.

Returns the command index (≥ 0) on success, -1 on failure.

```python
rbt.checkpoint("pick_done")
```

| Parameter | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `label` | Checkpoint label for progress tracking |

### `wait_checkpoint` 

```python
rbt.wait_checkpoint(label: str, timeout: float = 30.0) -> bool
```

Wait until a checkpoint with the given label has been reached.

```python
rbt.wait_checkpoint("pick_done")
```

| Parameter | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `label` | Checkpoint label to wait for |
| `timeout` | Maximum wait time in seconds |

### `delay` 

```python
rbt.delay(seconds: float) -> int
```

Insert a non-blocking delay in the motion queue.

Returns the command index (≥ 0) on success, -1 on failure.

```python
rbt.delay(1.0)
```

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/reference/python/tools/ -->

# Tools

Selecting a tool, the generic tool action, and the methods of the bound tool object `rbt.tool`. Tool actions are
queued with the motion; `tool.stop()` is immediate. [Tools and the TCP](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/programming/02-python-api/tools-and-tcp/)
in the guide.

## Registered tools

| Key | Tool | Variants (default first) |
|---|---|---|
| `NONE` | Bare flange - no tool attached | — |
| `PNEUMATIC` | Pneumatic gripper assembly (vertical/horizontal mounting) | `vertical`, `horizontal` |
| `SSG-48` | SSG-48 adaptive electric gripper (Spectral micro BLDC) | `finger`, `pinch` |
| `MSG` | MSG compliant AI stepper gripper (StepFOC) | `100mm`, `150mm`, `200mm` |
| `VACUUM` | Vacuum gripper (pneumatic valve I/O) | — |

## Selecting and acting

### `select_tool` 

```python
rbt.select_tool(tool_name: str, variant_key: str = '') -> int
```

Set the active end-effector tool on the controller.

```python
rbt.select_tool("PNEUMATIC")
```

| Parameter | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `tool_name` | Name of the tool ('NONE', 'PNEUMATIC', 'SSG-48', 'MSG', 'VACUUM') |
| `variant_key` | Optional variant within the tool type. |

**Returns:** Command index (>= 0) if queued, 0 on failure.

### `tool_action` 

```python
rbt.tool_action(
    tool_key: str,
    action: str,
    params: list | None = None,
    *,
    wait: bool = False,
    timeout: float = 10.0,
) -> int
```

Send a generic tool action command.

Returns the command index (>= 0) on success, -1 on failure. The action and its parameters are checked before anything is sent: a malformed one raises `ValueError`. A key naming a tool other than the selected one is refused by the controller.

A tool action is queued work: it runs in queue order with motion, the arm holding still while it does, so a wait on it covers the motion queued ahead of it, and one sent after a blended move ends the blend there. A `move` before a completed `calibrate` is refused when its turn comes, failing its own index; a tool action that fails cancels what is queued behind it (`MOTN_CANCELLED`). A pause holds the tool actions still queued. `stop()`, `estop()`, `reset_state()`, a teleport, or a jog or servo stream taking the arm discards them and halts the one running where the jaws are, keeping the grip.

`stop` alone acts at once, on the tool fitted now: it halts the action running, failing it as cancelled by a tool stop, keeps what is queued behind it, and holds the next queued tool action until the jaws are still.

Electric grippers take `move [position, speed, current]` (exactly three fractions in `[0, 1]`; current spans the tool's `current_range`), `calibrate`, `stop` (halt in place, keep grip) and `idle` (release, the jaws left where they are); `set_position`/`open`/`close` map onto `move`. Pneumatic grippers take `open`, `close`, and `move`/`set_position [position]`.

```python
rbt.tool_action("PNEUMATIC", "open")
```

| Parameter | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `tool_key` | Tool registry key (e.g. "PNEUMATIC", "SSG-48", "MSG") |
| `action` | Action name (e.g. "open", "close", "move", "calibrate") |
| `params` | Positional parameters (meaning defined by tool config) |
| `wait` | If True, block until action completes |
| `timeout` | Maximum time to wait in seconds (only used when wait=True) |

!!! note
    The actions of the electric grippers: `move` with `[position, speed, current]` as fractions, `calibrate`,
    `stop`, `idle` (release). Of the pneumatic and vacuum grippers: `open`, `close`, and `move` (or
    `set_position`) with `[position]`, below 0.5 opening and from 0.5 closing. The tool methods below call these.

## The electric gripper tool (SSG-48, MSG)

### `tool.set_position` (electric) 

```python
rbt.tool.set_position(
    position: float,
    *,
    speed: float = 0.5,
    current: float = 0.5,
    **wait_kwargs: Any,
) -> int
```

Moves the jaws to `position`, 0 open and 1 closed, at `speed` (a fraction of the gripper's speed range) and with
`current` as the current limit, the grip force. `current` is a fraction of the tool's current range: 100 to
1300 mA for the SSG-48, 100 to 2800 mA for the MSG, so `current=0.5` is 700 mA or 1450 mA. Queued: it waits for
the motion before it, and the motion after it waits for the jaws to arrive, stop on a part or stall. Refused
when its turn comes on a gripper that was never calibrated.

### `tool.open` (electric) 

```python
rbt.tool.open(*, speed: float = 0.5, current: float = 0.5, **wait_kwargs: Any) -> int
```

`set_position(0.0, ...)`: the jaws fully open.

### `tool.close` (electric) 

```python
rbt.tool.close(*, speed: float = 0.5, current: float = 0.5, **wait_kwargs: Any) -> int
```

`set_position(1.0, ...)`: the jaws close until they reach the end or stop on a part.

### `tool.calibrate` (electric) 

```python
rbt.tool.calibrate(**kwargs: object) -> int
```

Sends the gripper its calibration: it opens fully and closes fully to find its end stops. Queued. The API counts
it done after a fixed 2 s (200 control cycles) and does not read the gripper's calibrated bit; the SSG-48 needs
about 3 s and the MSG 5 to 6 s, so queue a `delay()` after it ([Calibrating](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/programming/02-python-api/tools-and-tcp/#calibrating)).
There is no clear-error action: a latched gripper error is cleared from the commander or Motor GUI.

### `tool.release` (electric) 

```python
rbt.tool.release(**kwargs: object) -> int
```

Drop the grip, freeing the jaws for manual handling, once the commands queued ahead of it have run. The jaws stay where they are.

### `tool.stop` (electric) 

```python
rbt.tool.stop(**kwargs: object) -> int
```

Halt the jaws where they are, keeping the grip, ahead of anything still queued: the action running fails as cancelled, and the queue behind it is kept. On an uncalibrated gripper, which has no position to hold, this releases instead.

## The pneumatic gripper tool (PNEUMATIC, VACUUM)

### `tool.set_position` (pneumatic) 

```python
rbt.tool.set_position(position: float, **kwargs: float | int) -> int
```

Binary position: < 0.5 opens, >= 0.5 closes.

### `tool.open` (pneumatic) 

```python
rbt.tool.open(**kwargs: float | int) -> int
```

Switches output 1 high, queued with the motion; the action lasts the tool's estimated stroke (a single control
cycle for the vacuum gripper). Which way the gripper moves depends on the tubing.

### `tool.close` (pneumatic) 

```python
rbt.tool.close(**kwargs: float | int) -> int
```

Switches output 1 low, queued with the motion; otherwise as `open()`.

Every tool object also has `status()`, returning the `ToolStatus` of the selected tool: `key`, `state`,
`engaged`, `part_detected`, `fault_code`, `positions`, `channels` and `variant_key`. For the electric grippers,
[Tool status](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/programming/02-python-api/tools-and-tcp/#tool-status) says where each field comes from.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/reference/python/io/ -->

# I/O

The control board's digital inputs and outputs. The firmware's I/O byte is `[in1, in2, out1, out2, estop, ...]`;
reads return the first five, writes take the logical output index 0 or 1. [I/O, delays and checkpoints](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/programming/02-python-api/io-and-delays/)
in the guide.

### `write_io` 

```python
rbt.write_io(index: int, value: int, *, timeout: float | None = None) -> int
```

Set digital output by logical index (0 = first output pin).

The firmware I/O byte layout is `[in0, in1, out0, out1, estop, ...]` so logical output index 0 maps to bit position 2.

Returns the command index (≥ 0) on success, -1 on failure.

`timeout` bounds command acceptance. TimeoutError leaves application unconfirmed; None uses the client defaults.

```python
rbt.write_io(0, 1)   # Set first output HIGH
```

The read side is `io()` under [Queries](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/reference/python/queries/#io), and `is_estop_pressed()`.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/reference/python/configuration/ -->

# Configuration

The hardware connection, the motion profile, the TCP corrections, the collision world and the status rate.
[Tools and the TCP](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/programming/02-python-api/tools-and-tcp/) and [The controller](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/programming/02-python-api/controller/)
in the guide.

### `connect_hardware` 

```python
rbt.connect_hardware(port_str: str) -> int
```

Connect to robot hardware via serial port.

```python
rbt.connect_hardware("/dev/ttyUSB0")
```

| Parameter | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `port_str` | Serial port path (e.g., '/dev/ttyUSB0' or 'COM3'). |

**Returns:** 1 if acknowledged, 0 on failure.

**Raises:**

- `ValueError`: If port_str is empty.

### `select_profile` 

```python
rbt.select_profile(profile: str) -> int
```

Set the motion profile (e.g. `"TOPPRA"`).

```python
rbt.select_profile("TOPPRA")
```

| Parameter | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `profile` | Motion profile type ('TOPPRA', 'RUCKIG', 'QUINTIC', 'TRAPEZOID', 'LINEAR') |
| `Note` | RUCKIG is point-to-point only; Cartesian moves will use TOPPRA. |

**Returns:** 1 once the profile is selected, 0 when no reply arrives.

**Raises:**

- `MotionError`: when `profile` is not a profile name.

!!! note
    The profiles of this version: `TOPPRA`, `RUCKIG`, `QUINTIC`, `TRAPEZOID`, `LINEAR`. [Motion profiles](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/theory/motion-profiles/)
    says what each does.

### `set_tcp_offset` 

```python
rbt.set_tcp_offset(x: float = 0, y: float = 0, z: float = 0) -> int
```

Set TCP offset in mm, composed on top of the current tool transform.

The offset shifts the effective TCP point in the tool's local frame. Subsequent motion (especially TRF relative moves) will use the new TCP. Returns the queued index; await `wait_command(index)` to confirm application. This translation-only setter clears user TCP rotation. Call with (0, 0, 0) to reset. Changing tools resets the offset.

```python
rbt.set_tcp_offset(0, 0, -190)  # pencil tip 190mm from gripper
```

### `set_tcp_transform` 

```python
rbt.set_tcp_transform(
    x: float = 0,
    y: float = 0,
    z: float = 0,
    roll: float = 0,
    pitch: float = 0,
    yaw: float = 0,
) -> int
```

*No docstring.*

### `tcp_offset` 

```python
rbt.tcp_offset() -> list[float]
```

Query current TCP offset in mm [x, y, z].

```python
offset = rbt.tcp_offset()
```

### `tcp_transform` 

```python
rbt.tcp_transform() -> list[float]
```

*No docstring.*

!!! note
    `set_tcp_transform(x, y, z, roll, pitch, yaw)`: millimetres and intrinsic XYZ degrees relative to the
    registered tool. Both setters return a queued index; wait for it before relying on the correction. The TCP
    queries raise `TimeoutError` instead of returning a misleading zero when the controller does not answer.

### `set_shapes` 

```python
rbt.set_shapes(shapes: list) -> int
```

Replace the program-layer collision-world shapes (keep-out barriers).

Collision-enabled shapes are added to the controller's checkers so motion is blocked against them; an empty list clears the program layer. Installation-layer shapes (robot config) are unaffected.

Acknowledged: returns 1 only after the controller confirms the world was applied; 0 on timeout. Raises MotionError if the controller rejects the shapes.

```python
rbt.set_shapes([Box(name="table", x=0.6, y=0.4, z=0.02,
                    pose=(0.3, 0, -0.01, 0, 0, 0))])
```

!!! note
    Shapes are the program layer of the collision world: boxes and other primitives with a pose in metres and
    extrinsic XYZ radians, collision-enabled or visual only, attachable to the flange as held objects. The
    installation layer, from the robot's configuration, is not affected.

### `set_status_rate` 

```python
rbt.set_status_rate(hz: float) -> int
```

Set the rate the controller broadcasts status at.

```python
rbt.set_status_rate(100)
```


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/reference/python/status/ -->

# Status fields

The fields of the status buffer the controller broadcasts, as `stream_status()` yields it and `status()`
summarises it, from the source at v0.9.1. Arrays are numpy arrays.

| Field | Type |
|---|---|
| `session_id` | `int` |
| `seq` | `int` |
| `mono_time_ns` | `int` |
| `pose` | `np.ndarray` |
| `angles` | `np.ndarray` |
| `speeds` | `np.ndarray` |
| `io` | `np.ndarray` |
| `tool_status` | `ToolStatus` |
| `joint_en` | `np.ndarray` |
| `cart_en_wrf` | `np.ndarray` |
| `cart_en_trf` | `np.ndarray` |
| `action_current` | `str` |
| `action_params` | `str` |
| `action_state` | `ActionState` |
| `executing_index` | `int` |
| `completed_index` | `int` |
| `last_checkpoint` | `str` |
| `error` | `RobotError \| None` |
| `queued_segments` | `int` |
| `queued_duration` | `float` |
| `tcp_speed` | `float` |
| `simulator_active` | `bool` |
| `collision_active` | `bool` |
| `collision_pairs` | `list[tuple[str, str]]` |
| `scene_epoch` | `int` |
| `accepted_index` | `int` |
| `homed` | `bool` |
| `enabled` | `bool` |
| `torques` | `np.ndarray` |
| `torques_ext` | `np.ndarray` |
| `warnings` | `list[tuple]` |
| `link_health` | `dict` |
| `drive_health` | `dict` |
| `loop_health` | `dict` |
| `homing` | `dict` |
| `cart_en` | `dict[str, np.ndarray]` |

## Meaning

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `session_id`, `seq`, `mono_time_ns` | The status publisher's lifetime (changes on restart), a sequence number (gaps mean missed broadcasts), and the monotonic time of the controller's snapshot |
| `pose` | The tool pose as a 4×4 matrix, flattened (16 values), in the WRF |
| `angles`, `speeds` | Joint angles in degrees and speeds in deg/s, J1 to J6 |
| `io` | `[in1, in2, out1, out2, estop]` |
| `tool_status` | The selected tool's `ToolStatus`; key `NONE` when no tool is fitted |
| `joint_en`, `cart_en_wrf`, `cart_en_trf`, `cart_en` | Enablement: whether each joint, and each Cartesian axis in each frame, can still move in the positive and negative direction (12 values: six axes, two directions) |
| `action_current`, `action_params`, `action_state` | What the controller is executing, its parameters, and the state: idle, executing, error |
| `executing_index`, `completed_index`, `accepted_index` | The index of the command running, the highest completed, and the latest accepted |
| `last_checkpoint` | The label of the last checkpoint reached |
| `error` | The current `RobotError`, or `None` |
| `queued_segments`, `queued_duration` | How much motion is queued, in segments and in seconds of estimated duration (tool actions included) |
| `tcp_speed` | The tool's linear speed in mm/s |
| `simulator_active` | Simulator mode |
| `collision_active`, `collision_pairs` | Whether the collision checker is on, and the pairs it currently reports |
| `scene_epoch` | Changes when the collision world changes: re-query `shapes()` |
| `homed`, `enabled` | Whether the robot is referenced, and whether motion is enabled |
| `torques`, `torques_ext` | Reserved for arms with torque sensing; zero on PAROL6 |
| `warnings`, `link_health`, `drive_health`, `loop_health` | Diagnostics: warnings, the serial link, the drives, the control loop timing |
| `homing` | The progress of a homing sequence |

The buffer's `freedrive` property is always false: PAROL6's steppers cannot be back-driven. `mode` is an alias of
`action_state`.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/reference/python/errors/ -->

# Errors

The error codes of the controller, with the catalog text a `MotionError` carries, from the source at
v0.9.1. The number ranges: 10 to 19 inverse kinematics, 20 to 29 trajectory planning, 30 to 39
motion execution, 40 to 49 communication, 50 to 59 system and safety. `MOTN_CANCELLED` uses the number shared
with the waldoctl interface, so that a client sees one code for a discarded command whichever arm raised it.
[Errors](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/programming/02-python-api/errors/) in the guide says how to recover.

| Code | Number | Title | Cause | Effect | Remedy |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `IK_TARGET_UNREACHABLE` | 10 | IK: target unreachable | Target pose has no valid IK solution. {detail} | Motion command rejected. Pipeline halted. | Verify target is within workspace. Try different orientation. |
| `IK_PARTIAL_PATH` | 11 | IK: partial path failure | Only {valid}/{total} poses along the path are reachable. | Motion command rejected. Pipeline halted. | Shorten the move, add intermediate waypoints, or adjust orientation. |
| `TRAJ_EMPTY_RESULT` | 20 | Trajectory: empty result | Trajectory generation returned no waypoints. {detail} | Motion command rejected. | Check motion parameters. Start and end may be too close. |
| `TRAJ_NO_STEPS` | 21 | Trajectory: no steps | Trajectory calculation produced zero steps. {detail} | Motion command rejected. | Increase duration or reduce speed fraction. |
| `MOTN_HOME_TIMEOUT` | 30 | Homing timeout | Robot did not start homing sequence within timeout. | Home command aborted. | Check serial connection and robot power. Ensure E-stop is released. |
| `MOTN_GRIPPER_TIMEOUT` | 31 | Gripper timeout | Gripper command timed out in state {state}. | Gripper command aborted. | Check gripper connection and calibration. |
| `MOTN_GRIPPER_UNKNOWN` | 32 | Gripper: unknown state | Gripper entered an unknown internal state. | Gripper command aborted. | Reset the controller and recalibrate the gripper. |
| `MOTN_SETUP_FAILED` | 33 | Command setup failed | Command could not be initialized. {detail} | Command rejected. Pipeline halted. | Check command parameters and robot state. |
| `MOTN_TICK_FAILED` | 34 | Command execution error | Unexpected error during execution. {detail} | Command aborted. Robot stopped. | Check robot state. May need to re-home. |
| `MOTN_NOT_HOMED` | 35 | Robot not homed |  |  |  |
| `MOTN_CANCELLED` | shared | Command cancelled | The command was cancelled by {scope} before it finished. | The motion did not run to completion. | Re-issue the command if the motion is still wanted. |
| `COMM_QUEUE_FULL` | 40 | Command queue full | Motion queue at maximum capacity. | Command rejected. | Wait for current motions to complete. |
| `COMM_UNKNOWN_COMMAND` | 41 | Unknown command | No handler for received command type. | Command ignored. | Check client library version matches server. |
| `COMM_DECODE_ERROR` | 42 | Command decode error | Failed to decode command. {detail} | Command ignored. | Check command encoding. Possible version mismatch. |
| `COMM_VALIDATION_ERROR` | 43 | Command validation error | Invalid parameters. {detail} | Command rejected. | Check parameter ranges and types. |
| `SYS_STATUS_RATE_INVALID` | 55 | Status rate not achievable | Status is broadcast every Nth control tick, so {requested} Hz does not divide the {control} Hz control loop evenly. | Broadcast rate unchanged. | Pick a rate that divides {control} Hz: {allowed}. |
| `SYS_CONTROLLER_DISABLED` | 50 | Controller disabled | Motion command sent while controller is disabled. {detail} | Command rejected. | Call reset() to re-enable the controller. |
| `SYS_ESTOP_ACTIVE` | 51 | E-stop active | Emergency stop is currently engaged. | All motion stopped. Queue cleared. | Release the E-stop button and call reset(). |
| `SYS_PORT_SAVE_FAILED` | 52 | Serial port save failed | Could not save serial port configuration. | Port may not persist across restarts. | Check file permissions and disk space. |
| `SYS_PROFILE_INVALID` | 53 | Invalid motion profile | Unrecognized motion profile: {detail} | Profile not changed. | Use one of: TOPPRA, RUCKIG, QUINTIC, TRAPEZOID, LINEAR. |
| `SYS_NOT_SIMULATOR` | 56 | Simulator-only command | {detail} is only available on the simulator. | Command rejected; the arm is unchanged. | Switch to the simulator with simulator(True), or drive the arm with a planned move. |
| `SYS_SELF_COLLISION` | 54 | Self-collision predicted | Planned configuration would self-collide at sample {sample} of {total}: {pairs} | Motion command rejected before dispatch. | Choose a different target, add intermediate waypoints, or disable via PAROL6_COLLISION_CHECK=0. |

A `RobotError` has the fields `code`, `title`, `cause`, `effect` and `remedy`, and `str(error)` joins them.
