<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/reference/python/controller/ -->

# The controller and its environment

## The command line

`parol6-server`, from the source at v0.9.1:

| Option | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `--host` | `0.0.0.0` | UDP host address |
| `--port` | `5001` | UDP port |
| `--serial` | — | Serial port (e.g., /dev/ttyUSB0 or COM3) |
| `--baudrate` | `3000000` | Serial baudrate |
| `-v`, `--verbose` | `0` | Increase verbosity; -v=INFO, -vv=DEBUG, -vvv=TRACE |
| `-q`, `--quiet` | flag | Enable quiet logging (WARNING level) |
| `--log-level` | — | Set specific log level (one of `TRACE`, `DEBUG`, `INFO`, `WARNING`, `ERROR`, `CRITICAL`) |

Without `--serial` the controller starts in simulator mode. The port can also come from `PAROL6_COM_PORT` or from
the file the last successful port was saved to.

## Environment variables

Read at the controller's start:

| Variable | Default |
|---|---|
| `PAROL6_BLEND_HOLD_S` | `0.1` |
| `PAROL6_BUSY_THRESHOLD_MS` | `1.0` |
| `PAROL6_COLLISION_CHECK` | `1` |
| `PAROL6_COLLISION_CLEARANCE_M` | `0.005` |
| `PAROL6_COLLISION_JOG_LOOKAHEAD_S` | `0.15` |
| `PAROL6_COLLISION_PATH_SAMPLES` | `16` |
| `PAROL6_COLLISION_SRDF` | `computed` |
| `PAROL6_COM_FILE` | `computed` |
| `PAROL6_COM_PORT` | — |
| `PAROL6_CONTROL_RATE_HZ` | `100` |
| `PAROL6_EXECUTION_OVERRIDE_TRANSITION_S` | `1.0` |
| `PAROL6_MAX_BACKLOG_COUNT` | `500` |
| `PAROL6_MAX_BLEND_LOOKAHEAD` | `100` |
| `PAROL6_MCAST_GROUP` | `239.255.0.101` |
| `PAROL6_MCAST_IF` | `127.0.0.1` |
| `PAROL6_MCAST_PORT` | `50510` |
| `PAROL6_MCAST_TTL` | `1` |
| `PAROL6_PATH_SAMPLES` | `200` |
| `PAROL6_SERIAL` | — |
| `PAROL6_SETTLE_MAX_TICKS` | `20` |
| `PAROL6_STATUS_RATE_HZ` | `50` |
| `PAROL6_STATUS_STALE_S` | `0.5` |
| `PAROL6_STATUS_TRANSPORT` | `MULTICAST` |
| `PAROL6_STATUS_UNICAST_HOST` | `127.0.0.1` |
| `PAROL_TRACE` | `0` |

A default marked *computed* is a path or an expression; see `parol6/config.py`. [The controller](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/programming/02-python-api/controller/)
in the guide says which ones matter.

## The wire protocol

Clients and the controller exchange msgpack messages over UDP: a command or query with a request ID, and an OK,
an error, a response or a status. The protocol version is checked in every status broadcast, and a client that
speaks another version raises `ProtocolVersionError`. The command and query types of this version:

**Commands:** `CmdType.PING` and the others, 54 in all, the queries among them; **queries:** `PING`, `STATUS`,
`ANGLES`, `POSE`, `IO`, `SPEEDS`, `TOOL`, `QUEUE`, `CURRENT_ACTION`, `LOOP_STATS`, `PROFILE`, `TOOL_STATUS`,
`ENABLEMENT`, `ERROR`, `TCP_SPEED`, `IS_SIMULATOR`, `TCP_OFFSET`, `SHAPES`, `STATUS_RATE`, `TCP_TRANSFORM`,
`EXECUTION_SPEED`, `COMMAND_COMPLETION`. The definitions are `parol6/protocol/wire.py`; a program in another
language can speak the protocol from them, though the Python client is the supported path.

## Python

The package needs Python >=3.11.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/reference/rbtscript/ -->

# RBTscript commands

The commands of the commander software's program language, as its interpreter accepts them. One command per
line; arguments in the order given; angles in degrees, positions in millimetres, speed and acceleration in
percent, time in seconds. [RBTscript](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/programming/03-commander/rbtscript/) in the guide has the rules and
examples.

| Command | Arguments | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `Begin()` | | Must be the first line, or the program is refused |
| `End()` | | Stops the program; the last line must be `End()` or `Loop()` |
| `Loop()` | | Restart at the line after `Begin()` |
| `Delay(t)` | `t` seconds, more than 0.01 | Wait; `Delay(0.01)` is refused |
| `MoveJoint(j1,j2,j3,j4,j5,j6, v=, a=, t=, trap\|poly, speed)` | six joint angles; `v`, `a` in % for the leading joint; `t` duration; the bare word `trap` or `poly`; the word `speed` | A move to joint angles, straight in joint space |
| `MovePose(x,y,z,Rx,Ry,Rz, v=, a=, t=, trap\|poly, speed)` | a WRF pose, then as `MoveJoint` | IK at the target, then a joint-space move |
| `MoveCart(x,y,z,Rx,Ry,Rz, v=, a=, t=, trap\|poly, speed)` | a WRF pose; `t`; `poly` or `trap`; `speed` | A straight-line move of the tool in the WRF; stops at a singularity. With `t`: trapezoidal unless `poly`. Without `t`: always 3.6 s |
| `MoveCartRelTRF(x,y,z,Rx,Ry,Rz, v=, a=, t=, trap\|poly, speed)` | a pose relative to the tool frame | A straight-line move relative to the tool; timing as `MoveCart` |
| `SpeedJoint()` | | No action: the program stops on it until Stop |
| `SpeedCart()` | | Not accepted: a program containing it is refused |
| `Output(n,HIGH\|LOW)` | output 1; `HIGH` or `LOW`, no space | Sets output 1; `Output(2,...)` is refused in the current version and stops the program |
| `Input()`, `Home()` | | No action: the program stops on it until Stop |
| `Gripper_cal()` | | Calibrates the electric gripper (clear its error in the Gripper tab first; activation is the tab's Activate option); follow with `Delay(4)` for the SSG-48, `Delay(7)` for the MSG |
| `Gripper(position, speed, current)` | whole numbers: 0 to 255; 0 to 255; mA, 100 to 1000 | Moves the electric gripper; continues at once, so follow with a `Delay()` |

Rules for `MoveJoint` and `MovePose`: `t` overrides `v` and `a` and makes the profile polynomial unless the word
`trap` follows; `v` with `a` makes it trapezoidal; neither gives a conservative trapezoid; `speed` as the last argument tracks the
speed curve only and may stop short of the target. `MoveCart` and `MoveCartRelTRF` are trapezoidal with `t` unless
`poly` follows, and take 3.6 s for any move without `t`. The list is in the commander's `PAROL6_ROBOT.py` as
`Commands_list`.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/reference/serial-protocol/ -->

# The serial protocol

The packets between the PC and the control board, from the firmware's `main.cpp` (`Unpack_data`, `Pack_data`).
Serial over USB at 3 000 000 baud; the PC sends one command packet per 10 ms cycle and the board answers each
valid packet with one telemetry packet. Multi-byte values are big-endian; positions and speeds are signed 24-bit
integers in motor microsteps and microsteps per second. [The serial protocol](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/board/10-serial-protocol/) in
the Control Board Manual explains the cycle.

## PC → board: the command packet

| Offset after the length byte | Size | Field | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| — | 3 | Start bytes | `0xFF 0xFF 0xFF` |
| — | 1 | Length | 52: the number of bytes that follow, CRC and end bytes included |
| 0 | 18 | Joints[6] | Commanded position of each joint, 3 bytes each, signed, microsteps |
| 18 | 18 | Speed[6] | Commanded speed of each joint, 3 bytes each, signed, microsteps/s |
| 36 | 1 | Command | The command byte, below |
| 37 | 1 | Affected joint | Bit per joint; reserved |
| 38 | 1 | InOut | Bits from the MSB: bit 2 = output 1, bit 3 = output 2; the rest reserved |
| 39 | 1 | Timeout | Reserved |
| 40 | 2 | Gripper position | 0 to 255 |
| 42 | 2 | Gripper speed | 0 to 255 |
| 44 | 2 | Gripper current | mA |
| 46 | 1 | Gripper command | Bits from the MSB: 0 activate, 1 action, 2 E-stop, 3 release direction |
| 47 | 1 | Gripper mode | 0 operate, 1 calibrate, 2 clear error |
| 48 | 1 | Gripper ID | The gripper's CAN ID |
| 49 | 1 | CRC | Reserved: carried, not checked by firmware 1 |
| 50 | 2 | End bytes | `0x01 0x02` |

## Command bytes

| Value | Name | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| 255 | Idle (dummy) | The joints stand still (speeds are set, no joint is stepped). Continues a homing in progress |
| 123 | Jog | Runs each joint at its commanded speed |
| 156 | Go to position with speed | Runs each joint at the average of the commanded speed and the speed that closes the position error in one cycle |
| 100 | Home | Starts the homing sequence |
| 101 | Enable | Enables motion, resets the homing state |
| 102 | Disable | Disables motion; the motors hold |
| 103 | Clear error | Resets the homing state |
| 69 | Repeatability test | A built-in two-pose cycle |

The gripper fields are forwarded over CAN every cycle: a move frame when any of them changed, a calibrate for
mode 1, a clear error for mode 2, an empty status poll otherwise.

## Board → PC: the telemetry packet

| Offset after the length byte | Size | Field | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| — | 3 | Start bytes | `0xFF 0xFF 0xFF` |
| — | 1 | Length | 56 |
| 0 | 18 | Position[6] | Actual position of each joint, 3 bytes each, signed, microsteps |
| 18 | 18 | Speed[6] | Actual speed of each joint |
| 36 | 1 | Homed | Bits from the MSB: joint 1 to joint 6 homed; bits 6 and 7 set |
| 37 | 1 | IO | Bits from the MSB: input 1, input 2, output 1, output 2, E-stop (1 = closed, not pressed); bits 5 to 7 set |
| 38 | 1 | Temperature error | Bits from the MSB: joint 1 to joint 6, reserved, reported cleared by firmware 1; bits 6 and 7 set |
| 39 | 1 | Position error | Bits from the MSB: joint 1 to joint 6, reserved; bits 6 and 7 set |
| 40 | 2 | Timing data | Ticks of 1.422 µs between the last two valid packets (90 MHz / 128); 7031 = 10 ms |
| 42 | 1 | Timeout error | Reserved |
| 43 | 1 | XTR2 | The last command byte received |
| 44 | 1 | Gripper ID | Always 0 in firmware 1 (not reported by the gripper) |
| 45 | 2 | Gripper position | 0 to 255 |
| 47 | 2 | Gripper speed | Always 1 in firmware 1 (not reported by the gripper) |
| 49 | 2 | Gripper current | mA |
| 51 | 1 | Gripper status | The gripper's status byte, bits from the MSB: activated, moving to a position, object detection (bits 5 and 4, bit 5 the low bit: 0 moving, 1 object while closing, 2 object while opening, 3 at position), temperature error, timeout error, E-stop error, calibrated |
| 52 | 1 | Object detection | Always 1 in firmware 1; the real value is in the status byte's object-detection bits |
| 53 | 1 | CRC | Reserved |
| 54 | 2 | End bytes | `0x01 0x02` |

The gripper's status byte and object detection are as the gripper manuals define them.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/reference/firmware-parameters/ -->

# Firmware parameters

The per-joint parameters of the control board's main firmware (`constants.h`, `motor_init.cpp`, `main.cpp` at
release V1): what a builder edits when mastering, fitting a different tool, reducing the currents, or fixing a
joint's direction. Steps are 32-microstep motor steps. [Firmware](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/board/08-firmware/) says how to upload a
change.

## Currents (`constants.h`)

| Define | Value | Note |
|---|---|---|
| `MICROSTEP` | 32 | |
| `MOTOR1_MAX_CURRENT` | 2000 mA | motor rated 2100 |
| `MOTOR2_MAX_CURRENT` | 2000 mA | motor rated 2100 |
| `MOTOR3_MAX_CURRENT` | 1900 mA | motor rated 2000 |
| `MOTOR4_MAX_CURRENT` | 1700 mA | reduced: the motor is enclosed in the forearm |
| `MOTOR5_MAX_CURRENT` | 1700 mA | reduced: enclosed |
| `MOTOR6_MAX_CURRENT` | 965 mA | motor rated 1000 |
| `VERSION` | 1 | |

The driver is set to `MOTORx_MAX_CURRENT × 0.85` as the running current and `hold_multiplier` of that for holding
(the per-joint table below has both); the driver rounds them to its own current steps.

## Per joint (`motor_init.cpp`)

| Parameter | J1 | J2 | J3 | J4 | J5 | J6 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `reduction_ratio` | 6.4 | 20 | 18.0952 | 4 | 4 | 10 |
| `standby_position` (steps at standby) | 10240 | −32000 | 57905 | 0 | 0 | 32000 |
| `homed_position` (steps from the switch to standby) | 13500 | 19588 | 23020 | −10200 | 8900 (`j5_homing_offset`) | 15900 |
| `joint_range_positive_steps` | 14000 | −1200 | 92605 | 7500 | 6400 | 64000 |
| `joint_range_negative_steps` | −14000 | −51587 | 34700 | −7500 | −6400 | 0 |
| `limit_switch_trigger` (input level when triggered) | 0 (inductive) | 1 (switch) | 1 (switch) | 0 (inductive) | 1 (switch) | 0 (inductive) |
| `direction_reversed` | 1 | 0 | 1 | 0 | 0 | 1 |
| `hold_multiplier` | 0.7 | 0.8 | 0.8 | 0.8 | 0.8 | 0.88 |
| Running current, `MOTORx_MAX_CURRENT × 0.85` | 1700 mA | 1700 mA | 1615 mA | 1445 mA | 1445 mA | 820 mA |
| Holding current, the running current × `hold_multiplier` | 1190 mA | 1360 mA | 1292 mA | 1156 mA | 1156 mA | 722 mA |
| Driver position / LIMIT input | 1 / 6 | 6 / 2 | 5 / 3 | 4 / 4 | 2 / 5 | 3 / 1 |

Joint 1's standby of 10240 steps is +90° (90 / 0.05625 × 6.4): the firmware homes to the pose the software
reports as J1 = 90°. The firmware's "standby" is what these pages call the after-homing pose: the standby
pose turned 90° about joint 1 ([Joint limits and directions](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/03-technical-data/joint-limits/#standby-and-after-homing)).

## Joint 5 and the tool (`main.cpp`)

| Variable | Value | Note |
|---|---|---|
| `j5_homing_offset` | 8900 | the pneumatic gripper holder; **8035** for the SSG-48 |

## Homing speeds and distances (`main.cpp`, `home_all`)

The approach speeds in steps/s: J1 −2050, J2 −2550, J3 −2550, J4 5550, J5 −5050, J6 −9550; the back-off
distances 850 (J1), 1050 (J2, J3), 1550 (J4, J5, J6) steps; the slow re-approach −750 steps/s for joints 1 to 3,
±4050 for 4 and 5, −8050 for 6. The firmware uses the second, slow trigger as the reference.

## The serial link

`Serial.begin(3000000)`; the timing counter runs at 90 MHz / 128 = 703 125 Hz.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/reference/test-firmware/ -->

# Test firmware commands

The commands the test firmware (`PAROL6 control board test code`) acts on: `#` followed by the name, case as
written, and a line feed (a terminal that sends only a carriage return gets no answer). None takes an argument.
[The test firmware](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/board/09-test-firmware/) in the Control Board Manual shows the output.

!!! danger "The motors turn from power-on"
    The test firmware turns all six motors slowly from the moment it boots until the power is switched off; no
    command stops them.

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `#IO` | Prints, once a second, the E-stop input, input 1, input 2 and the supply voltage in mV |
| `#LIMIT` | Prints, once a second, `Joint N is pressed` for every triggered limit switch |
| `#STOP` | Ends the `#IO` or `#LIMIT` printout; the motors keep turning |
| `#start` | Toggles the two LEDs |

The parser (`SerialPacketParser.cpp`) also recognises `STATUS`, `STEP1` to `STEP6`, `INPUT`, `ESTOP`, `OUT1TOGGLE`,
`OUT2TOGGLE`, `LED1TOGGLE`, `LED2TOGGLE`, `SUPPLYV`, `ONOFF`, `CAN` and `FLASH`, but `main.cpp` has no action for
them (the `FLASH` test is commented out): each is answered with `Unknown command`. The driver report (`joint N
Connection is: GOOD` or `BAD`, the currents and fault flags) is printed once, about three seconds after power-on,
not on a command.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/theory/ -->

# Theory corner

The theory behind a six-axis robot arm and its software, explained in the order you meet it: what a joint angle and a pose are,
which frames the numbers are in, how the software goes from one to the other, why some poses cannot be reached
and some moves cannot be made, what shape a move has in time, and who is in charge of the robot at any moment.
Each page says how the idea shows up in PAROL6's software. None of it needs maths beyond what is on the page,
and none of it is needed to run the robot: read it when you want to know why the robot does what it does.

## The pages

- [Units](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/theory/units/)
- [Joints, directions and the standby pose](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/theory/joints-and-poses/)
- [Reference frames](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/theory/reference-frames/)
- [Pose and orientation](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/theory/pose-and-orientation/)
- [Forward and inverse kinematics](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/theory/kinematics/)
- [Configurations and singularities](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/theory/configurations-and-singularities/)
- [Workspace and reach](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/theory/workspace-and-reach/)
- [Homing and mastering](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/theory/homing-and-mastering/)
- [Motion profiles](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/theory/motion-profiles/)
- [Blending](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/theory/blending/)
- [Target, commanded and actual](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/theory/target-commanded-actual/)
- [Control ownership](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/theory/control-ownership/)
- [Steppers, open loop and backlash](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/theory/steppers-and-open-loop/)
- [Further reading](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/theory/further-reading/)

## Robot types

Industrial robots are sorted by their joints and how they are arranged: vertically articulated arms, Cartesian
gantries, cylindrical and polar arms, SCARA arms, delta robots. PAROL6 is a **vertically articulated** arm with
six revolute joints, the most common industrial type, and the ideas on these pages are the ones every such
arm uses. The last three joints meet in a point, a **spherical wrist**, which the pages on kinematics return to.

![A robot with a spherical wrist (left) and one without (right)](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/assets/spherical.png){ width="650" }


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/theory/units/ -->

# Units

Robotics mixes units, and PAROL6's software converts between them at several places. The rule is: the interfaces
speak degrees and millimetres, the firmware speaks motor steps, and the maths in between is in radians and
metres.

| Quantity | At the interface (commander GUI, RBTscript, Python API) | Inside the software | At the firmware |
|---|---|---|---|
| Joint angle | degrees | radians | motor steps (microsteps) |
| Position | millimetres | metres | — |
| Orientation | degrees (three angles) | rotation matrices, radians | — |
| Joint speed | commander: percent of the maximum; API: a fraction of the maximum in (0, 1] | rad/s | steps per second |
| Tool speed | commander: percent; API: a fraction | m/s, rad/s | — |
| Acceleration | percent, or a fraction | rad/s², m/s² | steps/s² |
| Time | seconds | seconds | 10 ms cycles; the timing counter in 1.422 µs ticks |
| Gripper position | commander: 0 to 255; API: a fraction 0 to 1 | | 0 to 255 |
| Gripper current | commander: milliamps; API: a fraction of the tool's current range | | milliamps |

## Steps

The firmware knows nothing but steps: 200 full steps per motor turn, 32 microsteps each, 6400 per turn, times the
joint's gear ratio for a turn of the joint ([Drives, ratios and resolution](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/03-technical-data/drives-and-ratios/)).
The PC software converts with the two constants it keeps in its robot model:

```
degrees per step = 360 / (200 × 32) / ratio          # 0.05625° / ratio
steps = degrees / 0.05625 × ratio
```

## Speed fractions

The Python API's `speed` and `accel` are fractions of the robot model's maxima, in (0, 1], not percentages: a
`speed=0.5` joint move runs the leading joint at half its maximum speed, and the others proportionally so that
all finish together. A `duration` above zero overrides the speed: the move takes that long, whatever the speed
fraction says. The commander's speed slider is a percentage applied to its own, lower, maxima.

## Angles wrap

Joint 3 reports about 105° to 295° and joint 6 0° to 360°, both with the standby at 180°; joints 1, 2, 4 and 5
report signed angles. Orientation angles
wrap at ±180°: a pose with Rz = 179° and one with Rz = −181° are the same, and a program that compares angles
must take that into account.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/theory/joints-and-poses/ -->

# Joints, directions and the standby pose

## Numbering

Joints are numbered 1 to 6 from the base up: J1 turns the whole arm about the vertical axis, J2 is the shoulder,
J3 the elbow, J4 rotates the forearm, J5 pitches the wrist, J6 rotates the tool. The Python API indexes joints
from 0 in its jog calls (`jog_j(0, ...)` is J1) and lists angles in order J1 to J6 everywhere.

Joints 4, 5 and 6 are also called wrist 1, wrist 2 and wrist 3, as in the robot model and ROS.
The forearm is also called the lower arm: both names mean the link from the elbow to the wrist.

![Each joint turned 30 degrees in its positive direction, in colour, over the pose in grey](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/assets/kinematics/parol6_joint_directions.webp){ width="900" }
![Each joint turned 30 degrees in its positive direction, in colour, over the pose in grey](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/assets/kinematics/parol6_joint_directions_dark.webp){ width="900" }

## Positive direction

Each joint has a positive direction, the one in which its angle increases, drawn as the arrows in the figure on
[Joint limits and directions](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/03-technical-data/joint-limits/). The commander's left arrows jog
positive, the right arrows negative. The firmware has a per-joint flag that inverts the motor so that the
hardware agrees with this convention; a new build sets it per joint on the first run.

## Joint space and the standby pose

A set of six joint angles is a point in **joint space**: it describes the arm's configuration completely, and a
joint move is a straight line in it, every joint moving proportionally and finishing at the same time.

The reference point is the **standby pose**, the pose of the Denavit-Hartenberg table; after homing the robot
stands in it turned 90° about joint 1:

| Pose | J1 | J2 | J3 | J4 | J5 | J6 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Standby | 0° | −90° | 180° | 0° | 0° | 180° |
| After homing | 90° | −90° | 180° | 0° | 0° | 180° |

Every joint angle the software reports is measured in this convention. At J1 = 0° the arm points along the
base's X axis, away from the electronics box; homing ends with J1 a quarter turn further, at 90°, and the
software reports 90° there. The Python API calls that after-homing pose its standby.

## Limits

Each joint has a software limit in both directions, enforced by the planner and by the jog, and a mechanical
stop a little past it ([Joint limits and directions](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/03-technical-data/joint-limits/)). The limits are
in the robot model (`PAROL6_ROBOT.py` in both programs); a tool or a base that changes the real clearance does
not change them.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/theory/reference-frames/ -->

# Reference frames

A frame is a coordinate system: an origin and three axes, X, Y and Z, at right angles. A position is three
numbers in a frame; the same point has different numbers in different frames. PAROL6's software uses two frames
you choose between, and several it keeps to itself.

## The right-hand rule

All frames are right-handed: with the right hand's thumb along X and the index finger along Y, the middle finger
points along Z. For rotations, the thumb along the axis, the fingers curl in the positive direction. Every
orientation angle in the software follows this rule.

## WRF, the world reference frame

Fixed to the robot's base: the origin on the axis of joint 1 at the base's mounting surface, Z up, X and Y along
the base. Everything that does not move with the arm is described in it: the table, the parts, the positions a
program teaches. `MoveCart` in RBTscript and `move_l` in the API take WRF poses by default.

## TRF, the tool reference frame

Fixed to the tool: the origin at the tool centre point, Z along the tool's approach direction, X and Y across it.
It moves with the arm. A move **in** the TRF is relative to where the tool is now: "100 mm forward along the
tool" is `MoveCartRelTRF(0,0,100,0,0,0)` or `move_l([0,0,100,0,0,0], frame="TRF", rel=True)`, and it goes in a
different world direction every time, depending on the tool's orientation. Approaching a part along the
gripper's axis, retreating after a grip, and rotating the tool about its own axis are TRF moves.

![The tool frame at the end effector](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/assets/real_frame.webp){ width="600" }

## Jogging in a frame

The commander's Cartesian jog and the API's `jog_l` take the frame: WRF jogs move the tool along the base's
axes, TRF jogs along the tool's own. Switch to TRF to go straight in or out of a part whatever its angle.

## The frames inside

The kinematic model keeps a frame at every joint, each defined relative to the previous one by the
Denavit-Hartenberg parameters, and a frame at the flange. The tool frame is the flange frame moved by the
tool's transform; the Python API's tool definitions and `set_tcp_transform()` set that transform
([Tools and the TCP](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/programming/02-python-api/tools-and-tcp/)). The commander's model has the pneumatic gripper's
transform built in.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/theory/pose-and-orientation/ -->

# Pose and orientation

A **pose** is a position and an orientation together: where the tool is and which way it points. Six numbers:
x, y, z in millimetres and three angles in degrees, `[x, y, z, Rx, Ry, Rz]`, in the frame you name, the WRF
unless you say TRF.

## Position

The tool centre point's coordinates in the frame. For the standard pneumatic gripper the TCP is between the
finger tips; for a selected tool in the API it is the tool's registered point, moved by any offset you set.

## Orientation

Three angles describe how the tool frame is rotated relative to the reference frame. There are many conventions;
PAROL6's software uses **roll, pitch and yaw as rotations about X, Y and Z**, which is what the commander shows
as Rx, Ry, Rz and what the API's `pose()` returns and its motion commands take. The API's `set_tcp_transform()`
takes its angles as intrinsic XYZ rotations, `Rx · Ry · Rz`; its collision shapes take extrinsic XYZ in radians.
When a pose from one program goes into another, check the convention before trusting the numbers.

The same position can be reached with many orientations, and the orientation is what a program usually gets
wrong first: a few degrees off puts a finger into the table. The Python API examples on this site use
`[90, 0, 90]`, the orientation the tool has after homing: horizontal, pointing forward, away from the base. A
tool pointing down at the table has other angles; jog it there and read them.

![The same position with two orientations](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/assets/orientations.webp){ width="650" }

## Reading a pose from the robot

Jog to where you want to be and read the pose: the commander's position display, or `rbt.pose()`. That is how
poses are taught. A taught pose contains the tool's transform: taught with one tool, it is wrong for another.

## Rotating about several axes

A rotation about X followed by one about Y is not the same as Y then X, and three angles at once are hard to
predict. Rotate about one axis per command when you can, especially in the tool frame:

```
MoveCartRelTRF(0, 0, 0, 0, 45, 0)
MoveCartRelTRF(0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 45)
```


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/theory/kinematics/ -->

# Forward and inverse kinematics

Kinematics is the geometry of the arm: how the joint angles decide where the tool is, and the other way round.

## The kinematic diagram and the DH table

A kinematic diagram shows the links and joints without the shapes: six revolute joints, their axes, and the
distances between them. The Denavit-Hartenberg convention writes that down as four numbers per joint, a link
length, a link offset, a joint angle and a link twist, and PAROL6's table is in the Robot Manual
([Dimensions and kinematics](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/03-technical-data/kinematics/)). The commander software's robot model is
built from this table; the Python API loads the robot's URDF, which carries the same geometry, and computes the
kinematics numerically with Pinocchio.

The sheet below shows both at once for PAROL6 with nothing on the flange: the robot's real outline with every
joint at 0, the joint centres J1 to J6, the dimensions a1 to a7 between them, and under it the DH table those
dimensions make. The Robot Manual has the same sheet for every gripper.

![PAROL6, flange only: the dimensions a1 to a7 between the joint centres, and the DH table they make](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/assets/kinematics/parol6_flange.webp){ width="600" }
![PAROL6, flange only: the dimensions a1 to a7 between the joint centres, and the DH table they make](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/assets/kinematics/parol6_flange_dark.webp){ width="600" }

## Forward kinematics

From six joint angles to the pose of the tool. It is a chain of transformations, one per joint, multiplied
together, and it always has exactly one answer: the software runs it every cycle to show you where the tool is.
`rbt.pose()` is forward kinematics of the current angles plus the tool's transform.

## Inverse kinematics

From a pose of the tool to the joint angles that reach it. It is the hard direction. The spherical wrist helps:
the first three joints decide where the wrist centre is, and the last three decide the orientation from there,
so the problem splits in two. Even so:

- A pose can have **several solutions**: elbow up or down, wrist flipped or not, the base turned the other way.
  The software picks the one nearest the current configuration.
- A pose can have **no solution**: out of reach, or an orientation the wrist cannot make from that position.
  The move is refused (`IK_TARGET_UNREACHABLE` in the API, an inverse kinematics error in the commander).
- Near a **singularity** the solution exists but demands enormous joint speeds; the next page.

The Python API solves the inverse kinematics numerically, which is general but can fail on poses a closed-form
solver would find, especially around joint 4; re-planning from a slightly different pose or starting posture
usually helps. `MovePose` in RBTscript and `move_j(pose=...)` in the API solve the kinematics once, at the target,
and move in joint space; `MoveCart` and `move_l` solve it all along a straight line, which is where the next
page matters.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/theory/configurations-and-singularities/ -->

# Configurations and singularities

## Configurations

The same tool pose can be reached with the elbow up or down, the wrist flipped or not, the base facing the
target or turned 180° with the arm reaching backwards. Each combination is a **configuration**. A joint move
keeps the configuration it is in unless the target is in another; a Cartesian move cannot change configuration
at all, because that would mean passing through a pose where two configurations meet, which is a singularity.

Three choices with two answers each make eight configurations. The figure shows all eight for one tool pose:
PAROL6 with nothing on the flange, the tool centre point 250 mm in front of the base and 230 mm up, the tool
tilted 30° from vertical. The flange is in exactly the same place and orientation in every picture; only the
joints differ. The teal dot marks the centre of the flange and the arrow its axis, the same in every
picture.

- **Shoulder right or left**: the wrist centre in front of the joint 1 axis, or behind it with joint 1 turned
  about 180° and the arm reaching back over itself.
- **Elbow up or down**: the elbow above or below the line from the shoulder to the wrist centre.
- **Wrist flipped or not**: joint 5 positive or negative; joints 4 and 6 turn by 180° to keep the tool where it
  is.

![The eight configurations of PAROL6 for one tool pose: elbow up or down, shoulder right or left, wrist flipped or not; of these, only (a) is within the joint limits](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/assets/theory/configurations_parol6.webp){ width="700" }
![The eight configurations of PAROL6 for one tool pose: elbow up or down, shoulder right or left, wrist flipped or not; of these, only (a) is within the joint limits](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/assets/theory/configurations_parol6_dark.webp){ width="700" }

Mathematically all eight reach the pose. On the real robot, the joint limits rule most of them out: for this pose
only (a) is within every joint limit ([Joint limits and directions](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/03-technical-data/joint-limits/)), and
several of the others would also hit the robot itself. The poses were solved and drawn from PAROL6's model in
[robot_descriptions](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/robot_descriptions), the same model the limits come from.

The practical rule: teach the poses of a program in the configuration you want, and make the move between two
configurations a joint move (`MoveJoint`, `move_j`), never a Cartesian one.

How the software chooses, when a target is given as a pose:

- **The Python API** solves every pose starting from the joints where the robot is, so it keeps the current
  configuration, in Cartesian moves and in joint moves to a pose alike.
- **The commander software** solves `MovePose` starting from the standby pose, so it takes the configuration
  nearest to standby, whichever the robot is in; its Cartesian moves keep the current one.

To be sure of the configuration, give the target as joint angles.

## Singularities

When the arm moves in Cartesian space, the software converts a tool velocity into six joint velocities every
cycle. In most poses that works. In some poses two joint axes line up, and a motion of the tool in a certain
direction would need infinite joint speed, or the joints can turn without the tool moving: a **singularity**. The
maths divides by something that goes to zero. Near it, small tool motions ask for huge joint speeds; at it, the
move is impossible.

The three singularities of a six-axis arm with a spherical wrist:

| | When | Looks like | You meet it |
|---|---|---|---|
| Wrist | Joint 5 at 0°: the axes of joints 4 and 6 in one line | The wrist straight; the standby pose is a wrist singularity | whenever the tool points the way the forearm does |
| Shoulder | The wrist centre on the joint 1 axis. The shoulder axis is 23.4 mm in front of it, so the arm leans back to get there: with joint 3 at 180°, at joint 2 = −133.1° | The wrist straight above the middle of the base | working close to the joint 1 axis, above the base |
| Elbow | Joint 3 at 256.2°: the upper arm and the line from the elbow to the wrist centre in one line, the wrist centre 362.3 mm from the shoulder axis | The arm fully stretched | at full reach |

![The wrist singularity: joint 5 at 0°, so the axes of joints 4 and 6 lie in one line](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/assets/theory/singularity_wrist_parol6.webp){ width="571" }
![The wrist singularity: joint 5 at 0°, so the axes of joints 4 and 6 lie in one line](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/assets/theory/singularity_wrist_parol6_dark.webp){ width="571" }

![The shoulder singularity: the wrist centre on the joint 1 axis, here with joint 2 at −133.1° and joint 3 at 180°](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/assets/theory/singularity_shoulder_parol6.webp){ width="347" }
![The shoulder singularity: the wrist centre on the joint 1 axis, here with joint 2 at −133.1° and joint 3 at 180°](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/assets/theory/singularity_shoulder_parol6_dark.webp){ width="347" }

![The elbow singularity: joint 3 at 256.2°, so joints 2 and 3 and the wrist centre lie in one line, the arm fully stretched](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/assets/theory/singularity_elbow_parol6.webp){ width="517" }
![The elbow singularity: joint 3 at 256.2°, so joints 2 and 3 and the wrist centre lie in one line, the arm fully stretched](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/assets/theory/singularity_elbow_parol6_dark.webp){ width="517" }

The angles are the ones the software shows, from PAROL6's model. The wrist centre is where the axes of joints 4,
5 and 6 meet. The elbow singularity is the outer edge of the workspace
([Workspace and reach](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/theory/workspace-and-reach/)): singularities are part of its boundary, with the joint limits.

## What PAROL6 does

- **The commander software** stops a Cartesian move or jog when it reaches a singularity; the robot stays where
  it stopped. It does not deviate from the path to go around.
- **The Python API** refuses a Cartesian command whose path it cannot solve, before anything moves, and a jog
  that would enter a singular region stops.

Some industrial controllers can bend the path slightly to pass a singularity; PAROL6 keeps the path and stops
instead. The [demonstration video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=BJnZvwAE0PY) shows what singularities look
like on an industrial arm.

## Avoiding them

Singularities are a property of the geometry, so they are avoided by design, with trial and error:

- Keep the wrist bent: a few degrees of joint 5 away from 0° at the poses where you work.
- Place the parts so that the arm reaches them with a bent elbow, not at full stretch, and off the axis of
  joint 1.
- Mount the gripper at an angle, or on a plate that turns it, so that the working orientation needs a bent
  wrist.
- When a move keeps failing, make it a joint move, or add an intermediate pose.
- Run the program in the simulator: a stop or a refusal in the simulator is a singularity you can see.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/theory/workspace-and-reach/ -->

# Workspace and reach

## Reach

The furthest the flange centre gets from the axis of joint 1, within the [joint limits](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/03-technical-data/joint-limits/):
408 mm. The standard pneumatic gripper's tool centre point gets to 434 mm. A longer tool reaches further and
weighs on joints 4 and 5.

## Workspace

![Where the flange centre can go in the arm's plane, within the joint limits, in mm](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/assets/figures/parol6_workspace.webp){ width="760" }
![Where the flange centre can go in the arm's plane, within the joint limits, in mm](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/assets/figures/parol6_workspace_dark.webp){ width="760" }

The shaded region is everywhere the centre of the flange can go in the plane of the arm, within the joint limits
of the robot's model; the dotted line is the same for the wrist centre. It reaches 408 mm in front of the joint 1
axis and 359 mm behind it, 523 mm above the mounting surface and 25 mm below it. A tool adds its own length. The
region is computed from the limits only: the arm's own parts, the tool and the table can block some of it.

The volume the tool can reach. The **reachable workspace** is every point it can touch with some orientation: a
near-sphere of the reach, minus the base, minus the volume behind the elbow that the limits of joints 2 and 3
exclude. The **dexterous workspace** is the part of it where the tool can take any orientation, much smaller,
around the middle of the reach and in front of the robot. A program that needs a particular orientation at a
point needs that point in the dexterous workspace, and the way to find out is to jog there and try.

## Payload across the workspace

1 kg close to the base, 0.5 kg at full reach: the torque on joints 2 and 3 grows with the distance, and the
steppers' torque does not. A heavy tool shrinks the workspace in which the arm moves without losing steps.

## Placing the task

Faster cycles and a larger usable workspace come from the layout, not from the program: put the work in front of
the robot at mid reach, at a height that keeps the elbow bent, and away from the joint 1 axis. Move the robot or
the fixture rather than fighting the kinematics. The Python API's `reachable()` reports how much travel each joint
and axis has left from the current pose, which tells you how close to a limit the program works.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/theory/homing-and-mastering/ -->

# Homing and mastering

Stepper motors without encoders know nothing about where they are when the power comes on. Two procedures give
PAROL6 its position: homing, every time, and mastering, once per robot.

## Homing

Each joint drives to a switch or sensor whose position in the mechanics is known from the CAD model, then moves a
fixed number of steps from there to the after-homing pose. After that the firmware's step counters hold the joint
positions, and every move is counted from them. The process is the one 3D printers use. The sequence and what
can go wrong are in the Robot Manual's [Homing](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/05-operation/homing/).

In the software: the commander's **Home** button, the API's `home()`. The API tracks whether the robot is
referenced and refuses planned motion before it (`MOTN_NOT_HOMED`); a `home()` on a referenced robot is a
planned joint move back to the after-homing pose, and `home(calibrate=True)` runs the firmware's sequence again.

## Mastering

The fixed number of steps from the switch to the after-homing pose is measured on the reference robot. Printers and
switches vary, so on another robot the homed pose is a fraction of a degree off per joint. Mastering measures the
error with the witness marks, pins through holes in neighbouring links that line up in the after-homing pose, and corrects
the number in the firmware ([Mastering](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/05-operation/mastering/)).

![Witness marks on PAROL6](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/assets/parolw.webp){ width="650" }

Mastering affects the **absolute** accuracy, whether the pose the software reports is the true pose. It does not
affect the **repeatability**, whether the robot returns to the same place every time, which comes from the
mechanics and the switches alone. A program taught on an unmastered robot runs correctly on that robot; it runs
offset on another.

## When the position is lost

A collision, a stall, a move by hand or a power failure breaks the count, and nothing in the robot can tell.
Home again. A program that must not run with a wrong position checks something external before it starts: a
sensor on an input, a camera, a touch.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/theory/motion-profiles/ -->

# Motion profiles

A move has a start, an end and a time; the profile is how the speed changes in between. The profile decides how
smooth the move is, how much it shakes the arm, and whether the steppers can follow it.

## Trapezoidal

Accelerate at a constant rate, cruise at the maximum speed, decelerate at the same rate. The speed curve is a
trapezoid; the acceleration jumps between +a, 0 and −a, which is felt as a jerk at the three corners. With the
commander's `t=` argument, each third of the move is one phase.

![A trapezoidal velocity profile](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/assets/trap.webp){ width="700" }

## Polynomial

A quintic (fifth-order) polynomial through the start and end positions with zero speed and zero acceleration at
both ends: the speed rises and falls as a smooth bell, the acceleration is continuous, and the move starts and
ends from rest without a jolt. Slower in the middle for the same total time, and the arm likes it better.

![A quintic polynomial velocity profile](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/assets/poly.webp){ width="700" }

## In the commander software

`MoveJoint`, `MovePose`, `MoveCart` and `MoveCartRelTRF` take the bare word `trap` or `poly` after the other
arguments (`func="trap"` is ignored). A `MoveJoint` or `MovePose` with `t=` defaults to polynomial, with `v=` and
`a=` it is trapezoidal, and with neither it runs a conservative trapezoid. A `MoveCart` or `MoveCartRelTRF` with
`t=` defaults to trapezoidal, and without `t=` it always takes 3.6 s
([RBTscript](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/programming/03-commander/rbtscript/)).

## In the Python API

`select_profile()` sets the profile for all planned moves. The profiles of the version this site describes:
`TOPPRA`, `RUCKIG`, `QUINTIC`, `TRAPEZOID`, `LINEAR`.

| Profile | What it is |
|---|---|
| `TOPPRA` | Time-optimal path following: the fastest run along the given path within the joint speed and acceleration limits. The default |
| `RUCKIG` | Jerk-limited point-to-point motion: acceleration ramps instead of jumping. Joint moves only; a Cartesian move under it runs TOPPRA |
| `QUINTIC` | The quintic polynomial above, C² smooth |
| `TRAPEZOID` | Trapezoidal, with parabolic blends at the corners |
| `LINEAR` | Straight interpolation, no smoothing: for tests |

The move's `speed` and `accel` fractions scale the limits the profile works within; a `duration` fixes the time
instead. Streamed jogs and servo targets use their own jerk-limited profile in the controller, not the selected
one.

## Why the profile matters for a stepper arm

A stepper follows a speed command exactly until the torque runs out; a sudden acceleration demand at a corner
is where it runs out first. Smooth profiles, lower accelerations and lower currents go together: if a joint loses
steps at the start of moves, a quintic or jerk-limited profile at the same speed often fixes it.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/theory/blending/ -->

# Blending

A program with many waypoints stops at each one unless told otherwise, and every stop costs time and a jolt.
Blending lets the robot pass near a waypoint without stopping: when the tool comes within a radius of the
waypoint, it starts the next move, and the path rounds the corner.

- The tool does not pass **through** a blended waypoint; it cuts the corner inside the radius. A waypoint where
  the tool must be exactly, a pick or a place, is not blended.
- The blend radius is in millimetres of the tool's path.
- A blend needs the next move to be known when the current one starts: in the Python API the moves are queued,
  so the controller looks ahead and blends.

## In the Python API

`move_j`, `move_l` and `move_c` take `r`, the blend radius; `r=0` stops at the target. `move_p` is the
process move: a list of waypoints run at constant tool speed with automatic blending at every corner, for scan
and dispensing paths. A tool action or a `delay()` queued after a blended move ends the blend there: the arm
stops for it. The zig-zag example in the API's repository shows a raster scan with blends.

```python
rbt.move_l([200, 0, 250, 90, 0, 90], speed=0.5, r=15)
rbt.move_l([200, 160, 250, 90, 0, 90], speed=0.5, r=15)
rbt.move_l([250, 160, 250, 90, 0, 90], speed=0.5)          # stops here
```

## In the commander software

RBTscript has no blending: every move ends at rest. Make the path with fewer, longer moves, or with `MoveCart`
through points far enough apart that the stops do not matter.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/theory/target-commanded-actual/ -->

# Target, commanded and actual

Three positions exist at every moment, and they differ.

- The **target** is where you asked the robot to go: the end of the move.
- The **commanded** position is where the planner says the robot should be right now, on the trajectory it
  computed from the profile, sent to the control board in this cycle.
- The **actual** position is where the motors are, as the control board counts their steps: what `rbt.angles()`
  and the commander's display show.

## Why commanded and actual differ

The board receives a speed and a position every 10 ms and runs the stepper at that speed until the next packet.
Two things pull the actual position away from the commanded one:

- The PC is not a real-time machine; the packets are 10 ms apart on average, not exactly, and a late packet lets
  the motor run a little too long or short.
- A stepper cannot make the very small speed changes at the start and end of a smooth profile exactly; it
  rounds them.

If the board followed the speed alone, the errors would add up over a long move and the robot would miss the
target by a few steps. So the planners use the go-to-position command (156), in which the board runs each joint
at the average of the commanded speed and the speed that would close the position error within one cycle: the
speed curve gives the smoothness, the position curve pulls the error back to zero every cycle, and the robot
arrives exactly.

![Commanded (blue) and actual (red) speed on a trapezoidal move; the robot spends a third of the time in each phase](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/assets/trap_with_lines.webp){ width="700" }

![Position with speed-only tracking and with speed-and-position tracking: the second reaches the target exactly](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/assets/trap_position_ex.webp){ width="700" }

![The same with a polynomial profile](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/assets/poly_position.PNG){ width="700" }

The commander's RBTscript exposes the choice: a move with `speed` as its last argument tracks the speed curve
only, which is smoother and quieter and may stop short of the target; without it, speed and position are
tracked.

## What the software reports

The commander shows the actual joint angles and the actual tool pose; the Python API's status stream carries the
actual angles and speeds, plus `executing_index` and `completed_index` for where the queue is. "Actual" means
"counted steps": a lost step moves the real arm away from all three without any of them noticing
([Homing and mastering](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/theory/homing-and-mastering/)).


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/theory/control-ownership/ -->

# Control ownership

Only one program can own the control board, and inside the Python API only one source can drive the arm at a
time. Knowing who is in charge saves confusion and collisions.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph Clients
        G[GUI]
        P[Your script]
    end
    subgraph Controller["Controller: one owner of the arm"]
        Q["Planned queue: move_*, home, tools, in order"]
        S["Streamed motion: jog_*, servo_*, at once"]
    end
    B[Control board]
    G --> Q
    P --> Q
    P --> S
    S -. cancels .-> Q
    Q --> B
    S --> B
```

## One host on the serial port

The control board executes whatever packets arrive on its USB port. The commander software and the Python API's
controller each take the port exclusively; the second one to try gets an error or silence. Stop one before you
start the other.

## Inside the Python API

The **controller** owns the arm. **Clients** send it commands; it accepts commands from any number of clients on
the network, without authentication, so a GUI and a script can both be connected. What happens when they both
command motion:

- **Planned motion** (`move_*`, `home`, `delay`, tool actions, checkpoints) goes into one **queue**, in the order
  it arrives, and runs in that order, together with the output writes (`write_io`), the tool selection
  (`select_tool`) and the TCP corrections. Every queued command gets an index; `wait_command(index)` waits for
  that one.
- **Streamed motion** (`jog_*`, `servo_*`) takes the arm at once: it cancels the planned queue (every discarded
  command fails with `MOTN_CANCELLED`). A jog runs for its duration; a servo stream drives the arm while targets
  keep coming and ends about a quarter of a second after the last one. Then the arm brakes to rest and holds.
- **`stop()`** cancels the active move and clears the queue, from any client. **`estop()`** does the same and
  latches a protective stop until `reset()`.
- **`pause()`** holds the queue where it is; `resume()` continues it; `set_execution_speed()` scales it between
  10 and 100 %.
- **System commands** (`simulator`, `connect_hardware`, `select_profile`, `set_shapes`) take effect at once and
  change the controller's state for everyone. A queued `select_tool` does too, when its turn comes.

The rule for a program that shares the controller: own the arm for the duration of a task by queuing it, wait for
your indices, and expect `MotionError` if someone else stopped you.

## The firmware

The firmware's enable and disable commands (101, 102) decide whether it accepts motion at all; the E-stop makes
the PC software send disable or latch a stop ([Emergency stop](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/02-safety/emergency-stop/)). Between
packets the firmware keeps the last speeds it was given, which is why a host must never stop sending while a
joint is in motion.

## Simulator versus hardware

The controller runs against the hardware or in **simulator mode**, where the same planner drives a virtual arm
and the status stream reports it. `simulator(True)` switches; `is_simulator()` tells; `teleport()` sets the
virtual arm's pose. The **dry-run client** goes further: it runs the planner in the client's own process, with no
controller at all, for tests and previews ([Clients](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/programming/02-python-api/clients/)).


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/theory/steppers-and-open-loop/ -->

# Steppers, open loop and backlash

## Actuators

Robots are moved by actuators: servo motors with encoders, stepper motors, brushless motors, pneumatic and
hydraulic cylinders. PAROL6 uses **stepper motors**, which move in discrete steps on command, hold position
with their current, and need no sensor to be positioned: the cheapest way to get six precise axes, and the
reason the robot has no encoders and no brakes.

## How a stepper works

A stepper has 50 pole pairs and two windings; energising the windings in sequence pulls the rotor one step,
1.8°, at a time, 200 steps per turn. The driver can set the currents to intermediate values and hold the rotor
between full steps: **microstepping**, 32 positions per step on PAROL6, 6400 per turn. A microstep is a real
position only while the torque against it is small; under load the rotor lags up to a full step behind the
commanded microstep, which is why the resolution on paper is finer than the accuracy in practice.

A stepper's torque falls as its speed rises, because the windings' inductance limits how fast the current can
reverse. Above a certain speed, at a certain load, it **stalls**: it stops following the steps, buzzes, and the
position is lost. The speed and acceleration limits of the software exist to stay below that.

## Open loop and closed loop

**Open loop**: the controller commands and assumes the result. Simple, cheap, no sensors, and no way to know
when something went wrong. **Closed loop**: a sensor measures the result and the controller corrects the
difference; accurate, robust against load, and more complex. PAROL6's joints are open loop: the step count is
the position, and a lost step is an error nobody sees. The safeguards are the margins in the limits, the homing
that resets the count, and the user's eyes.

The electric grippers are different: their drivers run the motor in closed loop with an encoder, a brushless
motor on the SSG-48's Spectral Micro and a stepper on the MSG's STEPFOC. That is what makes a force-controlled
gripper possible ([End effectors](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/end-effectors/)).

## Position, velocity and torque control

A joint can be controlled in **position** (go there and hold), **velocity** (turn at this speed) or **torque**
(push this hard). PAROL6's firmware offers velocity (the jog command) and a velocity-plus-position tracking (the
go-to command); the planner on the PC turns position targets into those. Torque control, which collaborative
robots use to be safe around people, is not possible with open-loop steppers: the robot cannot feel.

## Backlash

The play between gear teeth, in a belt's mesh and in a coupler: when a joint reverses, the motor turns a little
before the output follows. PAROL6's planetary gearboxes have 15 to 20 arc-minutes of it, the belts less. It
shows as a small position error that depends on the direction of the last move, and as a slight looseness at the
tool. The cure is preload (tight belts), approaching a pose always from the same direction, and keeping the
couplers tight ([Couplers and threadlocker](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/07-maintenance/couplers/)).

## Encoders

An encoder measures a shaft's rotation: incremental ones count from a start, absolute ones know the angle at
power-up. PAROL6 has none on its joints; adding them is a common modification, and the community has closed-loop
driver projects. The gripper drivers have an absolute magnetic encoder on their motor.

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/theory/further-reading/ -->

# Further reading

Good places to go deeper into the concepts of this chapter:

- [Robot Academy](https://robotacademy.net.au/): Peter Corke's video lectures on kinematics, frames and control,
  the basis of the Robotics Toolbox the commander software uses.
- [Automatic Addison](https://automaticaddison.com/): practical tutorials, including
  [how to assign DH frames](https://automaticaddison.com/how-to-assign-denavit-hartenberg-frames-to-robotic-arms/)
  and [how to find the DH table](https://automaticaddison.com/how-to-find-denavit-hartenberg-parameter-tables/).
- [Robogrok](https://robogrok.com/): a robotics course with the maths worked out.
- [Robotics coursework collection](https://github.com/mithi/robotics-coursework): a curated list of courses and
  books.
- [Robotics Explained](https://robotics-explained.com/): short explanations of the vocabulary.
- [How do robot manipulators move?](https://roboticseabass.com/2024/06/30/how-do-robot-manipulators-move/) on
  Robotic Sea Bass: motion planning from the ground up.
- [How many axes does my robot need?](https://robohub.org/how-many-axes-does-my-robot-need/) on Robohub.
- [Singularities demonstrated](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=BJnZvwAE0PY) on an industrial arm.

The Python API's repository has a `docs` folder and a README that go into its architecture, the motion planner
and the collision checker beyond what this guide covers.

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/support/ -->

# Getting help

- **Questions and discussion**: the [Source Robotics Discord](https://discord.gg/prjUvjmGpZ).
- **A problem with the robot's hardware, its files or the control board firmware**: an issue in the
  [robot repository](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/PAROL6-Desktop-robot-arm/issues); see
  [Report a problem](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/support/report-a-problem/) for what to include.
- **A problem with the commander software**: an issue in
  [PAROL-commander-software](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/PAROL-commander-software/issues).
- **A problem with the Python API**: an issue in [PAROL6-python-API](https://github.com/PCrnjak/PAROL6-python-API/issues).
- **A mistake on a page of this site**: every page ends with a link to edit it and one to report it; see
  [Contributing](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/support/contributing/).
- **Orders and hardware**: [source-robotics.com](https://source-robotics.com/).

Before you ask, [Troubleshooting](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/08-troubleshooting/) goes through the common symptoms, and the
commander's terminal output or the API's `error()` tells most of what anyone will ask you for.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/support/report-a-problem/ -->

# Report a problem

A report that can be acted on says what you did, what happened, and what the robot said. Include:

1. **The robot**: bought or self-built; control board version (v2.0 with terminal blocks, or v1.2); the firmware
   (main, from which commit, and whether you changed `constants.h` or `motor_init.cpp`).
2. **The software**: commander (which commit, which Python version, which OS) or Python API (`pip show parol6`),
   or something else.
3. **What you did**: the exact steps, the program or script, the jog, the command.
4. **What happened**: and what you expected instead. A short video helps for anything mechanical.
5. **What the robot said**: the commander's response log and terminal output, or the API's exception text and the
   controller's log.
6. **The PC**: processor and OS, for anything about timing or communication.

Where to file it is on [Getting help](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/support/). A problem with a gripper goes to the gripper's own repository,
with the same facts.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/1/support/contributing/ -->

# Contributing

The documentation lives in [Source-Robotics/PAROL-docs](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/PAROL-docs). A small
fix, a typo, a wrong number, a missing link, can be made from the browser: every page ends with a link to edit it
on GitHub, which opens a pull request. For anything larger, open an issue first and say what you want to change.

## House rules

- Write for the reader who has the robot in front of them: what to do, in what order, and why when the why
  matters. Short sentences, one idea each.
- Facts come from the files: the firmware, the software's source, the BOM. When a page and the code disagree,
  the code is right and the page is fixed; a change to a command is made in the code first.
- Version facts live in `versions.yml`, never in a page. The API reference is generated from the Python API's
  source: edit the notes around the markers, not the markers' output.
- Link to a page of this site with its relative path, so that the build checks it; link to code on GitHub by
  its permanent URL.
- Images under 2400 px, with the exact file name (the live site is case-sensitive).
- Run `python tools/test_tools.py` and `mkdocs build --strict` before you open a pull request. Both run on every
  push.

The text and the images you contribute are published under CC BY-SA 4.0, the code examples under MIT.
